articles.title: 2018 WPT Master Final
articles.text:
2018 WPT Master Final

The 2018 Master Final (officially 2018 World Padel Tour Master Final) was the seventeenth and season-ending tournament of the sixth season organized by World Padel Tour, the most prestigious padel circuit at the time. For the second consecutive year, the tournament counted toward the rankings.
In the women’s category, for the seventh time this season, and the third consecutive time, the world’s top two-ranked pairs reached the final. In the decisive match, Alejandra Salazar and Marta Marrero, who played in their third Master Final together and their final tournament as a pair, faced twins Majo and Mapi Sánchez, who were appearing in their fifth consecutive Master Final. Salazar and Marrero, who had battled the twins for the world number one spot and competed against them in numerous tournaments between 2015 and 2018, defeated them in three sets to secure their sixth title of the season. This result meant that, despite finishing second in the world rankings, they ended the season as the most decorated pair of the year. Furthermore, they extended their head-to-head record in finals against Majo and Mapi to 6–1 and claimed their second Master Final title together (marking a fourth such victory for Salazar, who also won in 2009 and 2013).
In the men's category, the world number one's, Maxi Sánchez and Sanyo Gutiérrez, would reached their twelfth final of the season (out of a possible 16), having in previous years reached four finals in this competition, winning three of them (two as a pair in 2013 and 2014). Theirs opponents would be the defending champions and second-ranked pair, Fernando Belasteguín and Pablo Lima, who they had faced only once in 2018, with Belasteguín reaching the final in his first tournament back from injury. In the championship match, Belasteguín and Lima defeated Maxi and Sanyo, defending their title sucessfully and securing their fourth title together this season (the fifth for Lima). This victory marked Belasteguín’s seventh Master Final win (having previously won in 2006, 2007, 2009, 2010, 2011, and 2017), while Lima claimed his third (having won in 2012 and 2017).

articles.title: 2018 WPT Murcia Open
articles.text:
2018 WPT Murcia Open

The 2018 Murcia Open (officially 2018 World Padel Tour Murcia Open) was the sixteenth tournament of the sixth season organized by World Padel Tour, the most prestigious padel circuit at the time.
In the women’s category, for the sixth time this season, the world’s number 1 and number 3 ranked pairs reached the final. In the decisive match, Alejandra Salazar and Marta Marrero defeated the twins Majo and Mapi Sánchez in three sets, securing their fifth title of the season. This result allowed them to move up from world number 3 to world number 2 ranked pair, increased their head-to-head record in finals against the Sánchez twins to 5–1 in their favor, tied them with their rivals at five WPT titles each (six for the twins counting world pairs championship), and made them the first women's pair to win a title in Murcia.
In the men’s category, the world number one's, Maxi Sánchez and Sanyo Gutiérrez, reached their 11th final of the season (out of a possible 15), facing the second-ranked duo, Pablo Lima and Paquito Navarro, who reached their second final in as many tournaments since joining forces. In the title match, Sánchez and Gutiérrez, who by reaching the final had already mathematically secured finishing the year as the number one ranked duo (the first time in 16 years that Fernando Belasteguín didn't finish the season as world number one), defeated Lima and Navarro to claim their eighth title of the season, and their first-ever victory in Murcia.

articles.title: Alexander Xie
articles.text:
Alexander Xie

Xie Chujun Alexander (Chinese: 谢初筠; pinyin: Xiè Chūjūn; born 5 May 2007) is a Chinese professional footballer who plays as a midfielder for Chinese Super League club Qingdao West Coast.


== Early life ==
Xie was born on 5 May 2007 in Australia. He moved to Germany with his parents at age 11. He grew up in the youth system of FSV Frankfurt before joining VfB Stuttgart in August 2024.


== Club career ==


=== VfB Stuttgart U19 ===
In August 2024, Xie signed a two-year contract with VfB Stuttgart. During the 2025–26 season, he made 23 league appearances for Stuttgart U19, scoring 2 assists, and was part of the squad that won the German Youth Cup. On 3 June 2026, Stuttgart officially announced that Xie would leave the club upon the expiration of his contract on 30 June 2026.


=== Qingdao West Coast ===
On 9 July 2026, Qingdao West Coast officially announced the signing of Xie.  He made his Chinese Super League debut on 2 August 2026, coming on as a late substitute in the Qingdao derby against Qingdao Hainiu. As of 15 October 2026, he had made two substitute appearances in the league, accumulating 11 minutes of playing time.


== International career ==
In November 2025, Xie was called up to the China U18 training squad. In May 2026, he was named in the China U19 squad for the Maurice Revello Tournament. On 31 May 2026, he started and played 85 minutes in China U19's 1–0 victory over Saudi Arabia U21 in the opening match, and was named player of the match. In September 2026, he was again called up to the China U19 squad for a training camp ahead of the 2027 U20 Asian Cup.

articles.title: 1962 Michigan Senate election
articles.text:
1962 Michigan Senate election

An election was held on November 6, 1962, to elect all 34 members of the Michigan Senate for the 72nd Michigan Legislature. In the election, the Republicans maintained a 23–11 majority over the Democrats in the chamber.


== History ==
In the 1960 general election, the Republicans won a 22–12 majority over the Democrats, maintaining control over the chamber. In January 1962, Democrat William E. Miron died in office. Republican Kent T. Lundgren won the April special election to fill the vacancy. This left the state Senate with a 23–11 Republican majority.
The 1962 state primary was held on August 7. Two incumbent Republicans were defeated. Carlton Morris was defeated by Garry E. Brown and Charles Feenstra was defeated by Robert VanderLaan.
The general election was held on November 6. No incumbents were unseated. The Republicans maintained their 23–11 majority. On December 27, Republican Stanley G. Thayer was elected to serve as state Senate majority leader for the next session, succeeding Frank D. Beadle.
The state Senate was sworn in on January 9, 1963. The same day, Charles S. Blondy was elected minority leader by the Democrats, winning 6 of 11 votes. He succeeded Raymond D. Dzendzel, who'd been serving as acting minority leader since February 1962.

2007 All-Big East Conference football team

The 2007 All-Big East Conference football team consists of American football players from the Big East Conference who were chosen as the best at their respective positions during the 2007 NCAA Division I FBS football season.  The official All-Big East teams in 2007 were chosen by votes of the conference's head football coaches. The coaches chose both first- and second-team players. articles.title: 17 October Movement
articles.text:
17 October Movement

The 17 October Movement (Italian: Movimento 17 ottobre, abbreviated as M1710) is a spontaneous youth political movement that emerged in Milan in October 2026. The movement was formed in the aftermath of violent clashes between student protesters and law enforcement on October 17, 2026.
Operating without a formal leadership structure or official spokespeople, the collective advocates for permanent mobilization through grassroots assembly and direct action. The inherent violent nature of the group is debated amongst sources with contrasting opinions. Anonymous members which were interviewed stated that they did not condemn violent actions which took place during the 2026 Italian unrest.


== Background ==

The 17 October Movement emerged in October 2026 within the context of nationwide civil unrest in Italy driven by protests against public service degradation and the rising cost of living amongst various other causes. Following the riots, a distinct political faction detached itself from the broader platform to form the movement, establishing its presence online via social media platforms.


== History ==


=== Foundation ===
On 19 October 2026 the group announced their creation on their Instagram account where they also offered to assist people who had problems with the law enforcement at the protest, inviting people to join a Telegram group. The movement also declared that they'd be meeting every Saturday up until the Meloni government would have fallen. The movement then announced its next meeting to be on 24 October 2026 in Milan, Bologna, Turin, Rome, Florence, Padua, Bari, and Genoa. The movement also distributed copies of the 2004 book "Recipes for Chaos" and its own book "Safer in the Streets."
On 20 October 2026 it had already been reported that elements within the Telegram group of the site started to suggest moving to Signal as to avoid mediatic attention and to achieve better privacy standards.


== Ideology ==
Based on media coverage, sources are divided regarding the movement's association with violence. Il Fatto Quotidiano and Il Risveglio described the group in its early stages as factionalized between a reformist wing and a maximalist wing, characterizing the latter as prone to violence and influenced by the political models of Karl Marx and the French Revolution. articles.title: 1928 Valley City State Vikings football team
articles.text:
1928 Valley City State Vikings football team

The 1928 Valley City State Vikings football team represented Valley City State Teachers College—now known as Valley City State University—as a member of the Interstate Athletic Conference during the 1928 college football season. Led by fourth-year head coach Jim Morrison, the Vikings compiled an overall record of 5–2  with mark of a 5–1 record in conference play, placing second in the Interstate Athletic Conference.


== Schedule ==


== Season summary ==
Valley City State began the 1928 season with a shortage of linemen and an abundance of backfield players. The Teachers lost their opening two games to North Dakota Agricultural College, 12–0, and Moorhead Teachers, 19–7. By the third game, however, the team's line had improved considerably, and Valley City State completed the remainder of its schedule undefeated.
The Teachers earned their first victory with a 25–0 shutout of North Dakota State School of Science, followed by a 7–0 victory over Jamestown. Valley City State then defeated Minot Teachers, 12–7, before recording consecutive shutouts against Dickinson Teachers, 39–0, and Ellendale Teachers, 2–0.
Valley City State finished the season with a 5–2 record, outscoring opponents 122–38 and recording four shutout victories. James Eckel, Harris Simons, and John Fiola were identified as the team's leading players in the 1929 edition of Spalding's Official Foot Ball Guide.

articles.title: 2006 All-Big East Conference football team
articles.text:
2006 All-Big East Conference football team

The 2006 All-Big East Conference football team consists of American football players from the Big East Conference who were chosen as the best at their respective positions during the 2006 NCAA Division I FBS football season.  The official All-Big East teams in 2006 were chosen by votes of the conference's eight head football coaches. The coaches chose both first- and second-team players. Only two players were unanimously selected to the first team: West Virginia's senior safety Eric Wicks and Louisville's senior defensive defensive tackle Amobi Okoye. West Virginia quarterback Patrick White was chosen as the offensive player of the year, and Pittsburgh linebacker H. B. Blades was chosen as the defensive player of the year.


== Honorees by team ==
Louisville. The Louisville Cardinals won the Big East championship, compiled a 12–1 record, and placed six players on the first team: wide receiver Harry Douglas; offensive tackle Renardo Foster; offensive guard Kurt Quarterman; defensive tackle Amobi Okoye; cornerback William Gay; and kicker Art Carmody. Louisville placed another six players on the second team, including quarterback Brian Brohm.
West Virginia. The West Virginia Mountaineers finished second in the Big East with an 11–2 record. The Mountaineers were led by sophomore quarterback Patrick White who won first-team honors and was selected as the Big East offensive player of the year. For the 2006 season, White completed 109 of 164 passes (66.5%) for 1,524 yards and 11 touchdowns and rushed for 1,074 yards and 17 touchdowns. He was the first Big East player to gain over 1,000 yards by way of both passing and rushing in the same season. White was the second West Virginia quarterback in three years to win all-conference honors, following Rasheed Marshall in 2004. A total of six West Virginia players were named to the first team: White; running back Steve Slaton; offensive guard Jeremy Sheffey; center Dan Mozes; defensive lineman Keilen Dykes; and safety Eric Wicks.
Rutgers. Rutgers finished in third place in the Big East with an 11–2 record, and its head coach Greg Schiano was selected as the Big East coach of the year. He led Rutgers to a 10-2record, the program's first 10-win season since 1976. Five Rutgers players received first team honors: running back Ray Rice; tight end Clark Harris; offensive tackle Jeremy Zuttah; defensive tackle Eric Foster; and punter Joe Radigan.

articles.title: 1927 Valley City State Vikings football team
articles.text:
1927 Valley City State Vikings football team

The 1927 Valley City State Vikings football team represented Valley City State Teachers College—now known as Valley City State University—as a member of the Interstate Intercollegiate Conference during the 1927 college football season. Led by third-year head coach Jim Morrison, the Vikings compiled an overall record of 6–2 with a mark of 6–0 in the conference play, winning the Interstate Intercollegiate Conference championship for the second consecutive season. Valley City State outscored its opponents 116 to 67 and recorded five shutout victories. G. Burchill served as team captain.


== Schedule ==


== Season summary ==
Valley City State entered the 1927 season with only two players returning from the previous year's starting eleven. Despite the turnover, the Teachers captured their second consecutive Interstate Conference championship.
The Teachers lost to North Dakota, 19–0, and North Dakota Agricultural College, 36–0. They won their remaining six games, defeating North Dakota State School of Science, Jamestown, Park Region–Luther, Ellendale Teachers, Moorhead Teachers, and Minot Teachers.
Valley City State recorded shutout victories over North Dakota State School of Science (6–0), Park Region–Luther (33–0), Ellendale Teachers (14–0), Moorhead Teachers (7–0), and Minot Teachers (38–0). The team's only victory in which it allowed points was an 18–12 win over Jamestown.
The team was led by back Eckol, tackle A. Fiola, and end Salterman, who were identified as leading players in the contemporary season summary. Fiola was also identified as the team's leading tackler.

articles.title: Arthur Arent
articles.text:
Arthur Arent

Arthur Arent (1904-1972) was a 20th-Century American playwright of the twentieth century, best known for his 1936 Living Newspaper play Triple-A Plowed Under.


== Background ==
Arthur Arent was born on September 29, 1904, in Jersey City, New Jersey. He studied dramaturgy and performing arts in New York in 1923.


== Career ==
In the mid-1930s, Arent co-founded the Federal Theatre Project (FTP), a New Deal agency.  He was appointed as a creative drama writer specializing in "Living Newspaper". He wrote Triple-A Plowed Under for the FTP, which was performed in 1936.  Other plays included:  Ethiopia (1935), Power (1937), and One Third of a Nation (1938).
In 1937, Arent worked with Marc Blitzstein, Emanuel Eisenberg, Charles Friedman, and David Gregory on the magazine Pins and Needles of the International Ladies Garment Workers Union (ILGwU).
In the early 1940s during World War II, Arent wrote for Warner Brothers and then worked in the US Office of War Information.


== Death ==
Arthur Arent died on May 18, 1972.


== Works ==
Arent produced 59 works and worked on plays and adaptations for theater, radio, and television, as well fiction publications.   Radio works appeared on National Broadcasting Company (NBC) and "The Theatre Guild on the Air" presented by the United States Steel Corporation and "The Cavalcade of America" presented by DuPont. Television works appeared on "The United States Steel Hour", and "The General Electric Theater."

articles.title: 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships – Men's 100 metre backstroke
articles.text:
2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships – Men's 100 metre backstroke

The men's 100 metre backstroke event at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships was held on August 12 at the William Woollett Jr. Aquatics Center in Irvine, California. The event was won by Canada's Blake Tierney in a time of 53.18, ahead of American Will Modglin, who claimed the silver medal in 53.37. Modglin's compatriot Jack Aikins won the bronze medal in 53.46, while Mexico's Marcus Reyes-Gentry finished fourth in 54.04.
Earlier in the morning heats, Tierney recorded the fastest qualifying time of 53.13, narrowly ahead of Modglin, who finished in 53.17. Bermuda's Jack Harvey was the only swimmer advancing to the A final to establish a new personal best, lowering his own Bermudian national record by 0.05 seconds to 54.51. South Africa's Michael van Heerden qualified as the sole reserve for the finals, while his compatriot Matthew Mann, who finished 18th overall in 58.29, was ineligible for a reserve position due to the restriction on the number of swimmers from each nation. In the evening session, American Daniel Diehl won the B final in 53.67, a time that would have placed fourth in the A final.

articles.title: 2027 Rugby Championship
articles.text:
2027 Rugby Championship

The 2027 Rugby Championship is the scheduled fourteenth edition of the annual southern hemisphere competition, involving Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. The 2027 Rugby Championship marks the first edition of the tournament to be contested in full during the same year as a Rugby World Cup.
South Africa are the defending champions, having won the title in 2024 and 2025, respectively.


== Background ==

During the 2022 to 2024 negotiations between New Zealand Rugby (NZR) and the South African Rugby Union (SARU) for full traditional tours in 2026 and 2030, SARU chief executive Rian Oberholzer stated that although the Rugby Championship would be affected, it would still be possible to go ahead with a single round for its 2026 edition. The 2026 tournament was eventually scrapped, with three-Test tours between all four SANZAAR teams (Argentina, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa) rumoured as a potential replacement for the competitions 2028 edition as well. In October 2025, however, the Rugby Championship was confirmed to remain unchanged between 2027 and 2029, with the former edition being played in full (twelve matches) rather than its shortened format (six matches) commonly used during a Rugby World Cup year.


=== Format ===
The competition format consists of each team playing each other twice. Each team also host three matches, two making up a "mini-tour", which sees each nation play back-to-back Tests in one country, with the remaining three being away Tests.
SANZAAR confirmed in October 2025 that the 2027 Rugby Championship would kick off in July and finish in August, ahead of the 2027 Rugby World Cup. In September 2026, Rugby Australia confirmed the Wallabies' 2027 schedule. The tournament kicks off with Australia and New Zealand hosting Argentina and South Africa for two Tests, respectively. Rounds 3–4 take place between Australia/New Zealand and Argentina/South Africa on a home-and-away basis, with the latter two teams hosting New Zealand and Australia in the remaining two rounds.

articles.title: 1935–36 Kingston Colonials season
articles.text:
1935–36 Kingston Colonials season

The 1935–36 Kingston Colonials season was the fourteenth professional basketball season played by the Kingston Colonials franchise while competing in the revived version of the American Basketball League. It would also be their first season competing in the revived version of the ABL after previously competing in the Hudson River Basketball League, the New York State Basketball League (multiple times in their tenure), the Interstate Basketball League under a brief period of time, and finally the Metropolitan Basketball League before not being able to compete in a professional basis from 1928 until this season began in 1935. This season saw the ABL work with six teams throughout the entire season, although one of the teams would end up moving around multiple locations throughout the entire season. In any event, the Colonials would showcase themselves as a below-average team throughout the season, with the first half of the season seeing them get a 7–12 record for a fifth place finish that saw them be ahead of only the Paterson Panthers turned Trenton Bengals turned Passaic Red Devils to end that half of the season. The second half of the season would end up seeing relatively similar results occur as well, with Kingston getting a below-average 9–10 record for a fourth place finish to finish ahead of only the Philadelphia SPHAs / Hebrews and the Passaic Red Devils for that half. Due to the less than stellar results at hand from the Colonials, Kingston would fail to compete for the ABL's championship series for this season.

articles.title: 1934–35 New Britain Mules season
articles.text:
1934–35 New Britain Mules season

The 1934–35 New Britain Mules season was technically both the fourth and final professional basketball season played for this franchise and the second and final season of the team that was playing in New Britain, Connecticut after they previously played as the Hoboken Lisas in the briefly revived Metropolitan Basketball League, the Hoboken Thourots from Hoboken, New Jersey, the Camden Brewers in Camden, New Jersey, and the New Britain Palaces in New Britain, Connecticut. However, this can also count as the only proper season of play for the New Britain Mules franchise instead since this team would be formed from two teams who were considered to be struggling with their operations at the time in the New Britain Jackaways and the Newark Mules, with the Mules deciding to move their operations from Newark, New Jersey to New Britain in order to comply with the merger at hand for the second half of the season. Originally, the two teams operated just under the recently rebranded New Britain Jackaways and the Newark Mules names under the first half of the season before the combined fourth and seventh place finishes for that half of the season in the new seven-team league led to the two teams merging operations with each other to become the New Britain Mules for the second half of the season only. (However, it is recently believed that the team playing in the second half of the season is really just the Newark Mules while representing New Britain, Connecticut for the ABL this season in place of the New Britain Jackaways due to the original Jackaways team folding operations on January 18, 1935.) articles.title: 1934–35 New Britain Jackaways / Mules season
articles.text:
1934–35 New Britain Jackaways / Mules season

The 1934–35 New Britain Jackaways / Mules season was both the fourth and final professional basketball season played for this franchise and the second and final season of the team that was playing in New Britain, Connecticut after they previously played as the Hoboken Lisas in the briefly revived Metropolitan Basketball League, the Hoboken Thourots from Hoboken, New Jersey, the Camden Brewers in Camden, New Jersey, and the New Britain Palaces in New Britain, Connecticut. Originally, the team operated just under the recently rebranded New Britain Jackaways name under the first half of the season before the team merged operations with the recently renamed Newark Mules (previously known as the Newark Bears) from Newark, New Jersey to become the New Britain Mules for the second half of the season only. (However, it is recently believed that the team playing in the second half of the season is really just the Newark Mules while representing New Britain, Connecticut for the ABL this season in place of the New Britain Jackaways due to the original Jackaways team folding operations on January 18, 1935.) In any case, the New Britain Jackaways would end up struggling throughout the first half of the season, to the point where they finished the first half of the season with a 6–14 record for a last place finish for that half of the season before the Jackaways technically folded operations and were replaced by the Newark Mules under a sort of merger to become the New Britain Mules for the rest of the season (in the second half of the season) going forward. Once New Britain entered the second half of the season as the Mules instead of the Jackaways, the New Britain Mules would perform a fair bit better as a team during that half of the season, to the point where their overall placement would improve from last place (at 7th for New Britain (or 4th for the Newark Mules)) to tying for third place with the Jersey Reds, albeit with an average 9–9 record that still had them behind only the defending ABL champion Philadelphia SPHAs / Hebrews and the Brooklyn Visitations for a first place tie there. As such, New Britain would not only fail to qualify for the ABL's championship series once again, but both the Jackaways and the Mules teams that New Britain fielded this season would withdraw their operations from the league entirely following the season's conclusion as well.

articles.title: 2026 Italian unrest
articles.text:
2026 Italian unrest

The 2026 Italian unrest refers to a series of protests, demonstrations, strikes, and clashes in Italy beginning on 16 October 2026. The unrest involved student movements and other protesters expressing discontent over the cost of living, rising fuel prices, education policies, and public spending.


== Background ==

The unrest emerged amid concerns about the rising cost of living, higher fuel prices, and conditions within the education sector. Student movements criticized the policies of the government led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, calling for increased investment in public education and opposing military spending.
On 16 October, student demonstrations associated with the slogan “No Meloni Day” took place in several Italian cities. The same slogan used during the 2025 Italian general strikes and protests for Gaza by some groups of protesters.


== Timeline ==


=== 16 October ===
On 16 October, student demonstrations took place across Italy under the slogan “No Meloni Day”. The protests focused on the condition of school buildings, education funding, military expenditure, immigration policies affecting schools, and solidarity with French students.
Demonstrations were reported in Rome, Milan, Turin, Genoa, Bologna, Florence, Venice, Padua, Treviso, Cagliari and other cities. The nationwide mobilization followed several days of school occupations and student-organized actions.
In Turin, demonstrators threw eggs at police and clashes were reported between some protesters and officers. In Rome, some demonstrators threw firecrackers near the Ministry of Education, while flags of the United States and Israel were burned during a march. In Pisa, students at the Scuola Normale Superiore disrupted an academic-year opening ceremony.
The demonstrations coincided with climate mobilizations involving Fridays for Future and with a school-sector strike. Police unions reported that officers had been injured during confrontations in Rome and Turin. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence while the government defended the police response.
At the same time, a separate wave of protests by truck drivers and farmers spread across southern Italy in response to rising diesel prices and production costs. In Calabria, the transport stoppage organized by Fedralog began, with approximately 15 protest sites established near major roads and transport hubs, including the port of Gioia Tauro and the area around Lamezia Terme airport. articles.title: Aali Mothi Shahani
articles.text:
Aali Mothi Shahani

Aali Mothi Shahani (transl. Here Comes the Smart-Aleck) is a 2026 Indian Marathi-language fantasy comedy-drama film written and directed by Anand Dilip Gokhale and produced under the banners of Fine Brew Productions and True Hope Film Works. The film stars Hruta Durgule and Sarang Sathaye in the lead roles, alongside Guru Thakur, Rujuta Deshmukh and Suhita Thatte. The story follows an eleven-year-old girl who prays to Lord Ganesha to make her grow up instantly.
The film was announced on the occasion of Dussehra in October 2025, and principal photography began in Goa the following month. Aali Mothi Shahani was theatrically released on 2 October 2026 and received mixed reviews from critics.


== Plot ==
Gargi Kamat is an eleven-year-old girl who envies the freedom and privileges enjoyed by her elder sister Gauri, and wishes to grow up quickly so that her parents will allow her to do the same things. During the Ganpati festival, her grandmother tells her while putting her to bed that only Lord Ganesha has the power to make her grow up. The next day, Gargi skips school after missing her bus and goes to a nearby Ganpati temple, where she vows to keep circling the shrine until the deity grants her wish.
Gargi's life subsequently takes an unexpected turn, and she forms a friendship with a man named Atharva Shastri, which changes the way she sees the world. The story follows her journey through family relationships, friendship and faith as she tries to understand what growing up really means.

articles.title: Anonymous Syriac Commentary on the Apocalypse
articles.text:
Anonymous Syriac Commentary on the Apocalypse

The Anonymous Syriac Commentary on the Apocalypse is the earliest commentary on the Book of Revelation in the Syriac language, dating from before the year 1000.


== Manuscript ==
The Anonymous Syriac Commentary is known from a single manuscript, now London, British Library, Add. MS 17127. The copy of the Commentary was produced in the Syriac monastic community at Nitria in Egypt in 1088. The scribe was the priest Samuel, son of Quryaqos. He reused parchment from an existing manuscript of the eighth or ninth century, which contained the only known copy of Gessius of Petra's commentary on Galen, in Syriac translation. Add. 17127 is thus a palimpsest, with the Anonymous Syriac Commentary being the overtext and the erased work of Gessius the undertext. Samuel used leaves from the Gessian manuscript for at least four other works.
As Revelation was poorly received in the Syriac churches, few early copies survive. Add. 17127 contains the earliest mostly complete text of Revelation in Syriac, although it quotes only about 70% of the book.


== Authorship and date ==
The text of Revelation used by the Commentary is the translation of Thomas of Harkel, made in Egypt around 615. The anonymous commentator was working from the Syriac text and not a Greek one, as demonstrated by his comments on a mistranslation. Theologically, he was of the Miaphysite persuasion.
The "elaborate" commentary is a complete one, covering essentially the entire book. It takes up 92 parchment leaves or 184 pages. Like the manuscript and the translation, it was created within the Syriac community in Egypt. It must date later than 686, since it cites the Syriac translation of the Testamentum Domini made in that year by James of Edessa, and earlier than 1088, the date of the manuscript. Stan Larson, who edited the commentary and translated it into English, considers it a work of the 9th or 10th century. Thomas Schmidt places it closer to the year 700 because it mentions neither the rise of Islam or the Third Council of Constantinople of 680–681.


== Contents ==
The anonymous Syriac commentator identifies the author of Revelation with John the Apostle. articles.title: 1971 Kurchatov Institute criticality accidents
articles.text:
1971 Kurchatov Institute criticality accidents

In 1971, two criticality accidents occurred at the Kurchatov Institute of Moscow during nuclear reactor reactivity experiments. An incident in February resulted from improper safety procedures and a failure to calculate experimental parameters, resulting in the serious injury of two scientists. An incident in May occurred when improper reactor design and the improper use of an emergency relief valve resulted in the bottom falling out of a reactor, causing a prompt criticality that killed two and seriously injured two others. Both accidents stemmed in part from improper management of reactor water; the first experiment added water erroneously, while the second removed water too quickly. The details of the accidents were kept secret until after the fall of the Soviet Union.


== February 15, 1971 ==
At the SF-7 criticality facility, researchers were testing the difference in reactivity in a reactor design caused by using iron or beryllium neutron reflectors. The fuel rods were enriched to 20% uranium-235, a typical composition for nuclear-powered icebreakers. Two prior experiments had been run with uneven radial spacing of neutron poisons, with one using iron reflectors, and one with beryllium reflectors, which had shown that the reactor was not critical in either configuration, and that there was little difference between iron and beryllium.
A new experiment was to be carried out, in which the outer ring of fuel rods would not have any neutron poison. Because there had been little difference in reactivity in the first experiment between iron and beryllium, only the reactivity of an iron reflector was calculated for this new configuration. Later calculations would show that the beryllium was about 10% more reactive in this configuration than iron. The beryllium test was to be carried out first because it was still in the reactor core from the prior experiment. On the morning of February 15, D. A. Mastin, head of the experimental team, arrived early. Without the control operator or control physicist on duty, Mastin activated a pump to fill the reactor with water. Water is a neutron moderator which increases the reactivity of a reactor. No immediate accident occurred, and business continued as usual. Trainee scientist R. A. Lednev walked over to Mastin and began chatting.

articles.title: 2026-27 Kariobangi Sharks FC season
articles.text:
2026-27 Kariobangi Sharks FC season

The 2026-27 season marked the return of Kariobangi Sharks to Kenya's second tier league, the Kenyan National Super League, after ten straight seasons in the Kenyan Premier League following relegation after a promotion/relegation playoff played in October 2026.
Sharks endured a tough camapaign in the 2025-26 Kenyan Premier League season, ending up in 16th spot in what was their worst positional finish since qualifying and featuring in the Kenya's top flight from the 2017 season. 38 points earned from eight wins, 14 draws and 12 loses destined Sharks to relegation/promotion playoff berth with the third best team in the second tier league, Mombasa United FC. 
The playoff was shrouded in controversy and legal proceedings following the Football Kenya Federation applicaion of different rules governing the leagues for the season contrary to what had been applicable in the last ten seasons.The Federatrion declared the bpttom three sides relegated, Sharks included, as opposed to presenting them for a playoff leading to court cases.
The playoff eventually took off after both Mombasa United and Sharks agreed to it, despite the existence of court cases, following a meeting brokered by FKF. Mombasa United won the first leg played at Mbaraki Sports ground in Mombasa on 4 Oct 2026, 2-1, and in the return leg played at Ulinzi Complex on 6 October 2026, Sharks came from a goal down to lead 2-1 at half time to tie the game at 3-3 on aggregate. However, the game never ended though after fan trouble caused abaondonment of the game in the 62nd minute. The Football Kenya Federation Leagues and Competitions Department ruled that Sharks allegedly caused the abondment of the game and handed them a 'forefeiture' meaning they lost the game with a 2-0 score, hence a relgation on the basis of a 4-1 loss to Mombasa United.   
Away from the relegation controversy, Sharks announced the transfer of some key players; skipper Kevinluke Otiala and goalkeeper Stepstenios Wekesa to AFC Leopards, and the 2024-25 season top scorer Ally Salum to Tanzania's Kagera Sugar. The team replaced those departing with the arrival of two forwards David Polepole and Douglas Omanga from Tusker FC and Fidel Otieno from Mathare United, amongst other players.

2025–26 Amarante F.C. season

The 2025–26 Amarante Futebol Clube season was the club's 103rd season in existence and 92nd season since joining official competitions. It was Amarante's 25th season in the third tier of Portuguese football and the 2nd in the Liga 3. Amarante also played in the Taça de Portugal.
Eurico Couto began the campaign as head coach but was dismissed in October after a spell of poor results which left the club second to last at the league table. Alex Costa was then appointed head coach for the remainder of the season.
Under Costa, Amarante recovered strongly and qualified for the promotion phase of Liga 3. On 10 May 2026, Amarante secured the club's first promotion to the professional leagues and its return to the second level of Portuguese football for the first time since 1988–89 by defeating União de Santarém 1–0. Six days later, it defeated Vitória de Guimarães B 3–1 away to win the Liga 3 title. In recognition of the 2025–26 campaign, four Amarante players were selected for the Liga 3 Team of the Year, while Tiago Ventura received the league's Revelation Player award. In July 2026, the Municipality of Amarante awarded the club the Municipal Medal of Merit in recognition of its Liga 3 title and historic promotion to Liga Portugal 2.

articles.title: 17 October riots
articles.text:
17 October riots

On 17 October 2026, nationwide unrest in France regarding rising living costs, fuel prices, public services, education, and other issues escalated as student organisations joined protests against the cost of living, spearheaded by the yellow vests movement. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 110 marches drew 550,000 participants, including 110,000 in Paris; organisers estimated 800,000.
While initial protests and demonstrations throughout September and October had been conducted peacefully, recurrent violence climaxed across the country on the weekend of 17 October. Thousands of rioters and vandals exploited the tense situation to loot shops, set fires, and attack public buildings and police, resulting in what have been widely described as the worst riots in French history post-May 68. The riots caused hundreds of millions of euros in damage. Around 1,500 shops were severely damaged and a further 3,000 were looted. More than 1,500 fires involving vehicles and public equipment were reported. Public buildings and businesses were also attacked in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Lille and Bordeaux. Around 60 buildings suffered fire damage. The Associated Press reported about 400 arrests during the day. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu later said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers and gendarmes injured.
In Lyon, where about 20,000 people marched, hooded individuals were seen vandalising a branch of the tourist office, tearing letters from its sign and damaging the premises. The tourist office was set on fire by several individuals. In Marseille, shops and a municipal police station were damaged, and protesters briefly entered the lobby of city hall. In Limoges, the historic Hôtel de Ville was set ablaze during the evening; the fire continued into the following morning and partially destroyed the 19th-century building. A demonstrator lost a hand in Saint-Étienne; Nuñez said an investigation had opened and did not confirm reports that the injury was caused by a police grenade. In Paris, tens of thousands took part in the demonstration. The Associated Press reported that cars were set on fire and shops looted during clashes between police and groups of protesters.
Clashes and property damage were also reported during protests in Italy, Belgium and Portugal.

articles.title: 2010 Johor F.C. season
articles.text:
2010 Johor F.C. season

The 2010 season was Johor Football Club's 38th season in club history, their 4th season in the Malaysia Super League since its rebranding in 2004, and their 6th in the Malaysian first division.
Johor FC qualified to the Malaysia FA Cup quarterfinals with their coach Ramlan Rashid. They failed to advance further after being defeated by Negeri Sembilan FA. Johor  FC ended their Malaysia Cup campaign in the semi-finals, where they notably drew 2–2 against Negeri Sembilan FA in the first leg but were defeated 5–7 on aggregate after a high-scoring second-leg loss.


== Season overview ==
The 2010 season was a successful one for Johor FC, as the club finished fourth in the Malaysia Super League and reached the semi-finals of the Malaysia Cup, although they were unable to secure silverware in either competition.
Johor FC competed in the seventh edition of the Malaysia Super League, which had been established in 2004 following the rebranding of Liga Perdana 1. The team enjoyed a solid league campaign, finishing fourth with 43 points from 26 matches, recording 13 wins, 4 draws, and 9 defeats, with 44 goals scored and 29 conceded for a goal difference of +15. Their league campaign ran from January to August 2010, and the fourth-place finish placed them behind champions Selangor, Kelantan, and Terengganu. Notable results included a 5–0 home win over Penang and a 3–0 win over Kedah, though a heavy 6–0 away defeat to eventual champions Selangor in January was a low point.
In the Malaysia FA Cup, Johor FC's campaign was brief and ended in disappointment. After progressing through the early rounds, they faced Negeri Sembilan and drew the first leg 2–2 at home. However, they suffered a heavy 3–5 defeat in the second leg away, exiting the competition 5–7 on aggregate. The early exit meant Johor FC's only realistic chance of silverware that season rested on the Malaysia Cup.
The Malaysia Cup was the highlight of Johor FC's season, as the team went unbeaten through the group stage. Placed in Group C, Johor FC recorded three wins and three draws from six matches, scoring 7 goals and conceding 3, topping the group with 12 points and a +4 goal difference. Notable group results included a 1–0 win over Pahang and a 2–1 win over ATM FA. 2026–27 Syrian First Division

The 2026–27 Syrian First Division (Arabic: الدوري الدرجة الثانية السوري 2026–2027) will begin on 20 October 2026 and is planned to conclude on May 2027.


== Format ==
40 clubs representing all Syrian teams that have football programs (excluding those already in the Premier League) will split up in six groups of either 6 or 7 teams. Matches will be played in a home and away pure round-robin format within each group.
The top two finishers, as well as the two best third-place teams, would compete in the final round of the competition. Teams finishing between third and fifth (or sixth) from the first round will shape the upcoming Syrian Second Division. Teams that finish last from the first round will be directly relegated to the following Syrian Third Division season.
The final round consists of 14 total teams split into two groups of 7 teams. It will be in a single round-robin format held on neutral ground. The champions of each group gain promotion to the 2027–28 Syrian Premier League, while the 12 clubs that could not gain promotion will form the First Division for the upcoming season.
On 15 September 2026, a draw was held to determine the six groups.

articles.title: Balkove
articles.text:
Balkove

Balkove (Ukrainian: Балкове), formerly Fürstenwerder (Ukrainian: Фірстенвердер) and Poworotnoje (Ukrainian: Поворотне) is a village in Polohy Raion, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine. Administratively, it is part of Molochansk urban hromada. In 2001 its population was 501. 


== Geography ==
The village is located on the banks of the Behym-Chokrak River. The village is 16 kilometres southeast of Molochansk, 1.3 kilometres northeast of Kozoluhivka, and 6 kilometres northeast of Novomykolaivka. 


== History ==
Balkove was founded as Fürstenwerder in 1821 by 30 Flemish Mennonite families. Four families came from other parts of the Molotschna Colony, with the others coming from Prussia between 1816 and 1819. The village was named after a village of the same name in Prussia.  
In 1848, the village had 8 brick farmhouses and 22 brick houses.  
In 1869, there were 22 farms and 52 smallholdings, as well as a windmill and a brickyard.  
The village was renamed to Poworotnoje in 1915, but shortly renamed back to Fürstenwerder.  
The village was renamed to Balkove in 1946.  
The village became part of Molochansk urban hromada on June 12, 2020 following the abolition of the Balkove Rural Council and the Novomykolaivka Rural Hromada.   
The village became part of Polohy Raion on July 19, 2020, following the abolition of Tokmak Raion. 
The village has been occupied by Russia since March 2022. 


== Demographics ==
According to the 2001 Ukrainian census, there were 501 residents of the village with 91% spoke Ukrainian and 8% spoke Russian..

articles.title: 2026 Kolkata Durga Puja crowd crush
articles.text:
2026 Kolkata Durga Puja crowd crush

On 17 October 2026, at 19 people were killed and 35 injured in a crowd crush at a Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata, West Bengal, India.


== Incident ==
The Chorebagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal is located in North Kolkata, within the area of the Girish Park police station. The puja pandal had been in its 91st year of operation at the time of the crush. The 2026 theme was "Beyond Sound". According to Press Trust of India, prior to the crush, the West Bengal state government had had awarded the pandal the 2026 Best of the Best Durga Puja award. It had also won awards for lighting, environment-friendliness, and best pandal.
Per a Kolkata Police press release, the crowd crush occurred at the exit gate of the pandal at approximately 7:40 pm Indian Standard Time (UTC+05:30), though an eyewitness account reported by the Hindustan Times alternatively placed it around ten minutes earlier. The sudden onset of rain sent an influx of people into the pandal, surging through the entry and exit gates. This compounded the crowd with those inside, causing a bottleneck. According to a survivor interviewed by Indo-Asian News Service, two people fell in the dark and additional people fell on top of them.


=== Casualties ===
Thirteen of the nineteen victims were women, and four were children; the youngest victim was a 13-year-old boy from Agarpara. Many of the victims had travelled from outside the city to participate in Kolkata's Durga Puja festivities. 25 people were injured, and, as of 18 October 2026, three have been admitted to the ICU. One of the three was reported to be in critical condition due to crush syndrome.


== Response ==
Police halted entry to the pandal and began investigating the incident. Reports also said that members of the puja organising committee and security personnel had been detained as part of the investigation.
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari announced compensation of ₹2,500,000 (US$26,000) and a government job for a family member of each person killed. The state government also announced that it would cover the medical expenses of those injured and provide ₹500,000 (US$5,200) to each injured person. Prime Minister Narendra Modi separately announced ex-gratia payments of ₹200,000 (US$2,100) for the next of kin of each deceased person and ₹50,000 (US$520) for each injured person.

articles.title: A City Drowned in God's Black Tears
articles.text:
A City Drowned in God's Black Tears

A City Drowned in God's Black Tears is a collaborative studio album by American musicians Infinity Knives and Brian Ennals. It was released on April 4, 2025, through Phantom Limb.


== Background ==
Tariq Ravelomanana, better known under the pseudonym Infinity Knives, is an American record producer and multi-instrumentalist. American rapper Brian Ennals previously contributed vocals to Infinity Knives' album Dear, Sudan (2020). A City Drowned in God's Black Tears is the duo's third collaborative album, following Rhino XXL (2020) and King Cobra (2022). Most of the album was recorded at Frances Malvaiz and Griffin Murphy's home studio.
The album was released on April 4, 2025, through Phantom Limb.


== Critical reception ==

A City Drowned in God's Black Tears received online acclaim.
Justin Sayles of The Ringer stated, "A City is backdropped by moody, noisy production and filled with Modest Mouse references, self-medicating cocaine use, and pure aggression that'll be a good litmus test for how you view the world." Sumugan Sivanesan of Cyclic Defrost wrote, "Speaking truth to power, it is an exhilarating listen from start to finish, that makes clear to me how self-censorship has become normalised in my milieu." Andre Gee of Rolling Stone praised Infinity Knives' "adventurous, electronic-­driven tracks" and Brian Ennals' "sharp social commentary and self-effacing sense of humor". 
Arusa Qureshi of The Quietus commented that the album "is another bold progression in their DIY approach, but with even more contempt, exasperation and bitterness at the state of all things." She added, "Once again, the pair have created a project that underscores their propensity for social critique, while affirming a desire to remain authentically imperfect in their approach to creativity and experimentation." Hanif Abdurraqib of The New Yorker called it "among the most expansive and ambitious of the albums I loved this year."

articles.title: 1966 Oregon State Senate election
articles.text:
1966 Oregon State Senate election

Elections to the Oregon State Senate were held on November 8, 1966, to elect 15 candidates to the Senate to serve four-year terms, and one to fill the two-year remainder of an unexpired term. The Democratic Party won 9 seats to the Republicans' 7, resulting in a Senate composition of 19 Democrats and 11 Republicans, with no net gains for either party. The coalition of Republicans and conservative Democrats remained in power, electing Debbs Potts as Senate President, winning 17 votes to 12 against the leader of the liberal faction, Democrat Al Flegel.
This election used the same district boundaries used for the 1962 and 1964 general elections passed after the 1960 U.S. census. However, after the passing of a 1965 law, senators in multi-member districts were elected to designated single-member positions for the first time, as opposed to plurality block voting which had been used previously. Incumbent senators in multi-member districts were assigned numbers based on their vote totals at their most recent general election, with the highest voted candidate getting position 1, second-highest position 2, and so on.

articles.title: Anthon van der Horst
articles.text:
Anthon van der Horst

Anthon van der Horst (20 June 1899 ― 7 March 1965) was a Dutch organist, conductor,  composer and academic teacher. He directed the Nederlandse Bachvereniging from 1931 to 1965.


== Life and career ==
Van der Horst was born in Amsterdam on 20 June 1899. He received his musical training with Jean-Baptiste de Pauw for organ and Bernhard Zweers for composition, among others. He was a cofounder of the Musiklyzeum in Amsterdam in 1921, where he lectured from 1922 to 1927. He then directed the Musiklyzeum in Hilversum. In 1935 he became leading professor of organ at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam, where he at times also was professor of conducting and choral conducting. He influenced Dutch organists including Bernard Bartelink, Jan J. van den Berg, Piet Kee, Albert de Klerk, Gert Oost, Piet Post, and Charles de Wolff.
In 1931 Van der Horst succeeded Evert Cornelis, who was ill, as director of the Nederlandse Bachvereniging. He led the annual performances of Bach's St Matthew Passion as well as performances of his Mass in B minor until his death. The performances at the Grote Kerk in Naarden, where he was the organist, drew an international audience. He was also conductor of the Royal Choral Association in Amsterdam, the Excelsior choir in The Hague, the Sursum Corda choir in Leiden and the Christian Oratorio Association in Utrecht. He made several recordings, including with the Concertgebouw Orchestra and the Amsterdam Chamber Orchestra.
Van der Horst died in Hilversum on 7 March 1965, at the age of 65.


== Awards ==
In 1919 Van der Horst was the first in the Netherlands to receive the Prix d'Excellence for organ. As a notable scholar of Bach's church music, he received an honorary doctorate in theology from the University of Groningen in 1948.


== Compositions ==
Van der Horst composed more than 100 works, especially for organ, piano, and choir, but also art songs, three symphonies, two organ concertos and a violin concerto.

articles.title: Bhanwar Pal Deo
articles.text:
Bhanwar Pal Deo

Bhanwar Pal Deo (24 February 1864 – 3 August 1927) was Maharaja of Karauli from 14 August 1886 until his death in 1927.


== Early life, family, and education ==
Bhanwar Pal Deo was born on 24 February 1864 to Durjan Pal, the Rao of Padampura. He was educated at Mayo College in Ajmer. He was the first student from Karauli to attend Mayo and attended that school from 16 March 1878 to 29 April 1879. He was adopted by his uncle Arjun Pal II, the Maharaja of Karauli. He married six times. He married firstly, in 1878, to Hadiji, daughter of Apji Ajit Singh of Koela; secondly, in 1880, to Shekhawatji, a daughter of Kushal Singh, the Raja of Khandela (Senior); thirdly, in 1889, to Shekhawatji, a daughter of Ajit Singh, Thakur of Mandawa (Senior); fourthly, in 1898, to Sajjan Kumari, daughter of Akshay Singh, the Raja of Banera; fifthly, in 1900, to Gaudji, a daughter of Raja Sheo Singh of Sheopur; and sixthly, in 1902, to Sengarji, a daughter of Rup Shah, the Raja of Jagmanpur. His first wife died on 19 April 1897; his second died before 1893; his third died after 1914; his fourth died after 1914; his fifth died after 1914; and his sixth died after 1914.


== Reign ==
Upon the death of Arjun Pal II, he succeeded him on the throne of Karauli on 14 August 1886. However, as before, the administration of the state remained in the hands of the State Council under the supervision of the Political Agent. In 1887, he was granted increased powers, subject to certain conditions, and when in 1889 the State's financial difficulties had been resolved and its debts cleared, he was invested with full administrative powers. He used to conduct the administration of the State with a Council, of which he was the President, and used to attend the council meetings, which were held once a week. He had constructed bridges over the rivers on the Hindaun Road and built the tanks of Madanpur and Rundh Ka Pura at a cost of nearly a lakh of rupees. He attended the Delhi Durbar of 1903. In 1904, he ceded, free of charge, certain lands to the British Government of India for the construction of the Nagda–Mathura railway. During his reign, the state accumulated substantial debts, and this prompted the Political Agent for the Eastern Rajputana States to assume control of its administration in 1906. During this time, the state coinage was replaced by the British currency. His ruling powers were restored eleven years later. His ruling powers were restored to him eleven years later

articles.title: Alexa Kumiko Hatanaka
articles.text:
Alexa Kumiko Hatanaka

Alexa Kumiko Hatanaka (born 1988) is a Japanese-Canadian artist. She uses traditional East Asian papermaking and printmaking techniques in a primarily paper-based practice that reflects on themes of climate change, mental health, and survival.


== Life and career ==
Hatanaka was born in Toronto, Ontario, Canada in 1988. She studied printmaking at OCAD University in Toronto before learning traditional woodblock printmaking in China in 2011. Her research has since focused on the history of paper as well as efforts to revive papermaking traditions. Her practice is shaped by her queer identity and experience living with bipolar disorder.
Her predominantly paper-based practice incorporates traditional paper techniques and materials, combining approaches such as printmaking, ink drawing, natural dyeing, and sewing by hand to produce large-scale installations and wearable sculptures. Deliberately honouring the Japanese concept of mottainai in her work, she repurposes sewing offcuts in her patchwork paper textiles, reuses old printing blocks, and incorporates paper rice bags and vintage washi, some of which are over 50 years old. She uses konnyaku starch to treat her paper to make her textiles both flexible and durable. She also integrates kamiko in her work. Her work frequently depicts landscapes, bodies of water, and fish, particularly those found in ancient mythology.
She has also undertaken artist residencies, including twelve weeks at Black Rock in Dakar, Senegal in 2025 and four weeks at Arts Maebashi in Japan in 2026.


=== 61st Venice Biennale ===
Hatanaka was invited to participate at the 61st Venice Biennale in 2026. She presented Namazu (2023), a work that draws on the Japanese legend of a catfish whose movements cause earthquakes to occur; Faultlines and Loneliness (2024) and Instability (2024); and Susceptibility to Gravity (2026), exhibited in the Giardini, which draws inspiration from koinobori. The High Arctic features prominently in her work, informed by her involvement in community-based projects in that ecoregion for more than a decade. Moveable and Immoveable reflects on her time in the High Arctic, featuring linocuts depicting snowdrifts that have helped the Inuit peoples navigate their terrain for centuries.


== Awards ==
In 2026, Hatanaka received the Sobey Art Award from the National Gallery of Canada. She has also been awarded several grants from the Canada Council for the Arts.

articles.title: 2026 Girls' U19 South American Volleyball Championship
articles.text:
2026 Girls' U19 South American Volleyball Championship

The 2026 Girls' U19 South American Volleyball Championship was the 24th edition of the Girls' U19 South American Volleyball Championship, a biennial international youth volleyball tournament organised by the Confederación Sudamericana de Voleibol (CSV) for the girls' under-19 national teams of South America. It was held in Maracaibo, Venezuela from 7 to 11 October 2026.
Same as previous editions, the tournament acted as the CSV qualifiers for the FIVB Volleyball Girls' U19 World Championship. The top three teams qualified for the 2027 FIVB Volleyball Girls' U19 World Championship as the CSV representatives.
Argentina won their fourth title by beating Peru 3–0 in the final. Defending champions Brazil failed to retain their title but secured a spot on the podium after defeating the hosts Venezuela in the third-place match. Champions Argentina, runners-up Peru and third-place Brazil qualified for the 2027 FIVB Volleyball Girls' U19 World Championship.


== Host and venue ==

Maracaibo, Venezuela was confirmed as host city of the tournament on 25 July 2026, following a notification from the CSV to the Venezuelan Volleyball Federation. This was subsequently ratified at the 77th CSV Ordinary Congress held on 28 July 2026 in Lima, Peru. It was the fourth time that Venezuela hosted the tournament having previously done so in 1992, 2000 and 2002.
The competition was entirely played at the Gimnasio Pedro Elías Belisario Aponte, which is part of the Luis Aparicio Montiel Sports and Recreation Complex. The teams' training sessions took place at Gimnasio Dr. Antonio Borjas Romero owned by University of Zulia.


== Teams ==
Seven of the twelve CSV member associations entered the tournament.


=== Squads ===

articles.title: 1962 Oregon Ballot Measure 9
articles.text:
1962 Oregon Ballot Measure 9

Measure 9 was a ballot initiative concerning state legislative redistricting in the State of Oregon held on November 6, 1962. If ratified, it would have amended the Constitution of Oregon establish a new process for reapportioning the Oregon State Legislature effective after the 1970 U.S. Census, as well as introducing a new temporary plan. The Senate reapportionment process would have been largely left alone, but the apportionment of the state house would have been highly modified, creating a frozen 30-district map that representatives would be apportioned to.
A leading criticism of the proposed plan was that the apportionment formula used would have widened the population disparity between urban and rural districts, while proponents argued that the new formula would make the representative distribution more fair to rural areas, especially to Eastern Oregon. The measure was rejected by a 25-point margin. 


== Amendment ==
If ratified, the Measure 9 would have:

Repealed Sections 2 and 6 of Article IV of the Constitution of Oregon, which concerned the number and apportionment of state senators and representatives.
Established a minimum of 65 seats in the Oregon House of Representatives, up from its current number of 60, allotted among permanent, constitutionally-defined House districts in a multi-step process, with each receiving at least one representative. The boundaries of House districts would not have been changed following decennial censuses.
After each census, representatives would have been apportioned to the districts based on their population.
Then, if a population per representative number of a district exceeded four times that of that of the district with the smallest such number, it would receive an additional representative.
Established a minimum of 30 seats in the Oregon State Senate, its current number, with the Legislature permitted to increase the size of the Senate up to 35. The formula for apportionment would have remained "substantially unchanged."
The amendment would have become operative on Election Day, and for the purposes of nominating legislative candidates prior to Election Day.
The official explanatory statement of the measure stated that "the probable effect of this amendment will be to give somewhat more emphasis in the House of Representatives to representation from sparsely settled counties and to make some Representative Districts not so large in area as is now the case."

articles.title: 2018 WPT Portugal Master
articles.text:
2018 WPT Portugal Master

The 2018 Portugal Master (officially 2018 World Padel Tour Portugal Master) was the eleventh tournament of the sixth season organized by World Padel Tour, the most prestigious padel circuit at the time.
In the women's category, Mapi and Majo Sánchez reached the final once again to face Gemma Triay and Lucia Sainz, their fourth encounter in a final during the 2018 season. In the battle for the title, the Sánchez twins, who lead the world rankings, defeated Gemma and Lucia to secure their fifth title of the season, bringing them very close to finishing the year as the world number ones. Although other editions of the tournament had previously been held in Portugal, this was the first to include a women's draw, making Majo and Mapi the first players to win a title on Portuguese soil.
In the men’s category, Maxi Sánchez and Sanyo Gutiérrez reached their eighth final of the year (out of 11 possible), where they faced the veteran duo of Juani Mieres and Miguel Lamperti, who were making their first final appearance of 2018. In the battle for the title, Sánchez and Gutiérrez defeated their opponents in straight sets, securing their sixth title of the season, the first for both in Portugal, and reaching the world number 1 ranking as a team (with Sánchez also taking the top spot individually) for the first time in their carrers.

=== Belasteguín’s injury forces Lima to find a new partner ===
Following two tournaments with results that fell short of expectations, which caused him to lose ground to Maxi Sánchez and Sanyo Gutiérrez in the race for the world number one ranking, Pablo Lima has decided to part ways with Marcello Jardím. While awaiting Fernando Belasteguín’s recovery, Lima will team up with a new partner, Agustín Gómez Silingo, who underwent surgery last season and was ranked 50th.


=== Paquito Navarro hospitalized ===
During the tournament semifinals, Paquito Navarro was taken to São Francisco Xavier Hospital after a glass wall on the court collapsed on top of him following a collision. The athlete, and his partner Juan Martín Díaz, were forced to withdraw from the match, which they had been leading 1–0 in sets against Lamperti and Mieres, with the second set tied at 5–5 and the score at 30–30. articles.title: 2026–27 European Aquatics Champions League
articles.text:
2026–27 European Aquatics Champions League

The 2026–27 European Aquatics Champions League is the 64th edition of European Aquatics's premier competition for men's water polo clubs, and the 16th edition since being rebranded from the Euroleague to the Champions League. The season began on 18 September 2026 and will end on 15 May 2027 with the Final Four.
The winners of the European Aquatics Champions League will automatically qualify for next season's edition (if they choose to enter) and also will qualify for the 2027 Super Cup.
Zodiac Atlètic-Barceloneta are the defending champions.


== Format ==
Qualification round
Eleven teams participate in the qualification round in September 2026. The runners-up from national leagues ranked 1–10 and A-Polo Sport Management, the champions of Georgia take part. The teams were divided into three separate groups, held in centralised venues. After round robin play, the top two teams in each group progressed to the group stage.

Group stage
Sixteen teams will play in the group stage which will be held between October to December 2026. The champions of national leagues ranked 1–10 plus the six clubs who advanced from the qualification round will compete. The participants were distributed into four groups of four. After home and away double round robin play, the top two from each group will qualify for the quarter-finals round while the bottom two will drop down to the 2026–27 European Aquatics Euro Cup knockout stage.

Quarter-finals round
The eight advancing teams from the previous round will be present and will be split into two groups of four. The round will be organized between February and April 2027. After home and away double round robin play, the top two from each group will qualify for the Final Four.

Final Four
In May 2027, the four remaining clubs will travel to Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to try and obtain the Champions League trophy. Two semifinals, a third place game and final will take place to decide the champions.

The 1983–84 Tunisian National Championship was the twenty-ninth season of the Tunisian national football championship following the country's independence in 1956. The competition was won by CA Bizertin, who finished level on 62 points with Stade Tunisien and won the title on the goal difference of the first-leg ("aller") matches. Stade Soussien and Union Sportive Monastir finished level on 45 points, and Stade Soussien was relegated on the goal difference of the first-leg matches (−9 against −4). Club Olympique des Transports and Avenir Sportif de Gabès were promoted for the following season.

articles.title: Arnold Karskens
articles.text:
Arnold Karskens

Arnold Karskens (born 19 August 1954) is a Dutch journalist, writer, and former war correspondent. He is a co-founder and former chairman of the Dutch broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland.


== Early life ==
Karskens studied journalism at the School for Journalism in Utrecht.


== Career ==
Karskens worked as a freelance journalist for fifteen years and was employed part-time by Nieuwe Revu from 1995 to 2008. Between April 2008 and March 2012, Karskens worked for the free daily newspaper De Pers, and between 2013 and 2015 as a reporter and columnist for ThePostOnline (Magazine). Since 2016, he has maintained the website TheKarskensTimes, and in 2022 he became chairman of the public broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland. In August 2024, he was suspended from that position and dismissed in October of that year.


=== War correspondent ===
He began his career in 1980 with a visit to guerrilla soldiers of the People's Revolutionary Army in El Salvador. Since then, he has visited some thirty different conflict zones. In 2008, he worked in the war zones of Iraq and Afghanistan, mainly focused on the Uruzgan region. He insisted on working as an independent journalist and not as an embedded journalist. He has contributed to TV and radio programs, and several current affairs programs. He was a regular guest on talk shows.


=== Hunt for war criminals ===
Karskens gathered a great deal of information about Frans van Anraat and Guus Kouwenhoven, who were convicted of war crimes. He was also chairman of the Foundation for the Investigation of War Crimes, which sought to bring the fugitive Dutch Nazi and war criminal Klaas Carel Faber to justice. He helped arrange for co-plaintiff Theun de Groot to participate in the trial of Dutch SS member and Aktion Silbertanne participant Heinrich Boere in 2009 and 2010. In 2012, Karskens wrote the book De Beestmensch about the hunt for Faber. Since 2015, he has maintained a list of ten Dutch war criminals from the Second World War who may not yet have served their sentences.


=== Participatory journalism ===
On the night of 7 November 2010, Karskens was arrested at Brussels North Station on suspicion of disturbing public order. At the time, he was working on a report about people without residence permits when the police attempted to close off the train station. articles.title: 2026 Australian Short Course Swimming Championships
articles.text:
2026 Australian Short Course Swimming Championships

The 2026 Australian Short Course Swimming Championships were held from 29 September to 2 October 2026 at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre in Sydney, New South Wales. The event served as the official selection meet for the Australian team competing at the 2026 World Short Course Swimming Championships in Beijing, China. It had been announced in July 2025 that the Sydney venue would host both this meet and the 2026 Australian Swimming Trials, which took place earlier that year from 8 to 13 June. A total of 801 swimmers representing 186 clubs from across the nation competed over the four days of competition.
Notable absences from the championships included Kaylee McKeown, who withdrew from both the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacific Swimming Championships due to glandular fever, and Mollie O'Callaghan, who sat out following a back injury. Kyle Chalmers also skipped the event to prioritise time with his young family. Meanwhile, Olympic champion Cameron McEvoy opted out of the meet to compete on the Swimming World Cup circuit. During the Baku leg, McEvoy set a new Australian, Oceanian and World Cup record in the 50 metre freestyle, clocking a time of 20.22 seconds—a mark he lowered further to 20.13 seconds just a week later in Tashkent.
The meet was highlighted by numerous record-breaking performances across both able-bodied and multi-class disciplines. In the able-bodied individual events, Lani Pallister dominated the women's freestyle fields, winning gold in the 200, 400, 800, and 1500 metre events, alongside a silver-medal finish in the 100 metre freestyle. Her performances in the 400, 800, and 1500 metre events established new allcomers records. Samuel Short secured a golden treble in the men's distance events, winning the 400, 800, and 1500 metre freestyle, while Iona Anderson completed a clean sweep of the women's backstroke events. In the men's freestyle sprint disciplines, Edward Sommerville claimed gold in the 200 metre freestyle in an Australian record time and secured a silver medal in the 100 metre freestyle behind event champion Flynn Southam. Joshua Collett achieved a multi-event victory, winning the 50 and 100 metre breaststroke alongside the 100 metre individual medley, notably establishing a new Australian record in the 100 metre breaststroke. articles.title: 1996 Michigan Proposal A
articles.text:
1996 Michigan Proposal A

Michigan Proposal A was rejected by Michigan voters on November 5, 1996. The state ballot initiative, if successful, would have upheld a 1994 ban on the use of bingo, and other such games, for political fundraising.
The referendum was initiated by a Democratic-affiliated group in hopes of suspending and ultimately invalidating the ban on political bingo passed by the Republican-controlled Michigan legislature. Bingo was used extensively by the Michigan Democratic Party to raise campaign funds. The rejection of the referendum invalidated the 1994 ban.
A court ruling in 2000 upheld a law passed in January 1996, which banned political bingo, despite the referendum.


== Ballot language ==
The following was the language of the proposal on the ballot, as reported by The Ann Arbor News:

A referendum on Public Act 118 of 1994 — an act to amend certain sections of Michigan's bingo act.
Public Act 118 of 1994 would:
1. Change the definition of a qualified organization which is permitted to sponsor certain forms of gaming, including bingo, millionaire parties, and raffles, so that an organization which is organized under the Michigan Campaign Finance Act, including a candidate committee, political committee, political party committee, ballot question committee, or independent committee, is no longer qualified to receive a license to sponsor such gaming.
2. Permit a change in the single maximum prize or payout for a charity game sold by a licensed religious, educational, service, senior citizens, fraternal or veterans organization.

Should this law be approved?


== History ==


=== 1994 Bingo amendment ===
Bingo as a means of political fundraising was mostly utilized by the Democrats. Ingham County Democratic Chairwoman June Pallottini said that bingo was the largest individual source of campaign funds for the party. Bingo games raised an estimated $2 million for the party annually. Democrats argued bingo allowed middle-class people to support the party.
State Senate Majority Leader Dick Posthumus described political bingo as "one of the biggest single loopholes in the campaign finance law". Republicans argued that political bingo was a loophole on the basis that contributors were able to donate to political organizations anonymously. Republicans further argued that bingo was intended to be used for charities, not campaign fundraising.

articles.title: Athaliah (opera)
articles.text:
Athaliah (opera)

Athaliah is an opera in 2 acts with music by Hugo Weisgall. It uses an English-language libretto by Richard Franko Goldman that is based on the 1691 play Athalie by Jean Racine. The play in turn was based on the murderous Biblical figure Athaliah found in II Kings and II Chronicles. It premiered in a concert version at Philharmonic Hall, New York in 1964 with Shirley Verrett in the title role.


== Plot ==
Athaliah is the daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel and the wife of King Jehoram of Judah. After Jehoram's death, she murders her rival claimants to the thrown and rules the country in the belief that she has eliminated all rival members of the royal family. She abandons the Israelite religion for the worship of Baal. 
Meanwhile Athaliah's sister Yehosheba has successfully hidden Joash, the infant son of Ahaziah of Judah and his wife Zibiah. Yehosheba took Joash after seeing the child in a dream which led her to the Jewish temple to find him. She and her husband, the priest Yehohada, raise the child in secret and keep him safe. Ultimately Athaliah discovers the threat of Joash as a rebellion against her rises. The rebels barricade the Jewish Temple, and Athaliah unsuccessfully attempts to dislodge the rebellion. She is ultimately executed by Yehohada after he proclaims Joash as King.


== Composition and performance history ==
Athaliah was commissioned by the Concert Opera Association (COA). Weisgall spent several years creating the score; devoting much of the years 1960 to 1963 to this project. It was given its world premiere by the COA at Philharmonic Hall, New York on February 17, 1964. The opera was divided into two acts and included within them arias, duets, choruses, and a ballet interlude. 
At the premiere, conductor Thomas Scherman led the Little Orchestra Society and the singers of COA. While essentially performed in a concert version, the production was semi‐staged by director Edwin Levy and used lighting designed by Richard Casler. The cast in the premiere was led by Shirley Verrett in the title role with Irene Jordan as Yehosheba and John Reardon as Yehohada. Secondary roles were performed by Raymond Michalski (as Ahner), William Lewis (as Mattan), and Scott Kennedy (as Eliakim). The Choral Arts Society served as the opera chorus.

articles.title: 1906 United Kingdom general election in Wales
articles.text:
1906 United Kingdom general election in Wales

From 12 January to 8 February 1906, the 1906 United Kingdom general election was held in Wales, to elect all 670 members of the House of Commons, with 34 seats being in Wales. 34 seats represented territorial constituencies contested under the first past the post electoral system amongst 33 constituencies.
The election was held as a result of the resignation of the Conservative Government after a series of defeats in by-elections and internal disputes over tariff reform. The Liberal Party formed a minority Liberal Government and immediately requested a dissolution. It was the first of two general elections held during the reign of King Edward VII.
The Liberals under Henry Campbell-Bannerman won a landslide victory against the Conservative Party, with leader Arthur Balfour losing his seat. The Conservatives won the lowest number of seats it ever had in its history, a record unsurpassed until 2024. It was the first election since the creation of the Conservative Party in which it won no seats in Wales. This would only occur again in the 1997, 2001 and 2024 general elections.
