articles.title: Nar Singh Pal
articles.text:
Nar Singh Pal

Nar Singh Pal was Maharaja of Karauli from 1849 until his death on 10 July 1852.


== Birth ==
Pal was born to Madhu Pal, the Rao of Hadoti. He was a descendant of Kirti Pal, a son of Dharam Pal II, the Maharaja of Karauli.


== Reign ==
When Pratap Pal, the Maharaja of Karauli, died in 1849 without leaving a male heir, his family adopted Pal as his successor. Although his succession was undisputed, disputes arose over his guardianship. At the time, the state also owed the East India Company a debt of 1,54,312 rupees, and the British withheld recognition of his succession until arrangements had been made for its repayment. Before officially recognising him as Maharaja, they required him to undertake to pay an instalment of the state's debt. As Pal was still a child, his guardian assumed responsibility for managing the payment on his behalf. However, the instalment was not paid until after the deadline set by the British had passed. All this created an opportunity for his power-hungry family members, who tried to convince the British to depose Pal, install them, and, if this was to be done, they promised to pay back the state's debts faster. Seeing the growing instability in Karauli, the British decided to depose Pal. However, his guardian strongly opposed this and argued that removing Pal would be entirely unfair because they were fully prepared to pay their instalments on time. Later, the British realised that deposing Pal would actually trigger an even worse civil war, and gave up this idea. They then confirmed Pal as the ruler, and at the same time stationed a Political Agent in the state, to whose charge they committed the direct management of affairs of the state.


== Death ==
He died on 10 July 1852. He had, before his death, adopted Bharat Pal as his successor.


== References ==

articles.title: The Queens Closet Opened
articles.text:
The Queens Closet Opened

The Queens Closet Opened is a collection of manuscripts, first published in England in 1655. It comprises three sections: 'The Peal of Practise' (describing remedies), 'A Queens Delight' (confectionery), and 'The Compleat Cook' (cookery).
The book is presented by a W. M., who claimed that the recipes had been prepared by Henrietta Maria, Queen of England, Scotland and Ireland. Identifying themselves as "one of her late servants". W. M. wrote that the book's contents were:

As they were presented to the Queen by the most Experienced Persons of our Times, many whereof were honoured with her own practice, when she pleased to descend to these more private Recreations. Never before published. Transcribed from the true Copies of her Majesties own Receipt Books.
According to the food historian Gilly Lehmann, the title's reference to the Queen was a reflection of attitudes towards the ideal housewife, with The Queens Closet Opened representing "an example of domestic virtue at the very highest level". The notion of these recipes being private was further evoked in the title's imagery of the closet, a highly personal space.


== Publication ==
The Queens Closet Opened was first published during the Commonwealth of England, an 11-year stretch of Republican governance. This period followed the English Civil War, a series of wars which took place during the reign of Charles I. In contrast to the instability of Charles' tenure when few cookbooks were published, the comparative stability of England under the Commonwealth allowed the publication of a number of books containing information on cookery. The Queens Closet Opened was among the best-selling of these. It was one of several recipe collections published in 1650s England that associated with nobility—A Choice Manual, for instance, the other most popular recipe collection of the era, did the same. In doing so, some scholars have argued books like The Queens Closet Opened served a political purpose as a reminder of royalty, producing associations between the good management of the home and country by Stuart monarchs.
The Queens Closet Opened remained among the bestselling books of the 1660s and 1670s, and by 1700, it had been through ten editions. New editions continued to be published until 1713.

articles.title: Álex Campos
articles.text:
Álex Campos

Álex Campos Camí (born 2 February 2008) is a Spanish professional footballer who plays as a defender for Barcelona. 


== Early life ==
Campos was born on 2 February 2008. Born in Province of Lleida, Spain, he is a native of Aitona, Spain.


== Club career ==
As a youth player, Campos joined the youth academy of Atlètic Segre. Following his stint there, he joined the youth academy of La Liga side Barcelona, where he played in the UEFA Youth League.
Ahead of the 2025–26 season, he was promoted to the club's reserve team, where he was regarded to have established himself as a regular starter while playing for them. In 2026, he extended his contract with the Blaugrana until July 2029. On 20 October 2026, he was first called up to the Barça senior team during a 2–4 away loss to PSG in the UEFA Champions League.


== International career ==
Campos is a Spain youth international and has represented the country internationally at under-16, under-17, under-18 and under-19 levels. Altogether, he made two appearances and scored one goal while playing for the Spain national under-16 football team. 
During the spring of 2025, he played for the Spain national under-17 football team for 2025 UEFA European Under-17 Championship qualification. One year later, he played for the Spain national under-19 football team for 2026 UEFA European Under-19 Championship qualification.


== Style of play ==
Campos plays as a defender and is right-footed and has received comparisons to Spain international Pau Cubarsí. Initially, he played as a midfielder while playing for the youth academy of Atlètic Segre before switching to defender while playing for the youth academy of Barcelona.
Spanish newspaper Mundo Deportivo wrote in 2026 that "the... right-footed center-back stands out for his excellent aerial ability in both penalty areas and his decisive tackling in defense. He also possesses good ball control, with the ability to look up and distribute the ball effectively. Standing at 1.85 meters tall, he has the physical attributes to be an alternative in the center of defense".

articles.title: Violins (album)
articles.text:
Violins (album)

Violins is the third studio album by the American alternative rock musician Blondshell, released on September 25, 2026, via Partisan Records. It was produced by Yves Rothman and recorded in Los Angeles between EastWest Studios and Saturn Sound. The record was preceded by the singles "Heart Has to Work So Hard", "Violins", and "Fur Elise", and it was accompanied with a fourth single, "Stone Fruit", on the same day as the album. Upon release, Violins was met with positive reception from critics.


== Background and recording ==
Soon after completing her second album If You Asked for a Picture (2025), Sabrina Teitelbaum initially decided to take a break from recording but quickly found herself eager to write again. In preparation, she listened to a considerable amount of guitar-based music and amassed a playlist consisting of artists such as Arthur Russell, Brian Eno, Sade, Teenage Fanclub, and Television. After sharing the playlist with Rothman, she wrote for a period on the guitar at home and proceeded to make demos with Rothman and guitarist Sam Stewart. Violins was recorded in her base city of Los Angeles at EastWest Studios and Saturn Sound.


== Composition ==
Described as an alternative rock album, Violins generally retains the musical style of the first two Blondshell albums. It does, however, mark a shift in how Teitelbaum wrote the lyrics, with her opting for a more abstract approach as opposed to the blunt lyrics that previously characterized her work.


== Promotion and release ==
On May 18, 2026, Teitelbaum released the single "Heart Has to Work So Hard" in anticipation of a new album, whose title and release date had not yet been revealed. Violins was officially announced the following June 25, accompanied by the release of its title track as the second single. The music video for "Violins" was directed by Sabra Binder. The third single, "Fur Elise", was released on August 18, 2026, with a lyric video.
Violins was released on September 25, 2026, via Partisan Records, alongside the fourth single, "Stone Fruit", and its corresponding music video, directed again by Sabra Binder. The album debuted on the UK Independent and Scottish Albums Charts at no. 11 and 21, respectively.

articles.title: Locomotives of the West Lancashire and Liverpool, Southport and Preston Junction Railways
articles.text:
Locomotives of the West Lancashire and Liverpool, Southport and Preston Junction Railways

The West Lancashire Railway (WLR) and Liverpool, Southport and Preston Junction Railway (LS&PJR) both had a varied fleet of locomotives, although separate companies they shared a lot of facilities and staff. Their locomotives were administered separately until December 1888  when they combined their locomotive stocks and operated a single stable.
The WLR did not have a definite livery and their locomotives were a variety of colours, apparently being chosen by the manufacturer, the LS&PJR followed suit.


== West Lancashire Railway locomotives ==
The lines first Superintendent of rolling stock was Jack Willgoose until he retired in 1888, he was succeeded by John Edmondson who came from the  Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway, he stayed in the post until the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway (L&YR) take-over.
Upon opening in 1878 the line had two 0-4-2 tender locomotives built by Sharp, Stewart and Company, they were initially named Edwd Holden and Sir T. Hesketh and were painted bright blue with plenty of polished brass. Sometime later, probably in 1880 but by 1882, these locomotives were renamed no.1 Southport and no.2 Longton respectively. No.1 was scrapped in 1896. No.2 was renumbered 7 in 1893 then allocated 1367 in the L&YR list on take-over but was found to be unfit for service and was scrapped in 1897.
A third engine, no. 3 Banks was delivered from Sharp, Stewart and Company in 1878, it was similar to the first two locomotives except it was fitted with a saddle tank and therefore had no tender, it was rebuilt as a tender engine in 1885, it was also painted bright blue on delivery. No.3 was scrapped in 1895.
For the Tarleton branch a Manning Wardle 0-6-0ST was purchased in 1882, this locomotive was painted black, it was no. 4 named Tarleton with the name inscribed on the sides of the tank in yellow. No.4 was renumbered 10 in 1893 then allocated 1370 in the L&YR list on take-over but was found to be unfit for service and was scrapped in 1897.
Once the line was fully opened, and services to Blackburn had started, more locomotives were required, unfortunately the company was short of funds. They sought out second-hand locomotives and found four suitable locomotives for sale by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway (LB&SCR), two were purchased in February 1883 and the other two in April 1833. 
The first two were 2-2-2 tender locomotives built at Br

articles.title: Carl Edvard Wallerstedt
articles.text:
Carl Edvard Wallerstedt

Carl Edvard Wallerstedt (11 January 1882 – 27 June 1963) was a Swedish diplomat who served as consul and consul general in San Francisco from 1919 to 1947. He began his career as a journalist, working for several Swedish newspapers and becoming a member of the Swedish Publicists' Association. In 1907, he travelled to the United States as a newspaper correspondent but subsequently joined the Swedish legation in Washington, D.C.
Wallerstedt later served as vice-consul and consul in Minneapolis, where he participated in Swedish-American cultural organizations and initiatives promoting Scandinavian art. In 1919, he became acting consul in San Francisco, overseeing Swedish consular affairs across the American West Coast, Alaska, Hawaii, and several western states. During his tenure, he supported the Swedish-American community, promoted cultural and educational ties between Sweden and the United States, and oversaw the expansion of the consulate. He also participated in diplomatic and cultural events, including presenting the Royal Swedish Aero Club's gold plaque to Charles Lindbergh in 1927. Before retiring in 1947, he arranged for the purchase of a new building for the Swedish consulate general and the consul general's residence.


== Early life ==
Wallerstedt was born on 11 January 1882 in Karlstad, Sweden, the son of merchant Edvard Wallerstedt and his wife, Amina Lindberg. He attended Karlstad Higher General Secondary School from 1892 to 1900. From 1900 to 1901, he worked in the editorial department of the Svenska Telegrambyrån, followed by studies in Germany and England from 1901 to 1903.


== Career ==
From 1904 to 1906, Wallerstedt worked in the editorial departments of the Svenska Telegrambyrån, Stockholms Dagblad, and Nya Dagligt Allehanda. He was a member of the Swedish Publicists' Association. As a journalist in Stockholm, he specialized in foreign news and feature articles. In 1907, he was sent to the Jamestown Exposition in Virginia as a representative of a Swedish newspaper syndicate. After arriving in the United States, Wallerstedt met Sweden's minister in Washington, D.C., Herman Lagercrantz, who offered him a clerical position at the Swedish legation. He served there from 1907 to 1909 before being transferred to Minneapolis to handle consular affairs under honorary consul Charles Axel Smith. Initially appointed unpaid vice-consul in 1909, Wallerstedt became consul in Minneapolis in 1914.

articles.title: Sumner Jackson
articles.text:
Sumner Jackson

Sumner Waldron Jackson (1885–1945), called "Dr. Jack", served as a medical doctor in France during both World War I and World War II. Despite being an American and although the United States was at war with Nazi Germany, the Germans occupying France permitted Jackson to continue to work at the American Hospital of Paris during World War II. Jackson and his wife and son were involved in the French resistance to the German occupation. Jackson helped wounded British and American airmen elude Nazi capture and escape to Great Britain and the Jackson house served as a "drop box" and meeting place for Resistance members.  Jackson, his wife, and son were captured by the Germans in 1944. He died in the mistaken bombing by the British of a ship carrying prisoners shortly before the end of the war in Europe in May 1945. His wife and son survived.


== Early life ==
Sumner Waldron Jackson was born October 7, 1885, in Spruce Head, Maine. He attended Waldoboro High School and Lincoln Academy in Newcastle, Maine. He graduated from Bowdoin College in 1909. He was trained as a medical doctor at Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia. In 1915, he became a medical intern at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. Waldron was described by author Charles Glass as a "tall, strong, and silent Yankee...an outdoorsman of the harsh American Northeast."


== World War I ==

In 1916, Jackson joined the "Harvard Group" of Americans who volunteered to serve in the British Royal Army Medical Corps. He arrived in France in June 1916. He was assigned as a surgeon and medical officer in a British military hospital near the front lines where the Battle of the Somme began on July 1, 1916. British and French casualties in the five month-long battle totaled more than 600,000. Jackson was assigned to a medical group near the front lines. The medical personnel suffered casualties.
In 1917, with the entry of the United States in the War, Jackson joined the U.S. Army Medical Corps. He was of only a few American doctors with experience treating battlefield casualties. He was assigned to a Red Cross hospital in Paris treating American and French soldiers evacuated from the front lines.  Between July 1917 and August 19, worked on a mobile hospital unit as well as being a staff member of four different hospitals. At one hospital he met a Swiss nurse named Charlotte Sylvie Barrelet de Ricout, called "Toquette". He was 32 years old; she was 27. His wife Toquette was small in stature

articles.title: Naděžda Melniková-Papoušková
articles.text:
Naděžda Melniková-Papoušková

Naděžda Filartová Melníkova-Papoušková (23 November 1891 – 10 July 1978) was a Czech art historian, cultural researcher and folklorist.


== Early life and education ==
She was born on 23 November 1891 in Saint Petersburg, Russian Empire. In 1919, she traveled to Prague and four years, studied the art of Slavic peoples at the Faculty of Arts, Charles University under the supervision of Tomáš Masaryk. From 1922 to 1925, she studied at the École du Louvre in Paris.


== World War II ==
Melniková-Papoušková, together with her husband Jaroslav Papoušek, was one of the founders of the Resistance in the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia. Her husband was arrested in December 1941 due to his activities within this movement and died four years later, in January 1945, in a forced labor camp. She was also sent to the Ravensbrück concentration camp on 9 October 1941. Throughout the war, she had almost no information regarding her husband's fate. She ultimately survived her captivity and returned to a liberated Czechoslovakia in 1945.


== After war ==
From 1946 to 1950, she taught at the Palacký University Olomouc. In the early 1950s, she managed the Ars Gallery, located on the first floor of the Melantrich on Wenceslas Square. In Prague, she organized exhibitions for artists such as Vladimír Komárek, Marta Taberyová and Miloslav Chlupáč, among others. She was a collector of historical artworks; for instance, she owned an exquisite collection of Russian porcelain.


== Later life ==
Melniková-Papoušková died in Prague on 10 July 1978. Her ashes were placed in an urn and interred in the Samšiňák family tomb at the Sobotka cemetery.

articles.title: Widyalaya
articles.text:
Widyalaya

Widyalaya is a type of school in Indonesia under the regulation of the Ministry of Religious Affairs that teaches in accordance of Hindu religious curriculum, similar to how madrasah is for Islamic curriculum. It was established in 2024 in an effort by the government to increase the formalization of Hindu education in Indonesia.


== Establishment ==

Prior to the formalization, Hindu-based schools in Indonesia consists of what is called pasraman, a kind of education institution that focuses solely on Hindu religious education. After the establishment of widyalaya, it became the second kind of religious based school formalized after madrasah, another kind of Islamic school where it is a blending of both secular and Islamic topics, which widyalaya becoming its Hindu equivalent. The curriculum consists of 60% of secular subjects and 40% of Hindu religious subjects and is equivalent to regular general school education. It is organized into pratama widyalaya which is an equivalent of kindergarten, adi widyalaya which is an equivalent of elementary school, madyama widyalaya which is an equivalent of junior highschool (SMP), and utama widyalaya which is an equivalent to senior highschool (SMA), together with its vocational equivalent, utama widyalaya kejuruan that is equivalent to an Indonesian vocational highschool (SMK). This kind of education institutions is expected to be centered mainly in Bali, as it is the center of Hinduism in Indonesia, though it also exists in other parts of the country such as in Sulawesi and Kalimantan. Some of these widyalaya were converted from pasraman schools. After its establishment, several regional heads in Bali expressed interests to establish public widyalaya operated by the government. As of 2026, all of existing widyalaya have status as private schools, though nationalization of several have been proposed and regulation to nationalize one was added in 2025. As of 2025, thereare 110 pratama widyalaya, 10 adi widylaya, 18 madyama widyalaya, 5 utama widyalaya, and 3 vocational utama widyalaya kejuruan in Indonesia. The effort to establish and formalize widyalaya was followed by the upgrading of state Hindu institutes into state universities status.

articles.title: Cruz Azul in international football
articles.text:
Cruz Azul in international football

Club de Futbol Cruz Azul is a Mexican professional football club based in Mexico City. The club has taken part in international competition since 1969, when it made its debut in the CONCACAF Champions' Cup and won the title at the first attempt. As of September 2026, Cruz Azul has played 195 matches in international club competitions organised by CONCACAF, CONMEBOL and FIFA, and in tournaments run jointly by Liga MX and Major League Soccer.
Cruz Azul has won the CONCACAF Champions Cup, formerly known as the Champions' Cup and the Champions League, seven times, a record it shares with América. Under Raúl Cárdenas, it won three consecutive titles from 1969 to 1971; Luis Fernando Tena led the club to back-to-back titles in 1996 and 1997 and to a sixth in 2013–14, and Vicente Sánchez to a seventh in 2025. The club was also runner-up in 2008–09 and 2009–10. Its 1969 and 1997 titles formed part of continental trebles alongside the league and the Copa México, and as of the end of the 2025 edition Cruz Azul was the Mexican club with the most matches, wins and goals in the competition. Javier Orozco, who scored 23 of his 24 goals in the competition for the club, is its all-time top scorer.
Outside CONCACAF, Cruz Azul became the first Mexican club to reach the final of the Copa Libertadores in 2001, losing to Boca Juniors on penalties, and also took part in the 2003 and 2012 editions. It was runner-up in the 1971 Copa Interamericana against Nacional, finished fourth at the 2014 FIFA Club World Cup, and lost to Flamengo in the Derby of the Americas at the 2025 FIFA Intercontinental Cup. In the competitions organised jointly by Liga MX and Major League Soccer, the club won the inaugural Leagues Cup and was runner-up in the Campeones Cup in 2021 and 2026.


== History ==


=== 1969–1988: Early continental success ===
Under manager Raúl Cárdenas, and as champions of the 1968–69 Primera División, Cruz Azul made its international debut in the 1969 CONCACAF Champions' Cup. Drawn against defending champions Toluca in the second round, Cruz Azul lost the tie 1–0 on aggregate but advanced to the semi-finals after Toluca were disqualified on 19 June for fielding three ineligible players. Cruz Azul then eliminated Costa Rica's Saprissa 4–3 on aggregate and met Guatemala's Comunicaciones in the final. The second legs of both ties were played at the Estadio Azteca rather than at the club's home ground, the Estadio 10 de Diciembre in Ciudad Coo

articles.title: Lophocerine
articles.text:
Lophocerine

Lophocerine is an isoquinoline alkaloid reported from the cactus Lophocereus schottii. It belongs to the group of substituted tetrahydroisoquinoline alkaloids and has been investigated in research on cactus chemistry and alkaloid biosynthesis. The compound was first reported in a 1958 study by Carl Djerassi, Takashi Nakano and James M. Bobbitt, which described its isolation and proposed chemical structure. Subsequent investigations examined its chemical synthesis and the biological processes involved in its formation in the plant.


== Chemical structure and classification ==
Lophocerine is classified as an isoquinoline alkaloid, a broad class of nitrogen-containing natural products whose structures contain an isoquinoline-derived ring system. More specifically, lophocerine has a tetrahydroisoquinoline skeleton. Its reported structure contains an isobutyl substituent, an N-methyl group, a methoxy group and a hydroxy group.
The structure proposed in the original isolation study was 1-isobutyl-2-methyl-6-methoxy-7-hydroxy-1,2,3,4-tetrahydroisoquinoline. The researchers obtained lophocerine in an impure form from the phenolic alkaloid fraction of the plant. They supported the proposed structure by methylating the compound and obtaining a derivative identified as a known dimethoxy tetrahydroisoquinoline.
The compound is recorded in PubChem, the chemical database maintained by the United States National Center for Biotechnology Information. The record associates lophocerine with PubChem Compound Identifier (CID) 442313 and molecular formula C15H23NO2. The formula corresponds to a molecular mass of approximately 249.35 g/mol.


== Discovery and isolation ==
Lophocerine was reported during a systematic investigation of alkaloids from Lophocereus schottii published in 1958. In the same study, Djerassi, Nakano and Bobbitt described piloceredine, another cactus alkaloid, in addition to the previously known pilocereine. Their work formed part of the broader chemical investigation of the cactus and its naturally occurring constituents.
The researchers isolated lophocerine from the plant's phenolic alkaloid fraction. The material was not obtained in a completely pure form, so the proposed structure relied on chemical evidence and the behaviour of derivatives prepared from the isolated material. In particular, methylation produced a dimethoxy derivative that was consistent with the assigned substitution pattern on the tetrahydroisoquinoline ring.

articles.title: The Case Against Adolescence
articles.text:
The Case Against Adolescence

The Case Against Adolescence: Rediscovering the Adult in Every Teen is a 2007 non-fiction book by American psychologist Robert Epstein. It was published by Quill Driver Books.
The book argues that adolescence, as a long period between childhood and adulthood, is largely a modern social creation. Epstein argues that many teenagers have abilities similar to those of adults, but are separated from adult society and are subject to many age-based restrictions. He uses the term "infantilization" for this treatment and argues that it can contribute to conflict and psychological problems among young people.
Epstein proposes replacing some age-based limits with a system based on individual competence. Under his proposal, young people could receive particular adult rights and responsibilities when they show that they are able to handle them.


== Background and publication ==
Epstein said that his interest in adolescence developed partly from his experience with his own children. He described one of his teenage sons as mature and questioned why the law still prevented him from doing many activities open to adults.
The book was published in the United States in 2007 by Quill Driver Books. The National Diet Library lists it as a 490-page book and classifies it under adolescence, adolescent psychology, maturation and developmental psychology.
In 2010, Epstein published a revised and expanded version under the title Teen 2.0: Saving Our Children and Families from the Torment of Adolescence. Epstein described Teen 2.0 as an updated and retitled version of The Case Against Adolescence. The new edition included updated information, additional material about youth rights and practical advice for parents.


== Contents and arguments ==


=== Artificial extension of childhood ===
Epstein argues that the modern idea of adolescence developed mainly during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. He connects this change to compulsory education, restrictions on child labor and other laws that increasingly separated young people from adult work and adult society.
According to Epstein, these changes produced an "artificial extension of childhood". He argues that teenagers in many modern societies spend most of their time with people of the same age instead of learning and working with adults. In his view, this creates a separate youth culture and limits opportunities for young people to develop adult roles.

articles.title: Virtual cemetery
articles.text:
Virtual cemetery

A virtual cemetery is a digital space intended to commemorate deceased people or animals. It may take the form of a standalone website, a collection of memorial pages, or an interactive environment in which users can read biographies of the deceased, view photographs and videos, leave memorial messages and take part in online rituals. Unlike a single online memorial page, a virtual cemetery brings many memorials together in one shared space, often modelled on the structure of a physical cemetery.
In academic literature, virtual cemeteries and web memorials are treated as forms of digital memorialization that change the ways people preserve memory and relate to the dead.


== History ==


=== Early web projects ===
In 1995, Michael Kibbee and Steve Brower created the World Wide Cemetery, one of the earliest internet projects dedicated to commemorating the dead. It allowed users to publish virtual monuments with photographs, audio and video, and visitors to leave messages.
In the same year, Jim Tipton founded Find a Grave. The site was originally intended to record the burial places of famous people. It later expanded into an international database of burials that includes grave photographs, biographical information and memorial entries.
In the late 1990s, virtual cemeteries and memorial websites began to attract media attention. For example, The Irish Times described the World Wide Cemetery in the article "Death on the Net", published on 21 October 1997.


=== Growth of digital memorialization ===
With the spread of social networking services and multimedia web services, digital memorialization moved beyond specialized virtual cemeteries. Users became able to create memorial pages, publish memories and photographs, and maintain collective memory of the deceased on social networks.
The development of mobile devices, geolocation services and augmented reality has led to digital tools that link real burial sites with additional electronic information. Such technologies are used, among other things, for cemetery navigation and for providing biographical material accessible via mobile devices.


== Types and functions ==
Virtual cemeteries and related digital memorial services may include the following functions:

Personal memorials. Pages with the biography of the deceased, photographs, videos and memories of relatives and friends.
Interactive memorials. The ability to leave condolences, memorial messages, virtual flowers and other symbolic to

articles.title: 1970 Oregon State Senate election
articles.text:
1970 Oregon State Senate election

Elections to the Oregon State Senate were held on November 3, 1970, to elect 15 candidates to the Senate to serve four-year terms, and one to fill the two-year remainder of one unexpired term. The Democratic Party won 9 seats to the Republicans' 7, resulting in a Senate composition of 16 Democrats and 14 Republicans, with no net gain for either party, though six seats switched hands.
At the opening of the 1971 session on January 11, senators became deadlocked for 12 days as they repeatedly failed to elect a new Senate President. During the first week of the session, fifteen 15–15 tied votes were tallied between the same two candidates: Democrat Berkeley Lent, backed by the liberal Democratic caucus, and Republican L. W. Newbry, backed by all the Republicans and conservative Democrat Debbs Potts. Potts had led a conservative Democrat-Republican coalition during the 1967 and 1969 sessions. During the deadlock, Democratic senators repeatedly attempted to convince Potts to join the rest of the Democrats. On January 22, after the 54th tied vote, Portland Democrat John Burns announced to the chamber that he would nominate himself with the support of Potts and the entire Republican caucus. Taken by surprise, Senate Democrats attempted to call a recess and then proceeded to leave the chamber to prevent a quorum. On the 55th ballot, Burns was elected President 16–14, voting for himself over Lent.
This election used the same district boundaries used for the 1962–1968 general elections passed after the 1960 U.S. census. Since the passing of a 1965 law, senators in multi-member districts were elected to designated single-member positions beginning with the 1966 election, as opposed to plurality block voting which had been used previously. Incumbent senators in multi-member districts were assigned numbers based on their vote totals at their most recent general election, with the highest voted candidate getting position 1, second-highest position 2, and so on. This was Oregon's last state senate election to use a mix of single-member, multi-member, and floterial districts to elect senators, as for the 1972 election, all state legislators would be elected from single-member districts for the first time. Primary elections were held on May 26.

articles.title: Robin Boyd House I
articles.text:
Robin Boyd House I

The Robin Boyd House I, also known as the Former Robin Boyd House, is a house located at 664–666 Riversdale Road in Camberwell, in the City of Boroondara, in the inner eastern suburbs of Melbourne, in Victoria, Australia. 
The house was designed by Robin Boyd in 1946, which the Boyds moved into a year later. Boyd was known not only as an architect but also an architectural writer, educator and commentator. Born in 1919, as a member of the Boyd family, he came from a creative family background of sculptors, painters and architects. He and his wife Patricia occupied the Camberwell home with their two daughters for approximately twelve years, until 1959, when their Walsh Street home in South Yarra was completed.
Built between 1946 and 1947 on the traditional lands of the Wurundjeri people, the house was added to the Victorian Heritage Register on 2 October 1991 in recognition of its social, historical, and architectural significance; and was also added to a non-statutory list by the Victorian branch of the National Trust on 16 April 1987 and identified for possible future inclusion on the now defunct Register of the National Estate on an unknown date.


== History ==
The International Modernist-style house was built in two phases by Boyd. The house was originally located on the bank of a former creek. This creek, which ran along the eastern half of the site, was converted to an open horse-shoe drain and was subsequently enclosed and covered with fill. Hence, site for the house's construction was restricted to the western half of the site. The first stage was designed in 1946 and was completed in the following year. It is the first house built which Boyd designed himself. The second stage was designed in 1951 after Boyd had returned from his first overseas trip to Europe, made possible by winning the Haddon Scholarship, and was completed in 1952.


=== Heritage disputes ===
In 1973, the house was purchased by Maria Rajendran and her husband who, in 1975, further extended the dwelling to the south with a two-storey structure. As a result of these alterations to Boyd's 1952 additions, the original design was significantly altered. In 1987, the Victorian branch of the National Trust added the house to its non-statutory heritage list; and in November 1990 served an interim preservation order forbidding demolition or alteration of the house under the provisions of the Building Control Act 1981. articles.title: Hang Seng Credit Card Ltd v Tsang Nga Lee
articles.text:
Hang Seng Credit Card Ltd v Tsang Nga Lee

Hang Seng Credit Card Ltd v Tsang Nga Lee [2000] 3 HKLRD 33 is a landmark decision of the Court of First Instance of Hong Kong in which Yam J held that a clause in a credit card agreement obliging a defaulting cardholder to pay, on a full indemnity basis, all costs and expenses incurred by the card issuer in enforcing the agreement was unconscionable under the Unconscionable Contracts Ordinance (Cap. 458), and therefore unenforceable. The decision disposed of ten undefended debt actions brought in the High Court by card issuers and banks, and the court decided the question of unconscionability although none of the defendants had taken part in the proceedings, hearing argument instead from an amicus curiae. It has since been regarded as an exceptional case in which the court declined to give effect to a contractual agreement as to costs.
The judgment also remarked on the high effective rates of interest charged by the plaintiffs and declined to follow an earlier decision permitting claims of small value to be pursued in the High Court rather than in the District Court. Within three months the Hong Kong Monetary Authority issued proposals, later incorporated into the Code of Banking Practice, under which costs indemnity clauses in banking agreements were to be limited to costs of a reasonable amount that had been reasonably incurred.


== Background ==


=== The Unconscionable Contracts Ordinance ===
The Unconscionable Contracts Ordinance was the result of the 1990 report of the Law Reform Commission of Hong Kong on the sale of goods and supply of services, which recommended that a provision modelled on section 52A of the Australian Trade Practices Act 1974 be adopted to control harsh or unconscionable terms in consumer contracts for the sale of goods and the supply of services. Among the examples the Commission gave of terms that might be considered harsh or unconscionable was "the provision providing for a defaulting borrower to indemnify the costs of obtaining judgment against him" in credit card agreements. It observed that such provisions were "unpopular with the High Court Masters", and that solicitors acting for card issuers often sued in the High Court even where the debt was well within the jurisdiction of the District Court, so that the costs which the debtor was ordered to pay on a full indemnity basis were inflated.

articles.title: Sergejs Juhņevičs
articles.text:
Sergejs Juhņevičs

Sergejs Juhņevičs (born 1975) is a Latvian serial killer who committed three sexually-motivated murders in his hometown of Jelgava from 2008 to 2011. After his arrest, he confessed to three additional murders dating back to the 1990s, but investigators were unable to substaintiate them.
For his confirmed crimes, Juhņevičs was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment.


== Early life ==
Sergejs Juhņevičs was born in 1975 in Jelgava, the son of Polish immigrant Józef Juhņevičs and his Latvian wife. Despite the fact that Sergejs grew up in a stable family with no notable issues, he started displaying signs of a mental illness early on in his childhood. Due to this, as well as his struggles at school, his parents admitted him at the Ģintermuiža Psychoneurological Hospital in 1987.
During a psychiatric evaluation, he was diagnosed with schizophrenia and assigned a Group 2 disability status for psychiatric conditions. After that, Juhņevičs continued struggling with learning, and eventually stopped going to school or seeking work. Between 1987 and 2011, he was admitted to the hospital a total of 45 times due to his deteriorating mental health – during one such evaluation in 2005, his diagnosis of schizophrenia was reconfirmed.
According to investigators, Juhņevičs started to exhibit a heightened desire for women sometime in the late 2000s. However, women refused to start relationships with him due to his mental abnormalities, resulting in him frequently getting into conflicts with them.


== Murders ==


=== Confirmed murders ===
Juhņevičs' first known victim was killed on 12 July 2008. On that day, he met a 46-year-old woman and invited her for a drink, to which she agreed. After meeting up, the woman invited Juhņevičs to her apartment on Dobeles Street, where they continued drinking together. That same evening, Juhņevičs asked the woman to have sex with him, but she refused; he then flew into a rage and attacked her. During the attack, Juhņevičs beat the victim, then stabbed her several times in various parts of her body before ultimately strangling her to death.
On September 20 of that year, Juhņevičs committed his second murder. That evening, he met 45-year-old woman who was sitting on a bench near the "Tonuss" nightclub in Jelgava. The woman accepted his invitation to have a drink, after which she invited him to her garden shed. After several hours of drinking together, Juhņevičs began to sexually harass the woman, but she resisted him

articles.title: 5 St Sampson's Square
articles.text:
5 St Sampson's Square

5 St Sampson's Square is a Grade II listed building on St Sampson's Square in the city of York, England. Originating as an inn known as the Golden Lyon, it comprises an early 18th-century front range incorporating parts of an earlier 17th-century structure, with subsequent alterations in the 19th century. The building forms part of the Central Historic Core conservation area and is now occupied by the department store chain Browns of York, serving as its tea rooms.


== History ==
The building originated as an inn and dates from the second quarter of the 18th century, with later alterations. It was bought in 1729 by Thomas Crosby, an innholder, and was already known as the Golden Lyon. The front range is early 18th‑century, incorporating a rear block thought to be of early 17th‑century origin, with further changes made in the early and later 19th century.
In 1968 the site was included within the newly established Central Historic Core conservation area, and on 19 August 1971, No. 5 was designated a Grade II listed building. It forms part of a short row that includes the adjoining No. 6, also listed at Grade II, and stands next door but one to the Grade II* listed No. 7. All three buildings are now occupied by the department store chain Browns of York, with No. 5 serving as its tea rooms.


== Architecture ==


=== Exterior ===
The rear part of the building is timber‑framed. At the front, the ground floor is finished in colour‑washed stucco, with the upper storeys rendered and painted. A timber cornice marks the eaves, and the roofs are a mix of slate and pantiles. The façade has three storeys and three bays on a low plinth. The entrance, set slightly to the right, has a six‑panel door with an overlight and a surround of fluted half‑columns with a moulded top on scrolled brackets. All the windows are 12‑pane sashes in raised surrounds, with sills on the ground and second floors. A wide fascia runs below the first‑floor windows, and a plain band sits beneath the eaves, which are finished with a moulded cornice on small brackets. A wrought‑iron lantern hangs above the door.


=== Interior ===
The ground‑floor front room has 19th‑century boarded panelling at dado height, with the main ceiling beams and joists left visible. Further back, parts of the earlier timber structure can still be seen, including studwork on the left wall, and on the right the curved head of a former fireplace opening is exposed.

articles.title: Gnarpurt
articles.text:
Gnarpurt

Gnarpurt is a historic pastoral property and homestead complex near Lismore, in the Western District of Victoria, Australia. Established in the early 1840s, the estate was originally known as Little Corangamite or Kinloch Abbert before being renamed following its acquisition by the Manifold family in 1885. The property contains a bluestone homestead, an 1867 chapel, and a nineteenth-century woolshed and shearers' quarters. The chapel, measuring approximately 8 by 4.5 metres, is one of Victoria's smallest churches.


== History ==
Gnarpurt was established as a pastoral run in 1841 by Adam Swanston Robertson, initially in association with the Oliphant family. The property was originally known as Little Corangamite or Kinloch Abbert and formed part of the extensive pastoral holdings developed around Lake Corangamite during the early European settlement of the district. Robertson subsequently developed the station for sheep grazing, constructing a homestead and associated agricultural buildings.
Robertson undertook extensive improvements to the estate during the 1850s, including the planting of blue gum trees. A committed  Presbyterian, he also incorporated a purpose-built chapel room into the homestead, where he conducted religious services as a lay preacher. The room was distinguished by its vaulted ceiling and substantial exposed beams, providing a dedicated place of worship before the construction of a separate church building.
In 1867, Robertson commissioned the construction of a small bluestone chapel near the homestead for the use of the station's employees. The building was designed in the Gothic Revival style, drawing upon Robertson's recollections of rural churches in Scotland. A carved Celtic motif was incorporated above the entrance. Measuring approximately 8 metres in length and 4.5 metres in width, the chapel has been reputed to be the smallest church in Victoria.

Further improvements were undertaken in 1880, when architect and builder Alexander Hamilton was responsible for the construction of a bluestone woolshed and shearers' quarters. The large woolshed was capable of accommodating numerous shearers, and at its peak, the station reportedly processed approximately 15,000 merino sheep, with the woolshed containing as many as 20 shearing stands.
In 1885, the estate was purchased from Adam Swanston Robertson by members of the Manifold, who had extensive pastoral interests throughout the Western District. William Thomson Manifold initial

articles.title: Long Point Waterfowl
articles.text:
Long Point Waterfowl

The Long Point Waterfowl and Wetlands Research Program, known for much of its history as Long Point Waterfowl (LPW), is a Canadian research program that studies waterfowl, other wetland birds and their habitats in the lower Great Lakes. It takes its name from Long Point, a sand spit on the north shore of Lake Erie that is a major staging area for migrating waterfowl.
Begun in the 1980s as a research fund backed by a private hunting club and the federal government, it was run for much of its history by Bird Studies Canada. It briefly moved toward independence in 2015 and is today a program of Birds Canada, based in Port Rowan.


== History ==


=== Origins ===
The program grew out of the Long Point Waterfowl and Wetland Research Fund, established in the 1980s through an agreement between the Bluffs Club, a hunting club on Long Point, and Environment Canada. Its purpose was to develop scientific knowledge about waterfowl and wetlands in the Long Point region. Bird Studies Canada became a party to the agreement several years after it was signed.
Accounts of the program's founding date vary. An organizational history published in 2015 places its origins in the mid-1980s, while Western University, an early academic partner, dates its establishment to 1989.


=== Under Bird Studies Canada (c. 1990–2015) ===
For approximately 25 years, Long Point Waterfowl operated under the administration of Bird Studies Canada. Bird Studies Canada managed the program's finances and administration, employed its staff, and retained oversight through its board of directors. A separate Long Point Waterfowl board provided direction on program policy.
Wildlife biologist Scott Petrie was appointed executive director in 1997 and led the organization for 18 years.
During his tenure, Long Point Waterfowl strengthened its relationship with Western University. Petrie held an adjunct academic appointment, supervised student research, and taught the university's undergraduate course in wildlife ecology and management.
Petrie was also a director-at-large of the Ontario Federation of Anglers and Hunters, which recognized him with its Jack O'Dette Conservation Leadership Award in 2014.


=== Attempted independence (2014–2015) ===
In November 2014, the Bird Studies Canada board decided to end its administrative arrangement with Long Point Waterfowl, concluding that the program had grown sufficiently to operate independently.

articles.title: Jake Staines
articles.text:
Jake Staines

Jake Andrew Staines (born 13 July 1997) is an international field and indoor hockey player from Australia.
He competes in Hockey Australia's premier domestic competition, the ONE Active Hockey One.


== Personal life ==
Staines was born in Goulburn, New South Wales. His twin brother, Ben, is also an international field and indoor hockey player.


== Australian leagues ==
Throughout his career, Staines has competed in four premier Australian leagues. He is currently competing in the Hockey One and the Hockey WA Premier One competitions, and previously competed in the Australian Hockey League (AHL) and the Capital League 1 in Canberra.
Staines has been a member of the Canberra Chill in the Hockey One since the league's inception in 2019. Prior to this, he represented the Canberra Lakers in the AHL from 2015 to 2018, when the league dissolved.
During his youth and into his senior career, he represented the Goulburn Geckos in the Capital League 1 and Goulburn District Hockey Association competitions.
In 2022 he made the move to Perth to compete in the Hockey WA Premier One competition following his inclusion in the Australian Development Squad. In the league, he competes for Melville City HC.


== National teams ==


=== Under–21 ===
Staines has also represented Australia at international level. He was a member of the Australian U–21 side, the Burras, at the 2018 Sultan of Johor Cup. At the tournament, the team won bronze.


=== Indoor ===
He has also been a member of the Australian Indoor team since 2023. During his time with the squad, he has appeared at the 2023 and 2025 editions of the FIH Indoor World Cup in Pretoria and Poreč, the 2024 Indoor Oceania Cup in Canberra, and the 2025 Nkosi Cup in Cape Town.

articles.title: Huawei Mate 90
articles.text:
Huawei Mate 90

The Huawei Mate 90 series is a line of smartphones manufactured by Huawei, unveiled at an autumn launch event in Shanghai on October 1, 2026. The series comprises five models: the Mate 90, Mate 90 Pro, Mate 90 Pro Max, Mate 90 Pro Max Collector's Edition and Mate 90 RS Ultimate Design. Across 14 memory and storage configurations, prices range from CNY 5,999 (about US$890) for the base Mate 90 to CNY 18,999 (about US$2,830) for the top-specification Mate 90 RS Ultimate Design; Huawei has not announced a launch outside China.
As with earlier Mate series phones, the launch emphasised Huawei's in-house Kirin chips, developed by its HiSilicon subsidiary amid continued United States restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to the company. Huawei consumer business chief Richard Yu said the top-tier chip's "LogicFolding" architecture, which restructures chip wiring vertically to allow denser processing and shorter signal paths, was developed specifically in response to restricted access to advanced manufacturing technology. Yu also said rising memory component prices had added more than US$200 to the cost of each handset, and that Huawei's margins were under pressure as a result.


== Specifications ==


=== Chipset ===
The base Mate 90 uses the Kirin 9030, which Huawei says delivers 27% higher overall performance than the Mate 80. The Mate 90 Pro uses the Kirin 9035, a chip the company says is tuned to balance performance and power consumption, with battery life improved by 18% over the Mate 80 Pro. The Mate 90 Pro Max, Pro Max Collector's Edition and RS Ultimate Design use the Kirin 9050 Pro, which Huawei says is 31% faster overall than the previous generation and doubles on-device AI computing performance; the chip uses the LogicFolding architecture with an inter-die bandwidth of 125 terabytes per second. GSMArena reported that the Mate 90 Pro Max's base 12 GB RAM configuration instead uses the standard Kirin 9050, reserving the 9050 Pro for higher-memory configurations and the RS Ultimate Design. Huawei's performance figures are drawn from its own testing; as of October 2026, independent reviewers had not published benchmark results confirming them.


=== Display ===
The base Mate 90 has a 6.75-inch flat OLED display at a resolution of 1280×2832 pixels and a 120 Hz refresh rate. The Mate 90 Pro and higher models use a second-generation "Linglong" display with peak brightness of up to 12,000 nits at 1% average picture level (APL); the Mate

articles.title: Bridge Hotel, Hawthorn
articles.text:
Bridge Hotel, Hawthorn

The Bridge Hotel, and at one stage called the Bowling Green Hotel, was a hotel for a short period and then converted into a house, since 1866, located at 155 Church Street in Hawthorn, in the City of Boroondara, in the inner eastern suburbs of Melbourne, in Victoria, Australia.
Built as a hotel in 1854 on the traditional lands of the Wurundjeri people, the building was added to the Victorian Heritage Register on 16 May 1979 in recognition of its historical and architectural significance; and was also added to non-statutory lists by the Victorian branch of the National Trust on 21 April 1976 and the now defunct Register of the National Estate on 21 October 1980.


== Description ==
The former Bridge Hotel, a two-storey stuccoed-brick building, was constructed in about 1854 for the publican James Connell, one of Hawthorn's early settlers. Subsequently called the Bowling Green Hotel, it was converted to a private residence in 1866. The building incorporates a variety of styles including the Victorian Classical and Gothic. The building was built on bluestone footings, with a corrugated iron hipped roof, a detailed porch that faces the main facade, which has sash windows, string courses and a parapet. The buttresses and timber verandah are unusual features.
The former Bridge Hotel is important because of its association with the early settlement patterns of Hawthorn, one of Melbourne's rural outposts in the middle of the nineteenth century. Built in response to the construction of a timber bridge over the Yarra River in 1851, the former hotel illustrates early settlement patterns in the Village of Hawthorn prior to the arrival of the railway in 1861, and the movement of commercial interests closer to the station. The former hotel, which externally exhibits the principal characteristics of an 1850s public house, is important in demonstrating early Colonial hotel design and construction methods.
The renovated house with modern amenities sold in March 2024 for c.A$3 million. As of 2026, the four-bedroom two-storey house was leased, set on 840 square metres (9,000 sq ft), described as having an elegant mahogany and cast iron staircase, a living room with bay window that overlooked a private garden, a large dining room, study, and open-plan kitchen and dining area, with modern appliances. articles.title: Catch You If You Fall
articles.text:
Catch You If You Fall

"Catch You If You Fall" is a song by English singer-songwriter, drummer and model, Florrie. It was released on 28 August 2026 as the fourth single from her second studio album, Magic for a While, through Xenomania UK Limited and BMG.


== Background ==
"Catch You If You Fall" was written by Florrie Arnold, Brian Higgins, Ben Taylor, and Clara McHugh, with Arnold, Higgins, and Taylor also serving as producers. Described by The Guardian as "pensive balladry", it was written from the perspective of Florrie as a child, and pays tribute to her late uncle Martin, who was diagnosed with progressive multiple sclerosis as a teenager. According the song press release, Florrie spent the first four years of her life living with him and continued to visit him regularly until his death. She described the song as a promise to be there for him and a reflection of the significance he held in her life.

"Uncle Mart was diagnosed with MS when he was 17 and never moved away from home, so my nan became his full-time carer and they lived together in a little bungalow in Bristol. I spent five days a week with them until I was four and then went every day after school as I got older. I watched him struggle a lot as his MS progressed, he was in a wheelchair and had lost the use of half his body, but he was never defeated by it, and somehow he stayed so positive right up until the end. I loved helping him, and I think I absorbed all of the love my nan had for him too, because she essentially gave up her life to look after him. They showed me what real love and resilience look like, and I think so much of the empathy I have now comes from growing up with them. Mart taught me not to take anything for granted and to keep life in perspective, because if he could remain positive through everything he had to deal with, then I think there must always be a way through."


== Promotion ==
The song was released on 28 August 2026 as the fourth single from Florrie's second studio album, Magic for a While, on which it appears as the fifth track. An accompanying video featuring Florrie performing the song live with her band at Peckham Liberal Club was released on her YouTube channel.

articles.title: Khatmiyya in Eritrea
articles.text:
Khatmiyya in Eritrea

The Khatmiyya (Arabic: الختمية; Tigre: ኸትሚያ) is the largest and most influential Sufi order in Eritrea. It spread into the region in the early 19th century and became closely tied to the Egyptian and later the Italian colonial administrations, before losing much of its influence in the second half of the 20th century.


== Spread in the 19th century ==
The founder of the order, Muhammad 'Uthman al-Mirghani, made three missionary tours that reached the Eritrean region between about 1817 and the 1830s. In western Eritrea he initiated followers among the Halanqa, Sabderat, Algeden, Beni-Amer, Barya and Marya, and in the Sahel and Semhar he appointed local representatives (khalifas and khalifat al-khulafa'). The order expanded by attaching existing local religious figures and holy lineages to its network, a method that allowed communities to keep their existing social and political structures. This contrasted with the methods of its main local rival, the Ad Shaykh holy family.
The order's growth in the region accompanied the Egyptian conquest of Sudan from 1820, and it kept good relations with the Egyptian administration, especially after Egypt took Kassala in 1840. After the founder's death in 1852, his son Muhammad al-Hasan al-Mirghani (1819–1869), who had established the order's headquarters at al-Saniyya near Kassala around 1840, led its northern and eastern Sudanese branch, and under him the ruling class of the Habab came under greater Khatmiyya influence. In the 1860s and 1870s Muhammad 'Uthman Taj al-Sirr al-Mirghani (1849/50–1903) lived among the Habab and later among Saho-speaking groups, and did more than any other family member to consolidate the order in the Sahel, Semhar and Akele Guzai. After Egypt took over Massawa in 1865, the order gradually overtook the 'Ad Shaykh in the region, and at least eight mosques in and around Massawa came to be associated with it.


== Mahdist period and Italian rule ==
The Khatmiyya opposed the Mahdist movement of the 1880s, while leading elements of the 'Ad Shaykh supported it. Contrary to an earlier view that Sayyid Hashim al-Mirghani established the order at Massawa in 1860, Italian archival sources indicate that he settled there permanently only in April 1885, after fleeing Kassala during the Mahdist uprising. articles.title: Bet Asgede
articles.text:
Bet Asgede

The Bet Asgede (Tigre: ቤት ኣስገዴ; Arabic: بيت أسقدي), also spelled Bayt Asgade or Bet Asgäde, are a confederation of Tigre-speaking groups in northern Eritrea, made up of three branches: the Habab, the 'Ad Takles (also 'Ad Tekles) and the 'Ad Temariam (also 'Ad Tamaryam). They are traditionally associated with the Sahel region of northern Eritrea. Historically they were pastoralists, and their society was divided between a ruling aristocracy and a subordinate tigre class.


== Origins ==
According to their traditions, the Bet Asgede migrated to the Sahel from Akkele Guzay in the Eritrean highlands, perhaps in the 16th century, when the region was devastated by the religious wars of that period (see Ethiopian–Adal war). Miran cites them as an example of groups whose very formation was linked to migration into the contested borderland between the Ethiopian state and the Funj Sultanate.


== Relations with the Nayebs ==
The Habab were among the largest and wealthiest groups under the authority of the Nayebs of Hirgigo, and their submission made tribute a more important source of Nayeb revenue. The Nayebs confirmed the Habab chief, the kantibay; on one occasion a newly elected kantibay gave the Nayeb 100 camels, 100 cows, 100 goats and 100 woollen blankets in return for confirmation. After the Ottomans reasserted control over the coast in 1849, the old flexible arrangements were replaced in the early 1850s by fixed annual cash payments. The Habab were assessed at 3,000 thalers, and the 'Ad Takles and 'Ad Temariam at 1,000 each. In June 1850 a combined force of Ottoman soldiers and Nayeb militia met stiff resistance in Habab territory.


== Conversion to Islam ==
The Bet Asgede had followed local forms of Christianity before converting to Islam between the 1820s and the 1850s. The main agents of the change were the Ad Shaykh holy family and agents of the Nayebs. The preaching of the 'Ad Shaykh leader Shaykh al-Amin b. Hamid b. Naf'utay first attracted the subordinate tigre class, whose conversion and intermarriage with the holy family undermined their dependence on the Bet Asgede aristocracy. The aristocracy followed after al-Amin married the daughter of their kantibay. His grandson Shaykh Muhammad b. 'Ali b. al-Amin (d. 1877), based at Emberemi near Massawa, converted many Habab. The 'Ad Mu'allim holy clan served especially among the 'Ad Temariam, and the 'Ad Darqi among the Habab. Miran notes that how these nominally Christian communities converted

articles.title: Treva Brown
articles.text:
Treva Brown

Treva Brown is an American chemist and STEM advocate and specializes in microbial corrosion on Navy ships.


== Early life and education ==
Brown is a native of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, attending and graduating Baton Rouge Magnet High School. Brown credits the mentoring received from a physics teacher for persuading her to study science, stating that "as a young Black girl, I never thought I deserved a spot at the table when it came to being an integral part of the scientific community".
In 2011, Brown earned her Bachelor of Science from Louisiana State University followed by her PhD in chemistry from University of New Orleans in 2017.


== Career ==
Brown joined the United States Naval Research Laboratory at the Stennis Space Center in 2018. She studies organisms that contribute to corrosion on metal and microbial corrosion on Navy ships as well as biodegradation and corrosion mechanisms. Brown also helped investigate a fungi that caused deterioration in military tents forcing the tents to collapse.
Brown is a member of the Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority and the chemistry fraternity Alpha Chi Sigma.


== Advocacy ==
Brown is an advocate of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics, having organized outreach events for elementary and college level students. She cites the value of introducing young students to a scientist "who looks like them" in her outreach activities.


=== Beauty pageants ===
Brown has been the winner of several beauty pageants, including Miss Black Louisiana, Miss Black Empowerment Louisiana, and Miss Black St. Tammany Parish. Brown cites these pageants as a "means to an end", allowing her to engage with minority communities and promote the topic of science.


== Awards and honors ==
In 2017, Brown received the Winifred Burks-Houck Professional Leadership Award
In 2021, Brown received the Women of Color in STEM Community Service Award
In 2025, Brown received the Young Leadership Council Role Model Award which honors "business, community, and civic leaders"

articles.title: Ad Shaykh
articles.text:
Ad Shaykh

The 'Ad Shaykh (Tigre: ዐድ ሼኽ; Arabic: عد شيخ), also spelled Ad Sheikh, are a Muslim holy family of Eritrea that grew into a large and wealthy Tigre-speaking tribal group. In the first half of the 19th century they were among the most important agents in the conversion of the Tigre-speaking societies of the Eritrean lowlands to Islam. Their influence declined after the Khatmiyya Sufi order, backed by the Italian colonial government, displaced them in the early 20th century.


== Origins ==
The family traces its descent to a sharif named Husayn from Mecca. Like many holy clans of the region, the 'Ad Shaykh based their religious standing on claims of descent from the Prophet and on the possession of baraka, a spiritual power believed to be inherited. They first gained wide influence in the Sahel region of northern Eritrea in the early 19th century, mainly through the preaching and reputed miracles of Shaykh al-Amin b. Hamid b. Naf'utay.


== Expansion and conversions ==
Between the 1820s and the 1850s, the 'Ad Shaykh and agents of the Nayebs of Hirgigo converted to Islam the Bet Asgede (the Habab, 'Ad Takles and 'Ad Temariam), the Mensa', the Marya, the Bet Juk and parts of the Bilen, who had previously followed local forms of Christianity. The family worked closely with the Nayebs, to whom many of these groups paid tribute. They also drew followers into the Qadiriyya Sufi order, chiefly among the Marya and Mensa', although little is known about this aspect of their activity.
The Ad Shaykh attracted whole families from the subordinate tigre class, the serf-like stratum of Tigre-speaking pastoral societies. Conversion and intermarriage with the holy family weakened the dependence of these families on their aristocratic masters; among the Bet Asgede, the aristocracy itself followed after Shaykh al-Amin married the daughter of their kantibay (chief). Miran describes this as a form of social revolution that challenged traditional chiefs, including those of the Beni-Amer. The new adherents were absorbed into the family, which grew into an influential and wealthy independent group.
The family later divided and spread across the western, northern and eastern lowlands of Eritrea. Some branches settled in the Anseba and Barka valleys, others remained in the Sahel, and others moved north as far as Tokar in Sudan. Two of Shaykh al-Amin's sons settled among the Garabit and the Faydab under the patronage of the Beni-Amer.

articles.title: Anting West railway station
articles.text:
Anting West railway station

Anting West station (Chinese: 安亭西站), formerly known as Anting station, is located in Anting, Jiading district, Shanghai, China. It is a station on the Beijing–Shanghai railway and the Shanghai–Suzhou–Nantong railway. The station was put into operation on 1 July 2020. It handles passenger services for some trains running via the Shanghai–Suzhou–Nantong railway. About 10 trains stop there every day. In the first month of operation, the average number of passengers arriving and departing each day was about 500. It is expected to become a major terminal station for non-high-speed trains.


== Summary ==

Construction of the station, as an intermediate station on the Shanghai-Nantong Railway, began in August 2014. At the end of 2014, it was confirmed that the station would handle passenger services in a report entitled "Adjustment of Relevant Projects of the Shanghai–Nantong Railway from Shanghai Boundary to Fengbang Section". However, due to issues such as land acquisition and property division along the line, as well as the fact that the construction section would affect the operation of the Beijing–Shanghai railway, the amount of work was greatly increased compared to the original proposal. During the construction of the station, the trains on the Beijing–Shanghai railway were limited to a speed of 45 km/h (28 mph) when passing through this section.
In order to carry out the sheet pile structure construction of the Shanghai–Suzhou–Nantong railway on both sides of the Beijing–Shanghai railway, the double-track bypass line of the Beijing–Shanghai railway was put into operation at Anting West station at the end of October 2016. The original Beijing–Shanghai railway was closed and the trains used the bypass line to pass through the station. In early June 2017, the up line was realigned; the down line was realigned on 6 July. After the realignment was completed, Anting station was closed, and only tracks 1 and 2 were opened to ensure the passage of trains in order to meet the access and renovation of the Shanghai–Suzhou–Nantong railway.
In January 2019, the railway department put out a tender for the construction of the Anting West station building. Construction of the building started in March 2019 and was scheduled to be completed in April 2020. articles.title: Edwin B. Self
articles.text:
Edwin B. Self

Edwin Byron Self (1 May 1896 – 9 May 1980) was an American playwright, novelist, and businessman.


== Biography ==
The son of William E. Self and Sallie Self (née McCleane), Edwin Byron Self was born in Lexington, Kentucky on 1 May 1896. His father worked as a bookkeeper for the Tattersall's stables in Lexington. He received his primary school education at Harrison School in his native city. He started working for newspapers after completing the 7th grade; getting his first job with a paper in Knoxville, Tennessee. In his early life he worked in several different newspaper jobs; beginning as a "galley boy" and working his way up to business manager.
At the time of his father's death in 1916 Edwin was employed in the advertising department of The Lexington Leader. He took a job with The Cincinnati Post which was then part of the Scripps-McRae League of Newspapers, and there established the advertising service department. He married Elizabeth Christine Fundus in Cincinnati, Ohio on 10 Nov 1917. Elizabeth was also an employee at The Cincinnati Post, and they met while working together.
Self relocated to Dayton, Ohio in c. 1921 where he worked as a sales promotion and advertising manager for the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company. He translated Gabriela Zapolska's The Morality of Mrs. Dulska from Polish into English for a 1923 staging of the play at the Metropolitan Theater in Cleveland. He was the author of three plays that were staged on Broadway: Junk (1927, Garrick Theatre), Two Strange Women (1933, Little Theatre), and The Distant City (1941, Longacre Theatre). His play She Waar Different was staged at the Red Barn Theatre in Locust Valley, New York in 1932.
In 1930 Self relocated to Chicago where he established his own advertising agency. He left Chicago in 1937 when he was appointed advertising and merchandising manager for the Joseph Schlitz Brewing Company in Milwaukee. His novel, Limbo City, was published in 1946. That same year he moved to Los Angeles, California when he was appointed vice-president and chairman of Makelim Associates.  In the 1950s he worked as the director of advertising for the television program Schlitz Playhouse of Stars. His play Half a Miracle was staged at the Las Palmas Theatre in Los Angeles in 1969 with a cast led by Jack Bailey and Florence Lake.
Edwin B. Self died on May 9, 1980, in Los Angeles. His son was the American television executive and producer William Edwin Self.

articles.title: Theun Busser
articles.text:
Theun Busser

Theun Busser (born 10 December 1952) is a Dutch former marathon speed skater who finished fifth in the 1985 Elfstedentocht. Further, he won the Alternative Elfstedentocht twice (in 1985 and 1986) and earned three medals at the Dutch National Championships on artificial ice.


== Career ==
Busser was the first to cross the finish line after the lead group, which included the winner, Evert van Benthem, who won the sprint against Henri Ruitenberg, Jos Niesten, and Jan Kooiman. He finished 2 minutes and 23 seconds behind the lead group. Wim Westerveld crossed the line two seconds after him. He himself was disappointed with his fifth-place finish, which he attributed in part to a minor muscle injury. "At the start, I tore a small muscle in my leg," Busser said of the incident. "It held me back", I couldn't put in the necessary burst of effort, and as a result, I missed the decisive move."
Busser's nickname was "the Walrus", owing to the style of his moustache. He was not fond of skating on artificial ice rinks. "Regarding this former conscientious objector of Frisian descent, the story goes that he is too lazy to train and only shows up at the artificial ice rink when he needs to take a shower," Het Vrije Volk wrote about him in 1985. "In a winter like this one, however, training outdoors happens quite naturally, and Busser is getting into better shape than usual."
On 16 February 1985 – five days before the thirteenth Elfstedentocht – Busser won a speed skating marathon on artificial ice in his hometown of Utrecht. He finished ahead of Jan Kooiman (third) and Evert van Benthem (fifth), thereby besting two skaters who would go on to be part of the lead group in Leeuwarden.
On 2 March 1985, nine days after the "Tour of Tours" (de Tocht der Tochten, that is, the Elfstedentocht), Busser won the Alternative Elfstedentocht on Kallavesi, near the Finnish city of Kuopio. He defeated Jan Kooiman in the final sprint. Their finishing time was more than five minutes faster than what they had managed in the actual Elfstedentocht, a difference arising from the Finnish venue's lack of as much need for the participants to walk or klune. Busser viewed his victory as a form of redemption for his disappointing fifth-place finish in the "real" Elfstedentocht. Evert van Benthem, the winner of that race, did not participate in the alternative event. articles.title: Jen Fawkes
articles.text:
Jen Fawkes

Jen Fawkes is an American fiction writer. She has won the Pinch Award in Fiction (2019), John Gardner Memorial Fiction Prize (2019), Press 53 Award for Short Fiction (2020) for Tales the Devil Told Me, and the Phillip H. McMath Post-Publication Book Award (Fiction) for Mannequin and Wife. Her debut story collection, Mannequin and Wife (2020), was a finalist for the Shirley Jackson Award for Best Single-Author Collection.


== Career ==
Fawkes's short fiction has appeared in One Story, Lit Hub, The Iowa Review, Crazyhorse and Best Small Fictions, and has won prizes including the 2019 Pinch Award in Fiction and the 2019 John Gardner Memorial Fiction Prize from Harpur Palate.
Mannequin and Wife, published by LSU Press in September 2020, collects stories that range across psychological and magical realism, examining relationships between mothers and children, spouses, and mentors and protégés. It was a finalist for the 2020 Shirley Jackson Award for Best Single-Author Collection and won the 2023 Phillip H. McMath Post-Publication Book Award in fiction.
Tales the Devil Told Me won the 2020 Press 53 Award for Short Fiction and was published by Press 53 in October 2021. Its stories reimagine fairy tales and literary classics from the perspective of villains and minor characters, including Rumpelstiltskin, Medusa and the witch from "Hansel and Gretel". It was a finalist for the 2022 World Fantasy Award for Single-Author Collection. Reviewing it for Locus, Rich Horton described the stories as witty, dark, extravagant and savage.
Fawkes's debut novel, Daughters of Chaos, was published by the Overlook Press, an imprint of Abrams Books, on July 9, 2024. Set in Nashville during the American Civil War. Kirkus Reviews called it a "dazzling feminist tale" and the novel received a starred review from Publishers Weekly. Horton, writing in Black Gate, called it "a first rate first novel".

articles.title: Zach Barlev
articles.text:
Zach Barlev

Zachary Barlev (born June 23, 2003) is an American professional football offensive lineman for the Ottawa Redblacks of the Canadian Football League (CFL). He played college football for the Illinois Fighting Illini and Old Dominion Monarchs. 


== Early life ==
Barlev was born on June 23, 2003. He attended Plainfield East High School in Plainfield, Illinois, where he played baseball, football, golf, track and field and wrestling.


== College career ==
Barlev played college football for the Illinois Fighting Illini from 2021 to 2023 and Old Dominion Monarchs from 2024 to 2025. He redshirted his first year and only played in one game in the nine-overtime victory at Penn State. The next two seasons, Barlev played in 25 games on special teams. On December 1, 2023, he entered the transfer portal.
On December 15, 2023, Barlev committed to Old Dominion University. In 2024, he started all 12 games, three at left guard and nine at left tackle, earning third-team All-Sun Belt honors. The following year, Barlev started all 13 games at left tackle and was named to the first-team All-Sun Belt team.


== Professional career ==

After going unselected in the 2026 NFL draft, Barlev signed with the Ottawa Redblacks of the Canadian Football League (CFL) as an undrafted free agent. On May 31, he was signed to the practice roster. On August 6, Barlev was elevated to the active roster and made his first CFL start on August 14 against the Winnipeg Blue Bombers at right tackle. On September 7, he was moved back to the practice roster. On September 16, Barlev was promoted again to the active roster. On October 15, he was moved to the reserve roster to recover from an arm injury.
