articles.title: R (Hoareau and Bancoult) v Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs
articles.text:
R (Hoareau and Bancoult) v Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs

R (Hoareau and Bancoult) v Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs, also known as Bancoult (No 5), was a judicial review in the courts of England and Wales of the United Kingdom government's decision, announced on 16 November 2016, not to support the resettlement of the Chagossians in the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) and instead to fund a support package of about £40 million over ten years for Chagossians where they now live. The claimants were Solange Hoareau, a Chagossian born on Diego Garcia who was removed to Seychelles, and Olivier Bancoult, the chair of the Chagos Refugee Group.
A Divisional Court of Singh LJ and Carr J dismissed both claims on 8 February 2019. It held that the decision was rational, that the European Convention on Human Rights did not apply to the BIOT, that the public sector equality duty had been met, and that the 2015 consultation and the support package were lawful. It ended by observing that "Judicial review is not, and should not be regarded as, politics by another means."
The claimants appealed, relying in part on the 2019 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice and United Nations General Assembly Resolution 73/295, both issued after the Divisional Court's judgment. On 30 July 2020 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that neither the opinion nor the resolution decided anything about a right of resettlement, and that they did not bring the Convention into play or enlarge the common law right of abode. In 2026 the High Court treated the issues decided in the case as settled.


== Background ==


=== Expulsion and earlier litigation ===
The claims had their roots in the removal of the whole Chagossian population from the Chagos Archipelago between 1966 and 1972; no Chagossian has lived on the islands since 1973. The removal made way for a United States military base on Diego Garcia. The Court of Appeal noted that "no one now contends" that the expulsion was anything other than wrongful, that the claims arising from it had been compromised and paid, and that those settlements had not removed the wish of at least some Chagossians to live on the islands. In 1982 the United Kingdom paid £4 million to the Ilois Trust Fund in Mauritius in full and final settlement, but no payment was ever made to the Chagossians in Seychelles.

articles.title: Halid Doltmurziev
articles.text:
Halid Doltmurziev

Halid Doltmurziev (Georgian: ჰალიდ დოლტმურზიევი; Russian: Халид Долтмурзиев; born 22 May 2007) is a footballer who plays as a forward for Dinamo. Born in Belgium, he is a Georgia youth international.


== Early life ==
Doltmurziev was born on 22 May 2007 in Nieuwpoort, Belgium and is of Russian descent through his parents. The son of Umalat, he has two brothers. Growing up, he started playing football at the age of three.


== Club career ==
As a youth player, Doltmurziev joined the youth academy of Belgian side FA Nieuwpoort at the age of four. Following his stint there, he joined the youth academy of Cercle Brugge in Belgium in 2013, where he received interest from the youth academy of Belgian outfit Anderlecht.
Nine years later, he joined the youth academy of Club Brugge in Belgium, where he captained the club's under-16 team. Subsequently, he joined the youth academy of Georgian team Dinamo in 2025, where he played in the UEFA Youth League and was promoted to the club's senior team the same year.


== International career ==
Doltmurziev is a Georgia youth international and has represented the country internationally at under-17, under-19 and under-21 levels. Eligible to represent Russia internationally through his parents, he is eligible to represent Belgium internationally, having been born in the country. 
During the spring of 2024, he played for the Georgia national under-17 football team for 2024 UEFA European Under-17 Championship qualification. In 2026, he played for the Georgia national under-21 football team for 2027 UEFA European Under-21 Championship qualification.


== Style of play ==
Doltmurziev plays as a forward and is right-footed. Georgian news website Crystalsport wrote in 2023 that he "is very aggressive on the pitch, plays well with both feet... his natural position is center forward, but he sometimes plays as a left winger".

articles.title: 2026 FBI data breach
articles.text:
2026 FBI data breach

The 2026 FBI data breach was a cyberattack on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's recruitment portal, FBIJobs.gov, in September 2026, in which the extortion group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal data on nearly all current and former FBI employees and job applicants. The FBI designated the matter a cybersecurity incident on September 22, 2026, and later attributed the intrusion to a contractor's failure to apply a security patch to an Oracle PeopleSoft system; the contractor, reported to be employed by Accenture, was removed. Current and former officials described the breach as one of the most serious compromises of bureau data in years, citing counterintelligence risks to agents and their families. By mid-October 2026, authorities in the Netherlands, Jordan, and the United States had arrested or detained three people in connection with the investigation.


== Background ==
ShinyHunters is a cybercriminal extortion group, active since 2019, that steals data from organizations and then threatens to release it publicly unless a ransom is paid. On May 15, 2026, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center issued a public service announcement describing the group's tactics after its attack on the Canvas learning platform; the advisory said the group harassed victims and their families and sometimes exaggerated its access. In June 2026, Google's Mandiant reported that ShinyHunters was exploiting a vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft, CVE-2026-35273, against more than 100 organizations, chiefly in education; Oracle issued a security alert and fixes the same month.
The incident was the second reported compromise of an FBI system in 2026. In March, the bureau disclosed it was investigating suspicious activity on an internal system holding surveillance and investigative information, and a pro-Iranian group published personal documents it said came from an account belonging to Director Kash Patel.


== Breach ==
According to the group and to reporting by 404 Media, the intrusion began on the night of September 21, 2026, when attackers exploited a PeopleSoft server used by FBI recruiters and then moved into FBI-managed Amazon Web Services GovCloud infrastructure. Mandiant later assessed that the attackers had bypassed a recommended web-application-firewall rule for CVE-2026-35273 using URL encoding. articles.title: Ding Dong Merrily on Live
articles.text:
Ding Dong Merrily on Live

"Ding Dong Merrily on Live" is the 70th episode of the British sitcom Not Going Out, originally broadcast on 21 December 2018 as part of the show's ninth series. Written by series creator and lead actor Lee Mack and Daniel Peak and directed by Nick Wood, the Christmas special is the only episode of the show to be broadcast live.
In the episode, husband and wife Lee (Mack) and Lucy (Sally Bretton) put on a Christmas variety show for the benefit of their children's school. Mack wrote the episode to include difficult performances, and it features self-referential humour. He then wished for all episodes of Not Going Out to be live, but instead introduced episodes set in real time.


== Plot ==
Husband and wife Lee (Lee Mack) and Lucy (Sally Bretton) are organising "Ding Dong Merrily on Live", a variety performance to benefit their children's school. After other acts pull out, Lee hires Juan (Tom Benedict Knight), a knife thrower.
When the couple meet Juan, he says that he wants Lucy to be his assistant, and that he has seduced all his previous assistants. Lee's friend Toby (Hugh Dennis) advises him to write false negative reviews of Juan, to put Lucy off. After being convinced that Juan is an incompetent alcoholic, Lucy dismisses him from the show. It turns out that Juan has also been dismissed from a contract on a cruise liner, upsetting his wife who is recovering from cancer.
Feeling guilty, Lee invites Juan to the show and hires him again, but Toby walks in and inadvertently reveals that Lee left the false reviews, causing Juan to quit. Lee sends Toby and wife Anne (Abigail Cruttenden) on stage to sing "The Elements", which results in the couple singing improvised lyrics and arguing. For the finale, Lee dresses as Juan and throws the knives, with Lucy as his assistant. Later in bed, Lucy pleas for them not to do a live Christmas special again, and Lee proposes that next time will be on ice skates.


== Production ==
In March 2018, while promoting the ninth series of Not Going Out, Mack told Steve Wright of BBC Radio 2 that he was planning a live episode. He said that he used to consider live episodes to be self-indulgent as they did not aid actors' performances. Mack pointed out that as a stand-up comedian he could improvise if he forgot his lines, but factors such as camera and microphone control on a sitcom would complicate that; he revealed that he used hidden notes on set to remember lines. The BBC had broadcast a live episode

articles.title: Hôtel de Ville, La Chapelle-sur-Erdre
articles.text:
Hôtel de Ville, La Chapelle-sur-Erdre

The Hôtel de Ville (French pronunciation: [otɛl də vil], City Hall) is a municipal building in La Chapelle-sur-Erdre, Loire-Atlantique, in western France, standing on Rue Olivier-de-Sesmaisons.


== History ==
Following the French Revolution, the new town council initially met in the home of the mayor at the time. This arrangement continued until 1844 when the council led by the mayor, Anselme François Fleury, decided to establish a combined town hall and school. The site they selected was on the north side of what is now Rue François-Clouet.
The building, which was set back from the road, was designed in the neoclassical style and built in ashlar stone. The design involved a symmetrical main frontage of three bays facing onto the street. The central bay, which was rusticated, featured a square-headed doorway with an open pediment on the ground floor, a casement window with a cornice on the first floor, and a pediment above. The outer bays were fenestrated by casement windows with cornices on the ground floor and by casement windows with moulded surrounds on the first floor. There were pilasters at the corners of the building supporting the main pediment, which featured a small semi-circular window in the tympanum. After it was no longer required for municipal use, the building became home to the Centre Communal d'Action Sociale (CCAS).
In 1977, following significant population growth, the council led by the mayor, Donatien de Sesmaisons, decided to acquire a more substantial municipal building. The property they selected was the Château de la Gilière, which was set in a substantial parkland. The château had been commissioned as a private residence by a medical doctor, Adolphe Ollivery. It was designed in the neoclassical style, built in brick with a cement render finish and completed in 1840.
The design involved a symmetrical main frontage of seven bays, with the end bays slightly recessed and surmounted by Châteauesque-style roofs. The central bay featured a Venetian-style doorway on the ground floor, a casement window on the first floor, and a segmental-headed window with a pediment at attic level. The other bays were fenestrated by round-headed windows with moulded surrounds on the ground floor and by square-headed windows with moulded surrounds on the first floor.

articles.title: Enforcement and Compliance History Online
articles.text:
Enforcement and Compliance History Online

Enforcement and Compliance History Online (ECHO) is a public website and database operated by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). It brings together compliance and enforcement information for more than one million regulated facilities across the United States. ECHO lets users search facilities, find EPA enforcement cases, analyze compliance and enforcement data, use data services, and send information to the EPA.
ECHO shows how facilities are regulated, when they were inspected, whether violations were found, and whether enforcement action followed. The data cover permits, inspection and evaluation dates and findings, violations, enforcement actions, and penalties.


== History ==


=== Pilot (2002) ===
The EPA released ECHO as a pilot tool on 20 November 2002 and asked the public for comment. At launch it gave access to the compliance records of more than 800,000 regulated facilities, including nearly 60,000 in New England. The tool was built with the Environmental Council of the States (ECOS), the national association of state and territorial environmental commissioners.
The pilot combined EPA and state compliance information for facilities regulated under the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. Data were updated monthly and covered a two-year period. Use grew over the following years, and the system came to answer about two million queries a year.


=== ECHO 2.0 and later releases ===
In December 2013 the EPA released ECHO 2.0, a full redesign that replaced the old mainframe system with a faster and easier interface. The first 2.0 release supported cross-system searches but offered limited access to program-specific data. Further releases followed in 2014:


== Data ==


=== Sources ===
ECHO takes its data from several EPA national systems, including the Facility Registry System (FRS), which holds facility identification information, and the Integrated Compliance Information System (ICIS). ICIS Federal Enforcement and Compliance covers EPA inspections and enforcement under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, CERCLA, EPCRA, FIFRA, the Marine Protection, Research, and Sanctuaries Act, and the Toxic Substances Control Act. Clean Air Act stationary source data moved from the older Air Facility System to ICIS-Air, with the last AFS extract made in October 2014.

articles.title: R (Pompe) v Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs
articles.text:
R (Pompe) v Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs

R (Pompe) v Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs [2026] EWHC 529 (Admin) is a decision of the High Court of Justice of England and Wales on two linked claims for judicial review brought by Chagossians against the Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs. The claimants, Bertrice Pompe and the father and son Louis Michel Mandarin and Louis Misley Mandarin, challenged the government's failure to consult Chagossians before agreeing the 2025 treaty under which the United Kingdom accepts that Mauritius is sovereign over the Chagos Archipelago. On 22 May 2025 Pompe obtained an out-of-hours injunction which briefly delayed the signing of the treaty; it was discharged around noon that day, and the treaty was signed shortly afterwards.
On 10 March 2026 Mrs Justice Stacey refused permission for the claims to proceed and dismissed them. She held that the claims were in substance a direct challenge to the prerogative power to make treaties and were not justiciable. She also held that none of the six grounds was arguable, principally because "the Chagossians have never had any right of abode or settlement on the Islands since their ancestors were first brought there". The judge acknowledged a "long and shameful history" in the treatment of the islanders.


== Background ==

The Chagos Islands became part of the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) in November 1965, after the United Kingdom agreed their detachment from Mauritius. Between 1966 and 1972 the British government relocated all Chagossians to Mauritius and Seychelles, and a United States defence facility was established on Diego Garcia. The judge recorded that the courts in England and Wales and the European Court of Human Rights "have not upheld their claimed right of abode or right of return to the Islands". In Chagos Islanders v United Kingdom (2013) the European Court of Human Rights declared a complaint inadmissible, holding among other things that descendants not born on the islands could not claim to be victims because they had never had a home there. In the litigation known as Bancoult (No. 5), the Divisional Court and the Court of Appeal dismissed challenges to the government's 2016 decision not to support resettlement.
On 3 November 2022 the Foreign Secretary announced that the United Kingdom and Mauritius would begin negotiations on the exercise of sovereignty

articles.title: General Land Office Records
articles.text:
General Land Office Records

General Land Office Records (often shortened to GLO Records) is an online database operated by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) that provides public access to federal land conveyance records for the public land states of the United States. The site offers search access and document images for more than five million federal land title records issued from 1788 to the present. The database is maintained by the BLM Eastern States Office in Springfield, Virginia, the successor to the original United States General Land Office.
The records document the first transfer of title from the federal government to private owners, and are widely used by genealogists, land title researchers, historians, title companies and natural resource agencies. The BLM has described the site as its most popular website and one of the most popular websites in the Department of the Interior.


== Background ==
The records originate in the federal land surveys required by the Land Ordinance of 1785, which authorized the transfer of public land from the federal government to private individuals. As land was sold or granted, the government issued land patents, and General Land Office surveyors produced plats and field notes describing the land. The BLM notes that surveyors often travelled by horse and wagon, were frequently the first non-Native people to enter an area, and recorded events such as births and deaths in their field notes.
The BLM Eastern States Office holds the Secretary of the Interior's copies of the original land records for most of the United States from 1787 onward. It maintains more than nine million historic land documents, including survey plats, field notes, homestead patents, military warrants and railroad grants.


== History ==


=== Automation project ===
Since 1989, BLM Eastern States has been protecting and automating historic land patent documents on behalf of the Secretary of the Interior. This work is known as the General Land Office Records Automation Project.


=== Website ===
The first version of the GLO Records website launched in 1998. By 2010 it had received more than 500 million hits from 13 million visitors.
A redesigned site was tested in beta through 15 October 2010 and went live on 18 October 2010. New features included:

map-based searching;
sortable and bookmarkable results lists;
an integrated search across patents, survey plats and land status records from a single query;
land description mapping;

articles.title: California State Insectary
articles.text:
California State Insectary

The California State Insectary is a historic building  in Capitol Park in Sacramento, California. Designed by George Clinton Sellon, California's first State Architect, and completed in 1908, the Arts and Crafts-style building stands near 13th and L streets, east of the California State Capitol.
The insectary was built by the state Commission of Horticulture (reorganized as the Department of Agriculture in 1919) to provide laboratory, breeding, and storage space for its Bureau of Pest Control's pioneering work with beneficial insects to control agricultural pests. The Bureau collected, bred, and distributed beneficial insects to California growers and foreign governments without charge.
In 1923, a legislative reorganization transferred state insectary operations to the University of California Citrus Experiment Station. The state Department of Agriculture's Division of Chemistry operated out of the State Insectary through the 1920s. Since 1938, Capitol Park's grounds maintenance crew has used the State Insectary as its headquarters.
The State Insectary is included in the National Register of Historic Places as part of the California State Capitol listing. 


== Origins and previous insectaries ==
Pioneering Californian entomologists like Albert Koebele and Alexander Craw and fruit growers like Ellwood Cooper had already begun importing insects from Australia and China to fight agricultural pests in California in the late 1800s. Cooper was appointed to the first State Board of Horticultural Commissioners in 1881 and then appointed the first Commissioner of the reorganized Commission of Horticulture in 1903. Under Cooper, in the early 1900s, the state opened an insectary in San Francisco for studying and distributing beneficial insects. The San Francisco insectary was destroyed in the 1906 earthquake.
By 1905, the state had begun plans to construct a new insectary in Sacramento. In July 1906, a temporary insectary was established in Sacramento at a private residence. A temporary insectary was also reestablished in San Francisco.
In 1907, John W. Jeffrey was appointed State Commissioner of Horticulture after a stiff competition with Cooper in which both sides were supported by organized campaigns that made state pest control policy a political issue. articles.title: Polona Rifelj
articles.text:
Polona Rifelj

Polona Rifelj (born 30 August 1973) is a Slovenian economist and politician. She has been serving as Minister of the Environment and Spatial Planning of Slovenia since 2026.


== Early life and education ==
Rifelj was born on 30 August 1973 in Celje, PR Slovenia, Yugoslavia. She got a degree in communication studies and economics, and a master's degree in politician science. Rifelj also have studies in financial forensics.


== Career ==
She has worked as director of the Celje Central Library since 2013.
Rifelj is member of the Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS) and her political career began in her hometown's city council, and worked for the Ministry of Agriculture. She also worked for the European Commission and the International Organisation for Migration with responsabilities on democratisation processes in third world countries, and the Slovenian Equestrian Federetion and the Legal Affairs Committee of the Slovenian Olympic Committee. In 2021 Rifelj was appointed State Secretary for economy in the office of Prime Minister Janez Janša.
In the 2026 parliamentary election, Rifelj was a Let's Connect Slovenia candidate to the National Assembly for Celje 2 constituency, but was not elected. In May 2026 Rifelj was announced as the Minister of the Environment and Spatial Planning of the Janša new cabinet.
She presented her career and her main proposals to the members of the National Assembly on 2 June. Rifelj announced that she would prioritise flood prevention, the circular economy and recycling, as well as streamlining administrative permits and simplifying environmental impact assessments. She also proposed auditing controversial projects, such as the C0 canal, and updating the Natura 2000 document. On the issue of housing, she proposed increasing the amount of land available for development, speeding up construction and refurbishing empty buildings to facilitate access to housing, particularly for young people.
Rifelj was sworn in on 4 June 2026.

articles.title: HMS Charon (1783)
articles.text:
HMS Charon (1783)

HMS Charon was a 44-gun fifth-rate Roebuck-class ship of the Royal Navy launched in 1783. Initially kept in ordinary, the ship first saw service off the coast of Africa in 1792. Returned to Britain in 1793 for the French Revolutionary Wars, she was converted into a hospital ship for the Channel Fleet. In this role Charon was present at the Glorious First of June in 1794 and the Battle of Groix in 1795. The ship then joined the Leeward Islands Station, where she operated as a store ship and participated in the capture of St Lucia in 1796.
Returned to Britain in 1797, Charon was used during the Irish Rebellion of 1798 to convey reinforcements from Britain. From 1799 the ship was predominantly based in the Mediterranean Sea, being converted into a troop ship in the following year. Charon then formed part of the blockade for the Siege of Genoa, and in 1801 participated in the landings at the Battle of Abukir where she had five men wounded. Charon returned to Britain in 1804 and was broken up in the following year.


== Design ==
Charon was a 44-gun, 18-pounder Roebuck-class ship. The class was a revival of the design used to construct the fifth-rate HMS Roebuck in 1769, by Sir Thomas Slade. The ships, while classified as fifth-rates, were not frigates because they carried two gun decks, of which a frigate would have only one. Roebuck was designed as such to provide the extra firepower a ship of two decks could bring to warfare but with a much lower draught and smaller profile. From 1751 to 1776 only two ships of this type were built for the Royal Navy because it was felt that they were anachronistic, with the lower (and more heavily armed) deck of guns being so low as to be unusable in anything but the calmest of waters. In the 1750s the cruising role of the 44-gun two deck ship was taken over by new 32- and 36-gun frigates, leaving the type almost completely obsolete.

When the American Revolutionary War began in 1775 a need was found for heavily armed ships that could fight in the shallow coastal waters of North America, where two-decked third-rates could not safely sail, and so the Roebuck class of nineteen ships, alongside the similar Adventure class, was ordered to the specifications of the original ships to fill this need. articles.title: Awad Darawshe
articles.text:
Awad Darawshe

Awad Musa Darawshe (1999/2000) – 7 October 2023) was an Arab-Israeli emergency medical technician and paramedic who was killed by Hamas members at the Nova music festival massacre while in the act of providing first-aid treatment to civilians. Darawshe was raised in the predominantly Arab town of Iksal, before gaining medical education with the Israeli ambulance service, Magen David Adom. He was employed by Yossi Ambulances while also serving as a volunteer with United Hatzalah. At the outbreak of the October 7 attacks, Darawshe refused orders from his superiors and requests from his friends to evacuate from the music festival. Instead, he chose to remain behind, believing he could talk down the terrorists with his Arabic language skills. He was killed by members of Hamas, while bandaging a festival attendee under the festival stage.
After his death, Darawshe became an international symbol of Arab-Israeli sacrifice and interfaith solidarity. Over 20,000 people attended his funeral in Iksal, across multiple faith communities, including Muslim, Jewish, Christian, Druze, and Circassians. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Israel called him a hero and the President of Israel personally called his parents to offer condolences from the nation to his family. President of the United States Joe Biden met with his family to offer compassion, and heard about his story. 
Darawshe's emergency medical efforts and selflessness inspired an art exhibit, Names & Faces, in Jerusalem, and graffiti art in Tel Aviv. His story was featured in published books including Against All Odds, and One Day in October: Forty Heroes, Forty Stories, and a Spanish language book of poetry, Gaza en los Cielos. An ultramarathon runner in the 2025 Comrades Marathon in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa was motivated to run in honor of Darawshe.


== Early life and family ==


=== Iksal upbringing ===

Awad Musa Darawshe was from Iksal, a predominantly Arab town located 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) southeast of Nazareth. His family was of the Muslim faith, and had resided in the town of Iksal for multiple generations. His parents were Musa Darawshe and Huda Darawshe. He had three sisters and one brother. He was the youngest child among his siblings. His mother called him her "hugging son", because he would sit beside her and hug her as she watched programs on the television. articles.title: R (Mandarin) v Commissioner for the British Indian Ocean Territory
articles.text:
R (Mandarin) v Commissioner for the British Indian Ocean Territory

R (Mandarin) v Commissioner for the British Indian Ocean Territory is a 2026 judicial review case in the Supreme Court of the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT), brought by four Chagossians who landed without permits on Île du Coin, in the Peros Banhos atoll, on 16 February 2026. They challenged removal notices served on them two days later and the failure to grant them permits to enter and remain in the territory. The court granted an interim injunction against their removal on 19 February 2026.
In a judgment of 31 March 2026 the Chief Justice, James Lewis KC, held that the court had jurisdiction to review the territory's 2004 constitution, and quashed its section 9, which provides that "no person has the right of abode in the Territory", as "an unlawful and irrational exercise of the prerogative". He preferred the reasoning of the dissenting minority in the House of Lords' 2008 decision in Bancoult (No 2), and held that the 2025 treaty between the United Kingdom and Mauritius had removed the defence and cost reasons on which the majority had relied. He also quashed the removal notices as procedurally unfair, but held that the claimants had entered and remained in the territory illegally, that the immigration permit system remained valid, and that the claimants had "at least in part" misled the court.
The court granted the Commissioner permission to appeal and ordered that the effects of the declaration and quashing orders be stayed pending the final determination of the appeal; the interim injunction was continued. The appeal was listed before the British Indian Ocean Territory Court of Appeal for 15–17 July 2026.


== Background ==

The BIOT was created by Order in Council in 1965 from the Chagos Archipelago and islands previously administered from Mauritius and Seychelles, and in 1966 the islands were made available to the United States for defence purposes. The entire population was removed between 1966 and 1972, and no Chagossian has lived on the islands since 1973. Before the court the Commissioner expressly conceded that there had been a settled population in the islands by the 1960s, which the judge called "commendable".

articles.title: John Burness
articles.text:
John Burness

John Frederick Burness (May 16, 1945 – December 19, 2022) was an American college administrator. He served as the interim president of Franklin & Marshall College from 2010 to 2011. Before F&M, Burness spent 17 years as the Vice-President for Public Affairs and Government Relations at Duke University. 


== Early life ==
Burness was born in Durham, North Carolina on May 16, 1945. Burness married Anne D. Williams in 1975. The couple had two sons, Evan and Sam.


=== Franklin & Marshall student president ===
Burness attended Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Burness served as president of student government and graduated in 1967. Upset by lackluster food at the school cafeteria, Burness once marched to the home of college president Keith Spalding to complain about the food. Carrying an ill-prepared pork chop, Burness convinced Spalding to change the college's food supplier.


== Duke University ==
Burness became Vice-President for Public Affairs and Government Relations at Duke University in 1991.  
As Vice-President at Duke, Burness was sued by Duke Lacrosse head coach Mike Pressler in connection with the Duke lacrosse rape hoax. Pressler accused Duke and Burness of defamation in relation to his termination. 
Burness retired from Duke in 2008. He returned to Duke as a visiting professor of public policy, serving until 2010. 


== Durham Tech ==
Burness was appointed to the Durham Technical Community College Board of Trustees by the Durham Public School Board in 2009. Burness was elected as Chairman of the Board in 2017, holding the position until his death in 2022.


== Franklin & Marshall College ==
Burness was elected to the Franklin & Marshall College Board of Trustees in 2003.
After the resignation of John Anderson Fry in 2010, Burness was installed as interim president by the Board of Trustees on July 1, 2010. Burness highlighted campus development and expading the college financial endowment as priorities for his administration.
Burness left office on the installation of Daniel R. Porterfield as the 15th president of the college. He continued as a college trustee until 2015.

articles.title: Valentina Muñoz Rabanal
articles.text:
Valentina Muñoz Rabanal

Valentina Muñoz Rabanal, also known as Chica Rosadita (born 2002), is a Chilean influencer, activist, and programmer. She was a member of the first-ever all-female team to become FIRST Lego League Challenge champions, and became known as for her work on Artifical Intelligence regulations in Chile. She has also founded NGO Asociación de Mujeres Jóvenes por las Ideas, focused on supporting women in STEM, and was appointed a United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Advocate. 


== Biography ==
Rabanal was born in 2002. Her mother worked in sales for a technology company, and Rabanal was brought with her to the office. At 9, the office had a cyberattack. During the panic, she wandered over to the IT office, where she asked what they were doing. She has stated their response was "saving the world". This led to her becoming interested in cybersecurity: she stated "I dreamed of being a hacker since I was nine." She learned to program at 12, and audited programming classes starting when she was 14 at the University of Chile. In 2018, she became a part of the first female team to become the world champions of the FIRST Lego League Challenge.
At 15, she co-founded the Asociación de Mujeres Jóvenes por las Ideas, which focuses on supporting women in STEM. It was created at her school and soon spread. It is better known as AMUJI Chile. Through the project, she has worked on providing resources for helping women in public speaking, science, technology, and project management. She also advocated for women in the science by submitting proposals regarding increasing inclusion to the Ministry of Science of Chile. She also developed an alternative learning platform called AMUJIPEDIA, which collected information from and partnered with specialized sites, during the COVID-19 pandemic.
She worked on ensuring the comments of women and children would be taken into consideration by the Chilean government when they designed their artificial intelligence policy, as the comment sessions were restricted to adults. She did this by organizing dialogue sessions and collating notes. This led to her becoming known as the youngest contributor to the First National Policy on Artificial Intelligence of Chile. She also helped organize the Latin American and Caribbean consultation on the 25th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration. 
She was named an ambassador of UNICEF, UN Women, and the Children's ombudsman.

articles.title: Artie Ramsodit
articles.text:
Artie Ramsodit

Nalinidevi Urmila "Artie" Ramsodit-de Graaf (born 19 February 1975) is a Dutch politician for Progressief Nederland (PRO) and government official. She has been a member of the Dutch Senate since 13 June 2023, having previously served as a municipal councilor in Haarlem from 2010 to 2017.


== Biography ==
Artie Ramsodit was born on 19 February 1976 in Paramaribo, and is of Indo-Surinamese descent. She came to the Netherlands with her parents at a very young age and grew up in Haarlem and the Rotterdam region. After finishing secondary school, she went on to study Public Administration at the University of Twente. A year later, she also began studying law at the University of Amsterdam. After obtaining her degree in public administration, she began working at the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs. During her time there, she also completed her law studies. Ramsodit later transferred to the Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations. At these ministries, she held the positions of policy advisor and manager. After meeting a person there who was conducting doctoral research, Ramsodit decided to pursue a PhD focusing on policing as well. She pursued her PhD at Tilburg University from 2006 to 2014.
In 2010, Ramsodit became a member of the municipal council of Haarlem. As a municipal councilor, she held a portfolio which included housing, employment, youth, and economy. On February 16, 2017, she left the council to conduct research in Bangalore for a period.
Ramsodit is a member of the governing bodies of various organizations. She serves on the boards of several different organizations, including the University of Applied Sciences Leiden. She is also the owner of CitySolutions.nl, a start-up that is part of the Humanities Lab of the faculty of humanities at the University of Amsterdam. Since June 13, 2023, she has been a member of the Dutch Senate, where she wore a sari, a traditional Hindu garment, during her inauguration ceremony.


== Personal life ==
Ramsodit is married and has a son.

articles.title: Ferns Castle
articles.text:
Ferns Castle

Ferns Castle (Irish Caisleán Fearna) is a ruined 13th century castle in the town of Ferns, County Wexford, Ireland.


== History ==
Although the settlement had a monastic history stretching back to the sixth century, the borough was re-founded by Richard de Clare (Strongbow) as one of his demesne manors before 1176. an Anglo-Norman castle was first recorded in 1177, when it was erected by the sons of Maurice FitzGerald and immediately destroyed, suggesting that it was an earth-and-timber construction. A rampart excavated under the castle may represent this structure or an earlier Irish fortress of King Dermot.
The present stone castle was first recorded in 1232, and was probably built in the early 13th century, either by William Marshal or his son, William Marshal II. It takes the form of a turreted tower, i.e. a (rather irregular) square structure with a large round tower at each corner, which was an arrangement among some Anglo-Norman castles in Ireland, though not in England. Other roughly contemporary examples exist at Carlow and Lea, and slightly later at Terryglass. This type of castle is particularly associated with the Marshal family. It is unclear whether the central structure was a fully-roofed keep or a courtyard with timber-framed buildings leaning against the outer walls. The large size of the castle (18x20m) and the position of the hall fireplace suggest that the latter was more likely, The ground floor was on two levels, as only part of the castle stood upon the bedrock. The entrance was on the first floor, and the whole building was surrounded by a rock-cut moat and defended with a barbican. The first floor also contained the great hall, recognisable by its fireplace with a joggled lintel. The fine Gothic windows and vaulted chapel suggest that it was completed, remodelled or rebuilt in the mid-13th century under William de Valence.
The castle was the target of repeated Irish attacks, both for its strategic significance and its symbolic importance as the former seat of the Mac Murchada dynasty (also known as the MacMurroughs). As a result of these raids and English neglect, it became dilapidated and was considered worthless in a 1324 inquisition. In 1331, the castle was burnt by the Irish, who were subsequently defeated, with many drowning in the River Slaney while trying to escape the English. articles.title: Kasensero Genocide Memorial
articles.text:
Kasensero Genocide Memorial

The Kasensero Genocide Memorial (Kinyarwanda: Urwibutso rwa Jenoside rwa Kasensero) is a memorial to the victims of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. It is located in Kasensero, in Kyotera District (formerly part of Rakai District), Uganda.
The memorial holds the remains of genocide victims whose bodies were carried by Rwandan rivers into Lake Victoria. The bodies were recovered on the Ugandan shore and buried in Uganda.


== Location ==
The memorial is in Kasensero, in Kyotera District, near the Ugandan shore of Lake Victoria.
During the genocide, many victims were thrown into rivers, including the Nyabarongo and the Kagera. These rivers flow into the Lake Victoria basin. Bodies were later found in the water and on the Ugandan shores of the lake.
Uganda has three burial and memorial sites for these victims: Ggolo in Mpigi District, Lambu in Masaka District, and Kasensero in Rakai District.


== History ==
In 1994, during the genocide, people were killed in Rwanda and thrown into rivers. The water carried the bodies to Lake Victoria and to several places on the Ugandan shore. Local authorities and residents recovered and buried them.
Most of the victims buried at Kasensero could not be identified. The site preserves the memory of people killed in Rwanda and buried outside the country because the water carried their bodies away.
According to the High Commission of Rwanda in Uganda, the three memorials in Uganda hold the remains of 10,983 victims: 4,771 at Ggolo, 3,337 at Lambu and 2,875 at Kasensero.
In 2020, Rwanda and Uganda discussed the ownership or management of the land of these memorials, including Ggolo, Lambu and Kasensero. The stated aim was to allow Rwanda to maintain and clean the sites.


== Commemoration ==
Kasensero is one of the few genocide memorials located outside Rwanda. Each year, families, survivors, Rwandans living in Uganda and officials gather there to honour the victims. Ceremonies take place during Kwibuka, the annual commemoration of the genocide against the Tutsi.

articles.title: Cumarinia odorata
articles.text:
Cumarinia odorata

Cumarinia odorata, commonly known in Spanish as biznaga partida olorosa (which translates as "fragrant split barrel cactus"), is a species of succulent flowering plant in the family. Cactaceae It is the only member of the monotypic genus Cumarinia. It is endemic to northeastern Mexico, where it is found in the states of  San Luis Potosí, southern Nuevo León, and southwestern Tamaulipas. It is very small in size.


== Description ==
Cumarinia odorata is a species of small cactus that often forms irregular clumps with a few branches. The stems are globular or shortly cylindrical in shape, with a dark green epidermis. They grow to 4 cm in height and 3 cm in diameter, with a slightly sunken and glabrous apex.
The stems are covered in soft, flaccid cylindrical tubercles. They are blunt, with a shallow groove on top, and measure up to 1 cm in length and 0.4 cm in width. The axils are bare.

At the ends of the tubercles are areoles, which are covered in white wool when young. These have 3-4 strongly hooked central spines, which are black or dark reddish to yellow in color and 2-2.5 cm long. There are also 7-9 radial spines, which are white or yellow with a brown tip and measure 0.8-1 cm in length.

The small, funnel-shaped flowers open during the day. They are narrow and yellow-pink in color. The flowers first appear at an early stage of the plant's life and are self-fertile. They measure 1.5-2 cm in length and 0.8-1.2 cm in diameter. The stamens are inserted in two rows, and have white filaments and golden-yellow coffee bean-shaped anthers.

The fruits are small, narrow, and cylindrical. They are light green in color with a slight pinkish tint, and measure 1.5-2 cm in length. Inside the fruit, the black seeds are egg-shaped and laterally compressed.


== Distribution and habitat ==
This species is native to northeastern Mexico, specifically to San Luis Potosí, southern Nuevo León, and southwesterm Tamaulipas, where it is mainly found in desert or dry scrubland biomes.
It grows on limestone slopes and canyons at altitudes of 670 to 1430 meters above sea level.


== Taxonomy ==
Cumarinia odorata was first described as Coryphantha odorata, a name published in 1930 by the German botanist Friedrich Boedeker in the scientific journal Monatsschrift der Deutschen Kakteen-Gesellschaft 2: 169.

articles.title: Wrestle-1 Grand Prix 2005
articles.text:
Wrestle-1 Grand Prix 2005

The Wrestle-1 Grand Prix 2005 was an incomplete professional wrestling tournament held over two events produced by Fumihiko Uwai's Big Mouth company in partnership with Fighting and Entertainment Group, the parent company of the K-1 kickboxing promotion. The opening round took place on August 4, 2005 at the Ryōgoku Kokugikan and the second round took place on October 2 at the Yoyogi National Stadium, both in Tokyo, Japan. Due to financial difficulties and numerous disagreements between the stakeholders, the joint venture closed without concluding the tournament.
In the main event of the opening round, The Great Muta defeated Akebono, who was making his wrestling debut in Japan, to qualify to the second round. In other prominent matches, Jun Akiyama defeated Katsuyori Shibata in the first round of the tournament, Kaz Hayashi defeated AJ Styles in a special singles match, and Mil Máscaras teamed with Terry Funk to defeat the team of Tomoaki Honma and Katsuhiko Nakajima in the opening match. The event also notably featured a ceremony in honor of Shinya Hashimoto, who died on July 11, 2005. In the main event of the second round, Bob Sapp defeated Jun Akiyama to qualify to the semi-finals. In other prominent matches, Mitsuharu Misawa and Yoshinari Ogawa defeated Akebono and Scorpio, Team 3D (Bubba Ray and D-Von) defeated Voodoo Murders (Johnny Stamboli and Chuck Palumbo), Giant Bernard and The Predator defeated Sam Greco and Jan "The Giant" Nortje, and Abdullah the Butcher and Giant Kimala defeated Dory Funk Jr. and Katsuhiko Nakajima.


== Background ==
Wrestle-1 had originally been a professional wrestling project backed by K-1 that fell through in 2003 amid the rivalry between K-1 and Pride Fighting Championships. In 2004, Fumihiko Uwai, a New Japan Pro-Wrestling (NJPW) executive and matchmaker, left the company after clashing with newly appointed president Seiichi Kusama. Sadaharu Tanikawa, head of K-1 promoter Fighting and Entertainment Group (FEG), with whom Uwai had grown close during NJPW's move toward mixed martial arts under Antonio Inoki, then asked him to produce a professional wrestling event. Uwai founded Big Mouth, a company funded by FEG, and recruited Akira Maeda as its supervisor. articles.title: 1934–35 Newark Mules season
articles.text:
1934–35 Newark Mules season

The 1934–35 Newark Mules season was arguably seen as the second and final professional basketball season played by the Mules franchise in Newark, New Jersey, as well as their first and only season played under that particular name after previously competing as the Newark Bears. Originally, Newark was going to be one of seven teams competing for the ABL's championship this season before it later became a six team league by the start of the second half of the season. At first, the Mules would look like an above-average team in the league when they posted a 12–11 record for a middling fourth place finish in the first half of the season ahead of the Boston Trojans, Jersey Reds, and New Britain Jackaways, but behind the Brooklyn Visitations, the defending ABL champion Philadelphia SPHAs / Hebrews, and New York Jewels. However, when the New Britain Jackaways ended up deciding they wanted to fold operations before the start of the season half of the season, with the Mules facing their own struggles as a franchise behind the scenes, the ABL decided to allow a merger to occur between the two teams on January 18, 1935 where the Newark Mules would move to New Britain, Connecticut for the rest of the season to become the New Britain Mules instead, which essentially allowed them to take over both teams' positions in the ABL for that half of the season. As a result of the merger, the Newark Bears would essentially fold operations for the rest of the season despite them technically continuing operations in New Britain, Connecticut for the second half of the season. Regardless of whether one would count the New Britain Mules as a continuation of the Newark Mules' season or not, following an average 9–9 that had the New Britain Mules tie the Jersey Reds for third place, with both the Mules and Reds being behind a tied first place finish between Philadelphia and Brooklyn for the second half of the season, the Mules franchise would end up folding operations by the conclusion of the ABL's season all the same.

articles.title: Sapieha Madonna
articles.text:
Sapieha Madonna

The Sapieha Madonna (Lithuanian: Sapiegų Madona), also known as the Blessed Virgin Mary, venerated by St. Francis of Assisi and St. Bernardino of Siena (Lithuanian: Švč. Mergelė Marija, garbinama šv. Pranciškaus Asyžiečio ir šv. Bernardino Sieniečio) is a prominent Catholic Church painting of Mary, mother of Jesus, holding in her hands Jesus, as well as saints Francis of Assisi and Bernardino of Siena venerating her standing nearby.
It was originally painted by an unknown painter in the late 15th – 16th century, but was damaged by fire in 1610 and was repainted by an unknown painter in the early 17th century. The painting is of Baroque style. It is currently on display on the southern wall of the Goštautai Chapel within Vilnius Archcathedral in Vilnius, Lithuania.


== History ==
The painting initially belonged to the Bernardines Church of St. Francis and St. Bernardino in Vilnius and was painted in the late 15th – 16th century. However, in the late 16th century Lew Sapieha, a Grand Chancellor of Lithuania, commissioned a new Church of St. Michael in Vilnius and Poor Clares Monastery. The new religious complex was intended to serve as the Sapieha family's mausoleum and under the direction of Lew Sapieha the painting was moved to the High Altar of Church of St. Michael. Since then this painting also bear the name of Sapieha family. Historically the current painting was only the centerpiece of a triptych as two side paintings of Saint Peter and Saint Paul were attached to it.
During the Battle of Vilnius in 1655 the Army of the Tsardom of Russia devastated Vilnius and the Church of St. Michael was set on fire, which caused a burning beam fall on the triptych. According to historical sources, at the time the triptych's centerpiece (current painting) was only slightly damaged (the face of the Blessed Virgin Mary slightly turned black), while the triptych's side paintings of Saint Peter and Saint Paul were severely damaged and fell down. The survival of the triptych's centerpiece was considered as miraculous event and once Vilnius was liberated from the Russian Army in 1661 and the Church of St. Michael was restored the painting's veneration further increased. By performing the post-war restoration of the painting in the early 17th century, the saints Francis of Assisi and Bernardino of Siena were painted in the sides near the Blessed Virgin Mary with Jesus.

articles.title: 1934–35 New Britain Jackaways season
articles.text:
1934–35 New Britain Jackaways season

The 1934–35 New Britain Jackaways season was both the fourth and final professional basketball season played for this franchise and the second and final season of the team that was playing in New Britain, Connecticut after they previously played as the Hoboken Lisas in the briefly revived Metropolitan Basketball League, the Hoboken Thourots from Hoboken, New Jersey, the Camden Brewers in Camden, New Jersey, and the New Britain Palaces in New Britain, Connecticut. Originally, the Jackaways were going to be one of seven teams competing for the ABL's championship this season before it later became a six team league by the start of the second half of the season. Unfortunately for the Jackaways, they would end up struggling very badly in the first half of the season, as they would end up with a below-average 6–14 record that put them in last place behind that of even the newly added Boston Trojans expansion franchise (with them being a half-game behind the recently rebranded Jersey Reds for a sixth place finish instead). Following the conclusion to the first half of the season, the Jackaways would originally fold operations by the conclusion of the first half of the season before they ended up merging operations with the Newark Mules on January 18, 1935 to essentially have the Mules operate for them in New Britain for the second half of the season under the New Britain Mules name instead. In any case, this technically marked the official end for the New Britain Jackaways for the ABL this season, as their operations would essentially be replaced by the New Britain Mules for the rest of the season going forward. Despite the Mules performing a lot better than the Jackaways in the second half of the season, they not only failed to qualify for the ABL's championship series in the second half of the season (due to the tied record with the Jersey Reds still being behind both the defending champion Philadelphia SPHAs / Hebrews and the Brooklyn Visitations, who tied for first place in that half of the season themselves), but they would also end up failing to return to the ABL as well following this season's conclusion.

articles.title: Lucius C. Walker
articles.text:
Lucius C. Walker

Lucius Campbell Walker (March 16, 1823 – August, 1862), sometimes referred to as L.C. Walker, was an American businessman and politician who served a single term in the Minnesota Legislature and was an Indian agent for the Bureau of Indian Affairs.


== Early life ==
Walker was born on March 16, 1823 in Caledonia County, Vermont. Walker moved to Minnesota Territory in 1852 and settled in St. Anthony, Minnesota:196 where he worked as a real estate agent.


== Political career ==
Walker first served as the postmaster of St, Anthony from April 22, 1854, to December 22, 1855. Walker served as a Republican delegate from the 3rd District for the Minnesota Republican constitutional convention which helped ratify the Minnesota Constitution.:196 Walker later served during the 1st Minnesota Legislature as a member of the Republican Party of Minnesota representing Minnesota's 23rd House district. Walker resigned from his position in the Minnesota House on February 27, 1858.


== Indian agent career and death ==
Walker later worked for the Bureau of Indian Affairs as an Indian agent for the Ojibwe (also called the Chippewa) from March 23, 1861, until August 22, 1862. Walker was personally recommended by Governor Alexander Ramsey, as well as other prestigious Minnesota politicians, namely James H. Baker, Morton S. Wilkinson, Cyrus Aldrich, and William Windom to serve as an agent to the Mississippi Ojibwe.:196 Despite his recommendations, Walker was not a good agent to the Ojibwe, this was primarily due to the embezzlement of annuity funds with the help of Clark W. Thompson and Indian commissioner William P. Dole.:203
On August 18, 1862, the first day of the Dakota War of 1862, Walker heard rumors that the Ojibwe under the command of Chief Hole-in-the-Day were amassing near Gull Lake in Cass County, Minnesota in order to attack Walker's Indian agency.:193 Walker requested military assistance from Fort Ripley, which in turn sent a detachment of soldiers from the 5th Minnesota Infantry Regiment to the agency.:193 Walker eventually fled the agency and committed suicide near Monticello, Minnesota due to fears of an Ojibwe uprising under Hole-in-the-Day. Walker's death date is disputed, some sources report it as August 22, 1862, while others report it as August 23, 1862.:132

articles.title: Responses to the Flint water crisis
articles.text:
Responses to the Flint water crisis

Various organizations, private and political, reported on and responded to the water crisis in Flint nationwide. The media attention in Flint spread to encompass infrastructural problems in other cities, and studies on the crisis and its fallout proliferated. Media figures and organizations reported on the crisis extensively, and several called for Governor Rick Snyder's arrest or resignation. The event was described by civil rights advocates as an example of environmental racism.


== Lead poisoning and aging infrastructure problems in other cities ==
An investigative report by Reuters released December 19, 2016, found nearly 3,000 areas in the United States with lead contamination rates at least double those in Flint. The Trump administration blocked publishing a federal health study on the nationwide water-contamination crisis.
The water disaster called attention to the problem of aging and seriously neglected water infrastructure nationwide. The Flint crisis recalled recent lead contamination crises in the tap water in various cities, such as the lead contamination in Washington, D.C. drinking water (2001), Columbia, South Carolina (2005); Durham and Greenville, North Carolina (2006); Jackson, Mississippi (2015); and Sebring, Ohio (2015). The New York Times notes, "Although Congress banned lead water pipes 30 years ago, between 3.3 million and 10 million older ones remain, primed to leach lead into tap water by forces as simple as jostling during repairs or a change in water chemistry." Inadequate regulation was cited as one reason for unsafe lead levels in tap water and "efforts to address shortcomings often encounter push-back from industries like agriculture and mining that fear cost increases, and from politicians ideologically opposed to regulation". The crisis called attention to a "resource gap" for water regulators. The annual budget of the EPA's drinking water office declined 15% from 2006 to 2015, with the office losing over 10% of employees, and the Association of State Drinking Water Administrators reported in 2013 that "federal officials had slashed drinking-water grants, 17 states had cut drinking-water budgets by more than a fifth, and 27 had cut spending on full-time employees", with "serious implications for states' ability to protect public health".

articles.text:
Kidnapping of Elizabeth Thomas

On March 13, 2017, 15-year-old Elizabeth Thomas went missing with her 50-year-old health and science teacher Tad Cummins for 38 days. Cummins took Thomas across state lines to a remote cabin in Cecilville, California, where a gas station worker recognized them and turned him in. Cummins was sentenced to 20 years in federal prison. A true crime documentary of the kidnapping was premiered on Lifetime in 2023, titled Abducted by My Teacher: The Elizabeth Thomas Story.


== Background ==
Elizabeth Thomas was born to exterminator Anthony Edward Thomas and Kimberly Thomas and lived in Culleoka, Tennessee. In 2016, Thomas was homeschooled until mother was removed from their home and charged with child abuse and child neglect, after which she began going to public school at Culleoka Unit School.
Tad Cummins was a father and grandfather when he encountered Elizabeth Thomas. He was married to his wife Jill Cummins for 31 years at the time he abducted her. He started teaching at Culleoka Unit School in 2011 and was known for being an informal teacher. In fall 2015, Thomas first encountered Cummins as a 14-year-old freshman in his class; Thomas had her sit next to him during class, eat lunch in his class room, visit him during her open class periods, and receive "counseling sessions" with him during other teacher's classes.
In fall 2016, Cummins told Thomas he wanted to see her naked, and he began kissing and sexually abusing her during school hours. When Thomas confided in him about her mental health struggles and her want to seek professional help, he told her not to. At school, other teachers and students were well aware of the relationship, with one student asking to be removed from Cummins' class due to discomfort with their relationship and another witnessing Cummins kiss Thomas on January 23, 2017. The school investigated the incident but did not inform Thomas' parents, and kept Thomas in Cummins' class. On January 27, Cummins chaperoned Thomas' field trip and solicited Thomas for sex, which she refused. On January 30, Thomas was removed from his classroom and told to seek guidance from other counselors than Cummins, although other teachers refused to. articles.text:
Coryphantha clavata

Coryphantha clavata, commonly known in Spanish as biznaga de porra (which translates as "club barrel cactus"), is a species of succulent flowering plant in the genus Coryphantha, within the family Cactaceae. It is endemic to northeastern Mexico.


== Description ==
Coryphantha clavata is a species of cactus that usually has a solitary habit, although it can sometimes form clumps. The stems are erect, and although juvenile stems are globose in shape, they later elongate and become club-shaped; that is, they have a larger diameter at the apex than at the base. The epidermis is dark blue-green in color with red tones. The stem measures 10-30 cm in height and 4-7 cm in diameter. The apex is covered in dense, woolly trichomes, and the taproot is turnip-shaped.

The stems have widely-spaces and obliquely-conical tubercles, whose axils are covered in white wool when juvenile. The tubercles are up to 2 cm in length and are arranged in 5, 8, or 13 rows. They have a shallow groove that extends almost to their base, and on them are situated the round, white areoles. The areoles measure approximately 3 mm in diameter; they have spines and 1-2 large red nectar glands.
Among the spines, there is 1 central spine (which may be absent) that measures 2-3 cm in length and is yellowish to brown in color and usually has dark bands. It is straight to curved or even hooked. There are also 6-12 radial spines measuring 0.8-1.5 cm in length; these are brown in color, with reddish bases and dark apices.
The flowers develop in an apical position. They measure 2-5 cm in length and up to 4 cm in diameter. They are a bright light yellow color. The outer tepals are linear and acute, with a wide, brown central vein. The inner tepals are linear, narrow, and creamy white in color. The stamens are pinkish in color, and much shorter than the tepals. The style is pink in color, and the 5-6 lobes of the stigma are short and greenish in color.
The fruits are light green in color and measure approximately 2 cm in length. They are juicy and have a dark red skin. The seeds are kidney-shaped and brown, measuring approximately 1 mm in length.


== Distribution and habitat ==
Coryphantha clavata is native to northeastern Mexico in the states of Aguascalientes, Guanajuato, Jalisco, San Luis Potosí, and Zacatecas. It is found primarily in desert or dry scrubland biomes at elevations of 1700 to 1800 meters above sea level.

articles.title: Cam Porter
articles.text:
Cam Porter

Cameron Porter (born April 13, 2002) is an American professional football running back for the Toronto Argonauts of the Canadian Football League (CFL). He played college football for the Northwestern Wildcats.


== Early life ==
Porter was born on April 13, 2002. He attended La Salle High School in Cincinnati, Ohio, where he had 2,285 rushing yards, 690 receiving yards and 34 touchdowns, earning second-team All-State honors by MaxPreps.


== College career ==
Porter played college football for the Northwestern Wildcats from 2020 to 2025. As a true freshman, he rushed for 333 yards and five touchdowns with nine receptions for 57 yards. Porter missed the entire 2021 season after suffering a lower-body injury in the preseason. In 2022, he had 286 rushing yards, two touchdowns and seven receptions for 50 yards. The following season, Porter had his best season from scrimmage with 651 yards and four touchdowns on the ground while adding 21 catches for 121 yards and a touchdown. In 2024, he rushed for 501 yards and six touchdowns with 23 receptions for 174 yards. In his final season, Porter played in two games, before suffering a season-ending right leg injury. Prior to his injury, he tallied 137 rushing yards, one touchdown and three receptions for 37 yards. 


== Professional career ==

After going unselected in the 2026 NFL draft, Porter signed with the Toronto Argonauts of the Canadian Football League (CFL) to the practice roster. On October 15, he was elevated to the active roster and made his CFL debut the following day. Against the winless Ottawa Redblacks, Porter rushed the ball seven times for 31 yards and a touchdown while adding a 15-yard reception.

articles.title: Ocean Beach Park (Long Beach, New York)
articles.text:
Ocean Beach Park (Long Beach, New York)

Ocean Beach Park (more commonly known as Long Beach) is a public park and beach owned and operated by the City of Long Beach, in Nassau County, New York, United States. It fronts the Atlantic Ocean.
The beach is one of the region's best-known destinations, and both it and the city of Long Beach are often considered by the media and public as being synonymous with one another.


== Description ==
Ocean Beach Park is located along the southern shore of the Long Beach Barrier Island, within the City of Long Beach and fronting the Atlantic Ocean. The beach stretches for 4.1 miles (6.6 km) along the shoreline, and additionally contains a 2.1-mile (3.4 km) boardwalk. 
During the summer season, a fee or beach pass is required to use the beach. Revenues raised are collected by the city, and the beach is among the largest sources of revenue for the city.
On the north side of the boardwalk, there are various buildings, including condominiums, apartments, and eateries. It also serves as a center for the community, hosting events such as crafts fairs. The benches on the boardwalk contain plaques, which can be purchased to memorialize others. 
The Transcontinental Pipeline passes beneath the beach, where it comes ashore after traveling beneath New York Bay and the Atlantic Ocean from New Jersey across the New York–New Jersey Bight; from its landing point beneath Ocean Beach Park, the pipeline continues a short distance north to its terminus: the Island Park Energy Center on nearby Barnum Island.


== History ==

Ocean Beach Park can trace its origins in its modern form back to the development of Long Beach by William H. Reynolds at the turn of the 20th century into a resort community. Its original boardwalk was first built in 1907, with access by invitation only; it later became a public amenity open to the general public. To draw attention to the project, Reynolds brought in two elephants, named Roger and Alice, from the nearby Dreamland in Coney Island. The boardwalk was intended to be five miles, with two miles completed by 1909. Over time, the boardwalk sustained damage from storms and fires, and had sections rebuilt.

The beach sustained significant erosion and damage to many of its facilities in 2012 from Hurricane Sandy – including the destruction of its boardwalk. articles.title: Technical College of the Federal University of Minas Gerais
articles.text:
Technical College of the Federal University of Minas Gerais

The Technical College of the Federal University of Minas Gerais (Portuguese: Colégio Técnico da Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Coltec) is a Brazilian federal public secondary and technical educational institution based in Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais. It was established in 1969 as the result of an agreement between the British Council and the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG), with the goal of training technicians to meet the demands of the labor market.
The school ranks very highly, placing among the top four public educational institutions in Brazil according to the results of the 2013 national high school examination (ENEM): Coltec achieved a score of 660.80, establishing itself as the fourth-best public educational institution in the country.

At the state level, it ranks as the third-best public institution in the state of Minas Gerais, while at the municipal level, it is the best public institution in Belo Horizonte — holding the top spot in the rankings, a position it has achieved in several other years as well.
Backed by one of the country’s most renowned universities, UFMG, Coltec has consistently proven itself to be one of the best educational institutions in Brazil, achieving excellent results in performance assessments. In 2011 and 2008, it ranked among the top public educational institutions in Brazil — placing eighth and eleventh, respectively — according to the National Institute for Educational Studies and Research Anísio Teixeira (INEP).
The school offers five daytime technical courses integrated with high school, and two evening technical courses for those who have already completed high school. The daytime technical programs, offered integrated with secondary education, are chemistry, systems development, industrial automation, electronics, and clinical analysis, each one with 36 vacancies per year. The evening courses, offered to those who have already completed high school, are mobile application development and biotechnology, each one also with 36 vacancies per year.
The entrance selection test is annual and requires Portuguese Language, Natural Sciences, Mathematics, Geography, and General and Brazilian History.

articles.title: Józef Hartman
articles.text:
Józef Hartman

Józef Sławomir Hartman, noms de guerre "Roch", "Sławek", and "Tata" (27 October 1898 – 24 April 1979), was a Polish Army officer who attained the rank of colonel in exile. From 1934 to 1939, he served as personal aide-de-camp to Polish President Ignacy Mościcki. During World War II, he was assigned to Section VI of the Polish General Staff in London and served as Polish commander of Special Training School 43 (STS 43) at Audley End House in Essex, the primary clandestine warfare training facility operated by the Special Operations Executive (SOE) for the Cichociemni paratroopers of the underground Home Army. From December 1943, he directed the Training Division of Section VI, overseeing the preparation and dispatch of airborne agents into occupied Poland. He was widely known among the troops as the "Father of the Cichociemni".


== Early life and Polish–Soviet War ==
Józef Sławomir Hartman was born on 27 October 1898 in the village of Swaryszów, in Jędrzejów County, then part of the Kielce Governorate of Congress Poland within the Russian Empire. He was the son of Karol Hartman and Małgorzata (née Białek), growing up with four brothers—Antoni, Stanisław, Jan, and Tadeusz—and a sister, Jadwiga. He completed his primary and secondary schooling in Jędrzejów and Warsaw.
In 1915, at the age of sixteen, Hartman joined the clandestine pro-independence Polish Military Organisation (Polska Organizacja Wojskowa, POW), adopting the nom de guerre "Roch", and served as commander of the POW Jędrzejów District. On 27 October 1917, he enlisted as a sergeant in the 25th Infantry Regiment forming under the Regency Council.
Following the restoration of Polish independence in November 1918, Hartman joined the newly established Polish Army and was assigned in 1919 to the 4th Legions Infantry Regiment in Kielce. During the Polish–Soviet War (1919–1920), he served on the front line with the regiment, participating in operations in the eastern borderlands and in the Battle of Grodno in September 1920. He was wounded twice in combat during the campaign. For combat gallantry, he was decorated with the Silver Cross of the Virtuti Militari (Fifth Class) and three awards of the Cross of Valour.

articles.title: Fangguo
articles.text:
Fangguo

Fangguo, or Fang states, were a category of ancient Chinese states that existed from the Shang dynasty through the Zhou dynasty.


== Name ==
The term Fang is derived from the Pinyin spelling of the character 方 as spoken in Modern Standard Chinese. In Old Chinese, it is reconstructed by William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart as /*paŋ/.
Fang has meanings including "place" in Modern Standard Chinese,, while in Classical Chinese it has broader usage including as a continuous aspect marker. Eastern Wu scholar Yu Fan identified the Guifang as an example of a nation using the term fang as a suffix in their commentary on the I Ching.
In oracle bone inscriptions dating to the Late Shang period, fang is commonly used as a suffix for placenames (e.g. Tufang 土方). Therefore, these states are often called Fangguo in Chinese academia. The term was first coined by Sun Yirang (孫詒讓) in his text Examples of Bronze Inscriptions (契文舉例) during the Qing dynasty.
However, fang is not always used as a placename suffix, and thus the exact meaning of fang when referring to these states is debated. For example, You is not always referred to as a fangguo. Reviews of inscriptions using the term show that allies, neutral parties, and enemies of the Shang people could receive the term. Due to the relative ambiguity in what fang precisely meant, fangguo as used in academia generally only includes states that oracle bone scribes referred to as fang. However, in a broader sense, it can refer to any one state that existed during the time in which oracle bones were actively written. Attempts have been made to define fangguo as the Shang saw them, which requires context clues from the oracular records the Shang left behind. From these clues, scholars such as Wu Shuhui and David Keightley believe the term may be used as a broad reference to polities outside of the Shang people's influence, or more specifically, those outside of the Great Shang City (大邑商), known today as Yin.


== Overview ==

Due to a vanishing lack of written records from individual fangguo, details of how they operated, functioned, and lived, is largely made apparent by oracle bones that detail dealings between the Late Shang or Western Zhou royal courts and the fangguo in question. Given these states may have been illiterate, it is difficult to find autonyms for them, or their own perspectives. For example, the Tufang is only known as the Tufang from Shang sources; there are seemingly no written sources or artifacts

articles.title: William Hargrave (bass-baritone)
articles.text:
William Hargrave (bass-baritone)

William Kossuth Hargrave (June 28, 1900 – November 29, 1986) was an American bass-baritone, actor, and voice teacher. He worked as a church and radio singers in Philadelphia prior to making his stage debut as Emile in the national tour of Rose-Marie in 1925. He was active as a radio, church, oratorio, and operetta singer in California during the 1930s. He had roles in the Broadway musicals Tattle Tales (1933) and Saluta (1934). In 1944 he won the  Metropolitan Opera Auditions of the Air and was a singer with the Metropolitan Opera from 1944 to 1947. He later was a voice professor at Howard Payne College in Texas, and music director of First Baptist Church in Culver City, California.


== Early life and education ==
The son of Herbert and Nellie Hargrave, William Kossuth Hargrave was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on June 28, 1900. He had three brothers and one sister. His father worked as a Baptist minister, and ended his career as a pastor.
Hargrave studied at Temple University School of Law and was trained as an airline pilot at Essington Avation School. He was a singer on the music staff of St. Stephen's Episcopal Church, Philadelphia for four years during the early 1920s. By February 1923 he was performing in concerts broadcast on WIP-AM in Philadelphia. The following summer he competed as a pilot in sea-plane races held off the coast of Atlantic City, New Jersey. 


== Career ==
Hargrave began his stage career in 1925 touring nationally in the role of Emile in the operetta Rose-Marie. After this he sang for two seasons in the chorus of the Philadelphia Civic Opera Company and was also a singer with the Mendelssohn Club. In 1926 he was elected a member of the Philadelphia Stock Exchange. By August 1927 he was in Long Beach, California working as a singer for KGER radio. He was the bass soloist in Handel's Messiah with the Haydn-Handel Society in Long Beach in December 1927. He subsequently was a singer at Neighborhood Unitarian Church in Pasadena in the late 1920s.
In 1931 Hargrave starred in Adolf Tandler's operetta Co-Eds put on by the Los Angeles Opera (no relation to the current company). He was employed as a singer KHJ radio in Los Angeles in 1932. In 1933 he starred alongside Barbara Stanwyck in the Broadway musical revue Tattle Tales. articles.title: El Sadig El Foka
articles.text:
El Sadig El Foka

El Sadig Abdelkarim Adam (Arabic: الصادق عبد الكريم آدم), also known as El Sadig El Foka (الصادق الفوكا) is a Sudanese warlord who leads a faction of the Sudan Liberation Movement (SLM-El Foka). El Foka participated in the siege of El Fasher.


== Biography ==
El Foka initially was a commander in the Sudan Liberation Movement (SLM) faction led by Abdulwahid El Nur, and based in Tawila, North Darfur. He defected with 1,500 of his men to the Sudanese Armed Forces in 2016, and signed a peace deal with the Sudanese government in North Darfur. His new group was referred to as the Sudan Liberation Movement for Peace and Development (SLM-PD). In 2018, El Foka's forces detained 21 civilians from Sortony, North Darfur without trial in Kabkabiya and moved them to the notorious Shala prison in El Fasher. 
During the interwar period between 2019 and 2023, El Foka's forces clashed infrequently with SLM-AW near Jebel Marra. In one battle in 2021, five of El Foka's soldiers were killed at Aru. At another, between July 17 and 18, SLM-AW forces attacked herders near Sortony and ransacked livestock. Civilians called on El Foka's forces to fight back, and a battle ensued that left 17 civilians dead as well as several of El Foka's soldiers.
SLM-El Foka fought at the siege of El Fasher on the side of the Sudanese Armed Forces in 2023 during the Sudanese civil war. In July 2023, his forces were reported to be roaming around the city's markets, plundering and looting shops and civilian homes. On August 18, 2023, SLM-El Foka fought with the Rapid Support Forces in El Fasher. Several civilians were injured in indiscriminate shelling perpetrated by El Foka's men.
