articles.title: Shanghai Baoshan railway station
articles.text:
Shanghai Baoshan railway station

Shanghai Baoshan (Chinese: 上海宝山站) station, also known as Shanghai North, is a station being built in Baoshan district, for the construction of the Shanghai–Nanjing–Hefei high-speed railway (also called the North Yangtze River HSR), the second phase of the Shanghai–Suzhou–Nantong railway and Shanghai Metro Line 19.
This station is the eastern starting point of the Shanghai–Nanjing–Hefei HSR, part of the Shanghai–Chongqing–Chengdu high-speed railway), and is equipped with an elevated terminal station with 4 island platforms and 8 tracks. The second phase of the Shanghai–Suzhou–Nantong railway passes through this station. Because the Huangpu River Tunnel, which passes under the mouth of Suzhou Creek (Wusongkou), is adjacent to the east side, its station is located on the second underground floor with a scale of 4 platforms and 10 tracks. A platform for the Shanghai–Suzhou–Nantong railway is reserved on the south side of the station. Shanghai Metro Line 19 runs through this station from north to south, and a platform is set on the third underground floor on the south side of the station. The station integrates municipal supporting projects and online development, creating a three-dimensional transportation hub with "four venues in one and a double-layer station".
On 9 January 2025, the bidding announcement for the station project (including the Line 19 station and reserved civil engineering for the metro line) was issued, with a planned construction period of 852 days. The three sections of the West, East and Middle East were respectively won by China Railway 24th Bureau, China Railway Construction-Shanghai Baoye Consortium and China Railway Shanghai Bureau. The project would start construction no later than 25 April 2026.

articles.title: FPG Property Fund
articles.text:
FPG Property Fund

FPG Property Fund, also referred to simply as FPG, is a South African real estate investment firm, based in Cape Town. Founded in 1989, the company has investments in residential, retail, and other and commercial properties.
As of 2026, FPG has a total of 59 properties in its portfolio, with a combined gross leasable area (GLA) of over 409,000 m². Most of its assets are located in SA. Its total asset value that year was in excess of R12 billion.


== History ==
FPG Property Fund was established in 1989 as Foodprop, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Foodworld Group, then one of the largest independent retail chains operators in the Western Cape. Foodprop was established to develop a property-owning entity that could source sites for Foodworld's retail operations while also building a broader portfolio of industrial and office properties. Its first acquisition was a tenanted retail property in Bishop Lavis, Cape Town, which the company continues to own.
In 2006, the company completed The Claremont, a R300 million residential development comprising 322 condos in Claremont, Cape Town. It was the company's largest single development at the time and represented an expansion beyond its predominantly retail property activities.
In 2012, the group made its first overseas property acquisition with the purchase of a retail property in Rugby, England. In 2013, the company rebranded as the FPG Group to reflect its broader focus across property sectors and its expanding international activities.
By 2015, FPG had grown to a portfolio of 38 properties, primarily in the retail sector, with more than 160,000 m² of gross lettable area. That year, Nedbank Property Finance provided R323 million in financing for FPG's acquisition of the Cape Gate Lifestyle precinct from Hyprop, comprising six properties with a combined gross lettable area of approximately 30,000 m².
In 2020, FPG Holdings acquired Tokai Junction in Tokai, Cape Town, from Fairvest Property Holdings for R180 million. The 7,618 m² retail center became part of FPG's growing convenience-retail portfolio.
From 2024, FPG expanded its portfolio through a series of acquisitions from major South African retail corporation Shoprite Holdings. In September 2024, FPG Holdings acquired the Drakenstein Centre in Paarl, a 9,000 m² shopping center that had been developed by Shoprite Holdings. In November 2024, FPG acquired Sandown Retail Crossing in Parklands, Cape Town.

articles.title: Joseph Honeysett
articles.text:
Joseph Honeysett

Joseph Huxley Honeysett (1890 – 1968) was an English-born Australian pioneer of association football (soccer) and a World War I veteran. He was a centre-forward in Tasmania, captaining the state team to its first international victory in 1923, and later became a foundational administrator of the sport in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT). He was posthumously inducted into the Football Australia Hall of Fame in 2021.


== Early life ==
Honeysett was born in London, England, in 1910. He migrated to Australia as a young man, settling in Hobart, Tasmania, around 1910 at the age of 20.


== Football career ==


=== Tasmania ===
Upon arriving in Hobart, Honeysett became involved in local football administration and playing. In 1910, he was elected as a committee member of the Tasmania British Football Association. 
He played as a centre-forward for South Hobart FC, Southern Tasmania, and the Tasmanian state team. In 1912, representing Southern Tasmania against Northern Tasmania in an intrastate match, he scored seven goals in a single game - a Tasmanian record that remains unbroken.
His playing career was interrupted by military service during World War I, but he returned to the pitch following his repatriation. In 1923, Honeysett captained the Tasmanian state team to a 2–1 victory over a touring team from the Republic of China at the South Hobart Ground. It was the first time Tasmania had ever defeated an international side.


=== Australian Capital Territory ===
In 1924, Honeysett relocated to the newly establishing Federal Capital Territory (now the ACT). In 1925, he convened the inaugural meeting of the Federal Territory Soccer Football Association, laying the groundwork for organized football in Canberra. He served the association as a player, executive secretary, referee, and team manager during the league's formative years.


== Military service ==
Following the outbreak of World War I, Honeysett enlisted in the First Australian Imperial Force (AIF). He served initially with the 40th Battalion and later promoted to Captain and transferred to the 47th Battalion. 
During action on the Western Front on the evening of 11 April 1917 during the first attack on Bullecourt, Honeysett was severely wounded and subsequently captured by German forces. articles.title: Leave It to Me (1937 film)
articles.text:
Leave It to Me (1937 film)

Leave It to Me is a 1937 British comedy film directed by Herbert Smith and starring Sandy Powell. It was written by Fenn Sherrie and Ingram d'Abbes.


== Preservation status ==
The British Film Institute National Archive holds a collection of ephemera and stills but no film or video materials.


== Plot ==
Set in the London district of Limehouse, Sandy enters the Special Constabulary, having been unable to join the Police on medical grounds. In a series of adventures, he rescues a girl from her evil stepfather, sorts out a wrestling match, and then gets involved with a gang of Chinese criminals.


== Cast ==
Sandy Powell as Sandy
Iris March as Joan
Franklin Dyall as Sing
Garry Marsh as Sergeant
Davy Burnaby as Sir WIlliam
Jack Hobbs as special guest
Dora Hibbert as speciality dancer
Nicholas Bird as speciality dancer
George Pencheff as wrestler
Jack Pye as wrestler


== Reception ==
The Monthly Film Bulletin wrote: " Knockabout farce, starring Sandy Powell as a special constable on duty in Limehouse.  The plot is merely a peg on which to hang a series of misadventures which befall the 'hero.' Unfortunately these are no more novel than the gags. They include such old familiar friends as Sandy eating spaghetti with chopsticks, Sandy being robbed of his trousers, and Sandy falling, from a balcony into a water-butt. The supporting players do their best, but cannot make bricks without straw. The pace throughout is slow, and the film both sags and drags. Its appeal will be mainly to the many admirers of the north-country comedian."
Kine Weekly wrote: "Robust comedy extravaganza, built to mass measurements by resourceful and popular radio and music hall comedian, Sandy Powell. The star is not supplied with many original gags, but he knows his job from A to Z, and has no difficulty in turning all that comes his way to humorous account. ... Sandy Powell is seen as a policeman, harem queen, all-in wrestler, professional ballroom dancer, Chinese mandarin, and private sleuth, and in each robust masquerade he finds many opportunities to score laughs. He certainly does his stuff."
Picture Show wrote: "This film revolves round the solidly humorous personality of Sandy Powell, and relates his difficulties in achieving his ambition to become a policeman. He gets mixed up with a gang of Chinese who plan to steal a certain jewel, and manages to save the jewel and get a reward. Competent support and direction."

articles.title: Alex Pongrass
articles.text:
Alex Pongrass

Alexander "Alex" Pongrass  (10 November 1923 – 9 June 2000) was a Hungarian-born Australian businessman and football administrator. Co-founder of the National Soccer League (NSL) alongside Frank Lowy. Pongrass was a long-time chairman of St George-Budapest Soccer Club.


== Early life ==
Born into a Jewish family in 1923, he was the second of three brothers. He began a textile apprenticeship and studied bookkeeping. 
In 1939, following the outbreak of World War II, 16-year-old Pongrass left home to work in his uncle’s newspaper distribution business. His parents later perished in the Auschwitz concentration camp. His brother, George, survived internment in the Dachau concentration camp. 
In 1944, during the German occupation of Hungary, Pongrass joined the Jewish underground resistance. Utilising forged identity papers, he posed as a liaison officer with the SS guards command. He successfully escorted Hungarian Jews to the protection of Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who saved thousands of Jews from execution and forced death marches by issuing protective Swedish passports.


== Business career ==
Partnering with his brother George, Alex established an engineering works in Sydney (later Pongrass Brothers Pty Ltd). During the 1960s and 70s, the company expanded into commercial boatbuilding, metal furniture, and plumbing, eventually employing over 600 people.


== Football administration ==


=== St George-Budapest ===
Pongrass served as a benefactor and chairman of the St George-Budapest Soccer Club. In 1958, he became president for over 40 years until the late 1990s.  Under his leadership, the club became an powerhouse in Australian football, constructing its own rectangular venue, St George Stadium at Barton Park, which hosted local and international fixtures.
Pongrass is credited with elevating the professional standards of the sport in Australia by actively recruiting top-tier, professional coaching talent. He hired national team manager Rale Rasic and Hungarian-Australian coach Frank Arok. During his tenure, St George-Budapest won five NSW First Division championships and captured the National Soccer League title in 1983. Pongrass also acted as a long-time mentor to Australian football legend Johnny Warren.

articles.title: Ryan Rodriguez
articles.text:
Ryan Rodriguez

Ryan Rodriguez is an American college football center for the Miami Hurricanes.


== Early life ==
Rodriguez grew up in Miami and began playing football at age four, initially as a running back. He was close friends with Andy Borregales and the two played together on the Doral Broncos. Rodriguez also played basketball growing up. He attended Doral Academy Preparatory School for middle school, where he played varsity football as an eighth grader.
Rodriguez attended Christopher Columbus High School in Miami. He was teammates with future Heisman Trophy winner Fernando Mendoza. As a sophomore, Rodriguez became a starter at tackle for the Explorers. As a junior, he helped the team win the Florida High School Athletic Association Class 8A state championship. Rodriguez was selected to play in the U.S. Army All-American Bowl after his senior season. However, the game was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic.


=== Recruiting ===
Rodriguez was rated as a four-star recruit by ESPN and On3, and a three-star recruit by 247Sports and Rivals. On April 27, 2020, he verbally committed to playing college football at the University of Miami over offers such as Coastal Carolina, Indiana, Louisville, Ole Miss, Syracuse, Tulane, UConn, Wake Forest, and West Virginia. "It’s always been my dream to play [at Miami]", said Rodriguez. "So, it was gonna be hard for any other school to get me to buy into what they’re selling.


== College career ==
As a freshman in 2021, Rodriguez appeared in one game and was redshirted, primarily serving as a member of the practice squad. He then missed the entire 2022 season while recovering from offseason surgery. In 2023, Rodriguez played in six games. He also made his first career start at center in the Pinstripe Bowl against Rutgers. Rodriguez was named the Hurricanes' starting left guard ahead of the 2024 season, but suffered an ankle injury in their opener versus Florida. He missed the final 12 games of the season after undergoing surgery. Rodriguez appeared in all 16 games during the 2025 season as a reserve offensive lineman, helping Miami advance to the College Football Playoff National Championship.

articles.title: Guest houses under the Islamic State
articles.text:
Guest houses under the Islamic State

In the territory of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL), which declared a caliphate in war-torn Syria in 2014, guest houses, often called madaffas or maqqars, played a special role. Every town and city controlled by ISIL had one or more of these guest houses and they were all similar. 
Upon arrival in the Islamic State, foreign girls and women would stay in a madaffa. If married, they stayed there while their husbands underwent military and sharia training under ISIL, until their husbands could find them a place to live. If unmarried, they stayed until they accepted an ISIL fighter's proposal of marriage. Unmarried women were not allowed to live alone but had to either live with family or in the madaffa until they married. Widows and divorced women under ISIL were expected to remarry quickly, and had to live in the madaffa until they did.
Integration officers were responsible for helping childless widows leave their homes and move back into the madaffa; widows with children were exempt from having to stay there. Male ISIL members who wanted to marry consulted with the ISIL Marriage Bureau and described their general preferences for a wife. Integration officers with the Marriage Bureau would arrange for them to meet with women waiting in madaffas, who had also specified their preferences for a husband. If, after one meeting, the man and the woman decided to marry each other, the Marriage Bureau then arranged for the nikah, the Islamic marriage ceremony. If one of the parties did not agree to the marriage, the woman would return to the madaffa to await another meeting with another prospective husband. A woman was free to decline any man's proposal, but she was not permitted to leave the madaffa until she married someone.
The madaffas were intentionally squalid and overcrowded and the staff were authoritarian and unpleasant in order to encourage the women to marry as quickly as possible so they would be allowed to move out. Anna Zizola and Paolo Inghilleri, in their book Women on the Verge of Jihad, compared them to prisons. Journalist Azadeh Moaveni described them as places "of such deliberate torment and uninhabitability that few women could stay long without going mad." The madaffas' windows and outside doors were locked, there were guards posted in the yard, and trips outside were supervised by the staff. articles.title: Pretty Lil' Heart
articles.text:
Pretty Lil' Heart

"Pretty Lil' Heart" is a song by the American singer Robin Thicke featuring the rapper Lil Wayne. It was released on November 8, 2011, as the second single from Thicke's fifth studio album, Love After War. Wayne raps the opening verse over a mid-tempo piano beat, and Thicke takes over for the rest of the song.
Critics responded well to the single, and several described it as smooth and romantic. A music video, in which Thicke adopts a James Dean-inspired look, was released in March 2012.


== Background and release ==
Thicke and Wayne had worked together before. Wayne appeared on "Shooter", from Thicke's 2006 album The Evolution of Robin Thicke, and Thicke sang on "Tie My Hands", from Wayne's 2008 album Tha Carter III. Thicke had debuted the title track of Love After War in September 2011. Speaking to Rap-Up about the album, he said it was written and produced by himself, as his first few albums had been.
"Pretty Lil' Heart" was posted online on November 2, 2011, and went on sale through iTunes on November 8. Love After War followed on December 6, 2011, on Star Trak and Interscope.


== Composition and lyrics ==
Wayne opens the song with a spacey, romantic rap over a mid-tempo piano beat. Thicke comes in afterward, and in the chorus he reassures his partner. Tom Breihan of Stereogum described the track as a classic old-school soul glide, with a rippling guitar line and well-placed horn stabs. He added that Wayne's verse is brief and that the song is mostly Thicke's. Niki McGloster of Vibe called it a smooth, guitar-driven record.
Writers heard the lyrics in different ways. PopCrush called the song a tender ballad on which both artists show a softer side. It described Wayne as soft-spoken and sincere in his verse, and heard Thicke's verses as asking his partner to confirm that her devotion is real. In a column about relationships, McGloster read the song as being about a man who feeds his partner's insecurity by reassuring her constantly, and suggested that this is not always healthy.


== Music video ==
The music video was released on March 2, 2012. Rap-Up noted that Thicke takes on a James Dean-inspired look. Complex wrote that he confesses his love for a partner and seduces her outside a hotel while sharing his feelings.
Thicke also performed the song on The Ellen DeGeneres Show. In the same appearance he sang "Exhale (Shoop Shoop)" as a tribute to Whitney Houston, who had recently died.

articles.title: Embassy of France, Tehran
articles.text:
Embassy of France, Tehran


== Overview ==
The embassy is located on Neauphle-le-Château Street, in Tehran. It also contains the consulate of France.


== History ==
The embassy is located on Neauphle-le Château Street,(Persian: نوفل لو شاتو) referencing the Yveline commune where Ayatollah Khomeini lived during his exile in France in 1978 after being expelled from Iraq.


== Ambassadors of France in Iran ==

thumb|Embassy of France in Iran, 2023.


== Consulate ==


=== French community ===
As of 31 December 2016, 1,146 French nationals were registered with the consular authorities in Iran. The French community is primarily located in Tehran.


=== Electoral districts ===
Since thethe law of 22 July 2013 reformed the representation of French citizens living outside of France and the establishment of consular councils in the diplomatic missions, the French citizens in a district covering Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan elect 3 councillors for 6 years. Since June 2014, they are Armand Meimand, Yves Merer and Valérie Khan. These councillors have 3 roles:

They are the locally-based representatives of French citizens abroad;
They belong to one of the 15 districts who elect among themselves the members of the Assembly of French Citizens Abroad;
They become part of the electoral college which elects the senators representing French citizens living abroad.
For elections to the Assembly of French Citizens Abroad, Iran, since 2014, has been part of the electoral district of New Delhi, which also includes Afghanistan, Bangladesh, India (except for Pondicherry), the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, and account for 2 seats. Iran is currently part of the electoral district "Central Asia and Middle East" with its headquarters in Dubai and which elects 4 of its 23 consular councillors to serve as part of the 90 members of the assembly of French Citizens abroad.
For election of legislative deputies representing French citizens abroad, Iran is part of the 11th district.

articles.text:
Dr Deepak S.S.


== Dr. Deepak S. S. Subrahmanyam Siddavaram ==
Dr. Deepak S. S. Subrahmanyam Siddavaram, commonly known as Dr. Deepak Siddavaram, is an Indian physician specialising in internal medicine, cardiology and critical care. He is the founder chairman and managing director of Saideep Hospital in Ahilyanagar (formerly Ahmednagar), Maharashtra, India. He began practising medicine in the city in 1979 and has been associated with the development of cardiac care, critical care and diagnostic services in the region.


== Early life and education ==
According to his professional biography, Siddavaram was born on 24 August 1950 in Kalyan, Maharashtra, India. He completed his Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) and Doctor of Medicine (MD) in Medicine at B. J. Medical College, Pune, in the 1969–1978 period.
He subsequently undertook specialised training in cardiology, critical care and echocardiography at the Texas Heart Institute in Houston, United States, and Northwick Park Hospital in London, United Kingdom.


== Medical career ==
Siddavaram began practising in Ahilyanagar in January 1979 as a consultant physician. His professional profile states that he established a coronary care, critical care and trauma unit in the district that year. He entered private practice in 1981 and subsequently developed Deepak Hospital, which provided intensive cardiac care and related diagnostic facilities.
In 1986, he introduced two-dimensional echocardiography into his practice and continued to develop cardiac diagnostic services. His work has included clinical diagnostics, internal medicine, critical care, echocardiography and hospital administration.


== Saideep Hospital ==
Siddavaram founded Saideep Hospital in Ahilyanagar, Maharashtra, and serves as its founder chairman and managing director. The institution was established to expand access to specialised medical services in the region.
The hospital developed into a multispecialty healthcare facility offering services in cardiology, critical care, diagnostic imaging and other medical specialties. In August 2024, Saideep Healthcare & Research Pvt. Ltd. announced a partnership with Sahyadri Hospitals, after which the institution became known as Saideep Sahyadri Hospital. Siddavaram continued as chairman under the partnership.

articles.title: Muslim students of France
articles.text:
Muslim students of France

Étudiants musulmans de France (EMF; English: Muslim Students of France) is a French student association founded in 1989. It operates through local branches and provides student support and representation. Its activities and alleged links to the Muslim Brotherhood have attracted public debate. EMF describes itself as independent and rejects allegations of ideological or political affiliation. 


== History ==
The association was established in Bordeaux in 1989 under the name Union islamique des étudiants de France (UISEF). According to its institutional history, it initially sought to provide support and a solidarity network for students, particularly those arriving from abroad. It adopted its current name at a congress in Limoges in November 1996.
In 1997, twenty-two left-wing organisations issued a statement accusing EMF of religious proselytism and pressure on students of North African origin, including encouraging young women to wear the hijab.
After the November 2015 Paris attacks, EMF released a video expressing solidarity with the victims and calling for national unity. Entitled Nous sommes unis ("We are united"), it featured students holding signs with the corresponding hashtag.


=== Student elections ===
EMF participates in elections to the regional student welfare bodies known as CROUS. In 2002, it received 7,191 votes (6.4% nationally) and won eleven seats.
In Grenoble, EMF won 22% of the vote in 2002, reaching 82% in one student residence. In 2004, it obtained two seats, in Créteil and Grenoble. It won five in 2006.


=== Cooperation with left-wing organisations ===
In March 2025, EMF joined RED Jeunes, the Union syndicale lycéenne and the antifascist organisation La Jeune Garde in establishing Génération Espoir Dignité Résistance (Génération EDR), a collective campaigning against Islamophobia. In an interview published by Politis at the collective's launch, its representatives described a campaign against Islamophobia and the far right that would bring together the networks and experience of participating organisations.
In April 2026, StreetPress reported that the Ministry of the Interior had notified Génération EDR of its intention to dissolve the collective. The ministry alleged that it continued the activities of La Jeune Garde and encouraged violence against political opponents. Génération EDR disputed these allegations. articles.title: Members of the Western Australian Legislative Council, 1880–1884
articles.text:
Members of the Western Australian Legislative Council, 1880–1884

This is a list of members of the Western Australian Legislative Council from February 1880 to September 1884. When the Council first met it had 21 members. Fourteen were elected and seven were appointed by the Crown. Three of the appointed members sat as the Colonial Secretary, the Attorney-General and the Surveyor-General. The other four were private citizens chosen by the Governor. They did not represent a district.
The Legislative Council Act Amendment Act 1882 (46 Vict, No. 24) raised the number of members to 24, with 16 elected and 8 appointed. It divided the North District in two. The southern part became the Gascoyne District, with one member. The rest stayed as the North District and returned two members instead of one. From July 1883 the Director of Public Works also sat in the Council as an appointed member.
Writs for the general election were issued on 10 January 1880. The results for every district except the North were announced on 28 February, and for the North on 16 April. The new Council first met on 19 July 1880 and re-elected Luke Leake as Speaker. It sat for the last time on 13 September 1884. 


== Notes ==
a  George Walpole Leake sat as Acting Attorney-General when the Council first met. Alexander Onslow became Attorney-General on 21 March 1881 and took his place. Onslow left the Council on 9 April 1883 and Leake filled the seat again until 10 July 1883, when Alfred Hensman became Attorney-General.
b  Roger Goldsworthy resigned as Colonial Secretary on 7 September 1880. Edric Gifford became Colonial Secretary and took the seat on 2 November 1880. He left the colony in January 1883. Malcolm Fraser, until then the Surveyor-General, became Colonial Secretary on 5 January 1883, and John Forrest became Surveyor-General. Forrest joined the Council on 10 January 1883.
c  The 1882 Act added an eighth appointed member. James Henry Thomas, the Director of Public Works and Commissioner of Railways, was appointed on 10 July 1883. He died on 16 July 1884. Clayton Mason, who succeeded him as Director of Public Works, took his seat on 18 July 1884.
d  Stephen Stanley Parker, Lockier Burges and George Randell were appointed on 5 July 1880, and Edward Stone on 15 July 1880.  Stone left the Council on 3 July 1882, the day after George Glyde was appointed. Burges left on 2 July 1884 and William Loton was appointed on 14 July 1884.

articles.title: Kothamba
articles.text:
Kothamba

Kothamba is a village in Mahisagar district, Gujarat, India. Since 2 October 2025, it has served as the headquarters of the newly created Kothamba taluka, formed by dividing the former Lunawada taluka into two.


== Geography ==
The village covers an area of 1,410.1 hectares (14.10 km2) and has the postal pincode 389230 (also listed as 389220 in some more recent directories). It lies approximately 20 km from Lunawada town and 40 km from Godhra, within Mahisagar district (formerly part of Panch Mahal district until 2013).


== Administration ==
Until 2 October 2025, Kothamba was part of Lunawada taluka. By a notification of the Revenue Department, Government of Gujarat (No. GHM/2025/194/M/PFR/102025/918/L.1, issued under section 7 of the Gujarat Land Revenue Code, 1879), the Gujarat government divided Lunawada taluka into a reconstituted Lunawada taluka and a new Kothamba taluka, with effect from 2 October 2025. Kothamba taluka was one of 17 new talukas created statewide that day. The new taluka has its own Taluka Development Officer (TDO), who took charge shortly after formation. Local news reports note increased traffic congestion in the village following its elevation to taluka headquarters.
For state and national representation, Kothamba continues to fall under the Lunawada Vidhan Sabha (state assembly) constituency and the Panchmahal Lok Sabha (parliamentary) constituency. At the village level, local governance is led by an elected Sarpanch under the Panchayati Raj system.


== Villages of Kothamba taluka ==
Per Schedule-B of the Revenue Department notification, Kothamba taluka comprises the following 58 villages, with Kothamba itself as headquarters:


== Demographics ==
According to the 2011 census of India (which predates the 2025 creation of Kothamba taluka and reflects the undivided Lunawada taluka), Kothamba had a population of 8,157: 4,233 males and 3,924 females, across 1,690 households.


== Infrastructure ==
The village reportedly has all-weather road access, local bus stops nearby, a post office, and a Community Health Centre (CHC). The nearest Primary Health Centre is said to be at Hathivan, a neighbouring village. Sources differ on whether Kothamba also has a police station.

articles.text:
Endea Owens

Endea Owens (born 1988 or 1989) is an American bassist and composer. She fronts the band Endea Owens and The Cookout, and was a member of Stay Human, the house band on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. 


== Early life and education ==
Owens was born and raised in Detroit, Michigan. Beginning at the age of eight, the first musical instrument she learned was the piano, followed by the violin. Owens was first exposed to jazz in the YouthVille Detroit music program, and learned the bass at the Detroit School of Arts. She was mentored by Marcus Belgrave.
Owens studied at Michigan State University and took bass lessons with Rodney Whitaker. In 2015, she graduated from the College of Music with a bachelor's degree in Jazz Studies.
Owens auditioned for the Juilliard School and the Manhattan School of Music, as she wanted to move to New York "to push myself harder and find my voice as an artist." She was accepted to and enrolled in the Manhattan School, but dropped out after three months as "it wasn't the right fit". She was encouraged by a professor at Juilliard to apply to that school again, did so, and was accepted. Owens graduated from Juilliard in 2018 with a master's degree in music.


== Career ==
Owens got her first gig at the age of 15. After graduating from Juilliard, she was selected by Wynton Marsalis as a Lincoln Center emerging artist.
In 2019, Owens met Jon Batiste. Later that year, she was hired as a substitute bassist for Batiste's band Stay Human, the house band on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. She was asked to stay on, and remained with the band until the end of series, seven years later.
In 2020, Owens founded The Community Cookout, a nonprofit organization hosting a monthly series of free meals and concerts. Originally launched in Harlem, she has expanded the series worldwide.
Owens fronts the band Endea Owens and The Cookout, whose members are all Juilliard School alumni. In 2022, the band performed in a Tiny Desk Concert during a celebration of the 20th anniversary of Juilliard Jazz. Owens also performed in a Tiny Desk Concert with Jon Batiste in 2019.
In 2022, Owens composed "Ida's Crusade", a suite dedicated to the life of Ida B. Wells, for the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra.
In 2023, Owens released her debut album, "Feel Good Music".
Recordings Owens has performed on include Jon Batiste's album We Are and the film Judas and the Black Messiah.


== Honors and recognition ==
Owens has received Emmy, Grammy, and Peabod

articles.title: Bank of China (Europe)
articles.text:
Bank of China (Europe)

Bank of China (Europe) S.A., known until January 2022 as Bank of China (Luxembourg) S.A., is a bank incorporated in Luxembourg and wholly owned by the Bank of China. Founded in 1991, it operates alongside the Bank of China Luxembourg Branch, which the parent bank opened in 1979 as the first foreign branch set up by a Chinese bank after the founding of the People's Republic of China. From its head office in Luxembourg City, the subsidiary has opened branches in the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Sweden, Portugal, Greece and Ireland. Since 2022 it has also owned the group's subsidiaries in Hungary and Serbia, and it serves as the Bank of China's intermediate parent undertaking in the European Union.
The Bank of China was the first of seven Chinese banking groups to make Luxembourg the base of their operations in the European Union.


== History ==


=== Luxembourg Branch (1979–1991) ===
The Bank of China, which had operated a branch in London since before 1949, opened a branch in Luxembourg in 1979. It was the first branch that a Chinese bank had established abroad since the founding of the People's Republic. The move followed the establishment of diplomatic relations between Luxembourg and the People's Republic in 1972. Luxembourg served during the Cold War as an unobtrusive venue for international payments and already hosted a Soviet-owned bank as well as American banks.
For roughly two decades the branch remained the only Chinese bank in the Grand Duchy. The Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) opened a representative office there in 1998, which became a full branch in 1999.


=== Subsidiary and dual structure (1991–2007) ===
In 1991 the bank incorporated Bank of China (Luxembourg) S.A. under Luxembourg law in order to adapt to the development of the European common market. From then on the group operated in Luxembourg through both a branch of the parent bank and a locally incorporated subsidiary. This "branch-cum-subsidiary" arrangement has been described as the model that the other Chinese banks reproduced when they established themselves in Luxembourg after 2013.


=== Expansion in the European Union (2007–2021) ===
The subsidiary opened its first branch outside Luxembourg in Rotterdam in 2007; it was the first Chinese financial institution in the Netherlands. A branch in Brussels opened in 2010. articles.title: Honduras–Taiwan relations
articles.text:
Honduras–Taiwan relations

Honduras–Taiwan relations are foreign relations between Honduras and Taiwan. Honduras maintained official diplomatic relations with Taiwan from 1941 to 2023. Relations between Honduras and China began on 26 March 2023. As of 2026, Honduras does not officially recognize Taiwan, instead recognizing the People's Republic of China as the one official government of China but still maintains unofficial relations with Taiwan.


== History ==

The Honduran Foreign Ministry began to maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan under the Empire of Japan in 1935, under the dictatorship of General Tiburcio Carias Andino. Taiwan's relationship with Honduras continued after Japan was defeated in WW2 and the the Republic of China took over the rule of the island in 1945. 
On 12 November 2021, Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández visited Taiwan for a 3-day trip to celebrate the 80th anniversary of diplomatic ties.
During the campaign for the 2021 Honduran general election, candidate Xiomara Castro stated her wished to establish diplomatic relations with China, at the expense of Taiwanese authorities.
On 26 March 2023, Honduras's Foreign Ministry posted on Twitter Inc. announcing the severance of official diplomatic ties with Taiwan and the establishment of ties with China.
Before the tie break, Taiwan was a major market for Honduras, especially the whiteleg shrimp. In 2022, almost 40% of Honduras's whiteleg shrimp exports went to Taiwan. After the  diplomatic shift, Honduran shrimp exports to Taiwan plummeted, reportedly affected more than 14,000 workers in the industry. 
One year after the tie break in March 2024, the Taiwanese government stopped providing scholarships for Honduran students, leaving 90 Honduran students in Taiwan without financial support.
In 2025, opposition presidential candidate Nasry Asfura stated that Honduras was “100 times better off” when it maintained diplomatic relations with Taiwan. He pledged that, if elected, he would restore diplomatic ties with Taiwan and forge partnerships with the United States, Taiwan, and Israel in order to revitalize the Honduran economy. 
According to a 2026 report by Taiwan News, Honduras still owes Taiwan more than US$400 million more than three years after cutting diplomatic ties with Taipei and recognizing Beijing.

articles.title: Robert Cochrane Kindergarten
articles.text:
Robert Cochrane Kindergarten

The Robert Cochrane Kindergarten is a preschool located at 2A Minima Street in Hawthorn, in the City of Boroondara, in the inner eastern suburbs of Melbourne, in Victoria, Australia. Historically significant, the Robert Cochrane Kindergarten is a single-storey timber building that was constructed between 1948 and 1950 as part of the Free Kindergarten movement in Victoria.
Built on the traditional lands of the Wurundjeri people, the preschool was added to the Victorian Heritage Register on 14 February 2013 in recognition of its historical, social, and architectural significance. 


== History ==
A free kindergarten was first established in Auburn in 1911, only a few years after the first kindergartens were established in inner-city Melbourne suburbs. The establishment of the Free Kindergarten Union (FKU) in 1909 resulted in an increase in pre-school facilities throughout the Melbourne metropolitan region, particularly in poor areas. Robert Cochrane, chairman of directors of Brooks Robinson Pty Ltd – a Colonial supplier of building materials – a philanthropist with a particular interest in child welfare, and prominent figure in the establishment of Congregationalism in Victoria, organised the establishment of the Auburn Free Kindergarten in the denominational school hall at the rear of the Augustine Congregational Church.
In 1934 Cochrane donated land at the rear of the church to enable construction of a purpose-built kindergarten, and after his death the following year it was decided to name the new building in his honour. Financial difficulties and World War II delayed progress, however in 1946 the architectural firm Martin and Tribe were commissioned to design the kindergarten. Marcus Martin was involved in kindergarten design, most significantly in the design of the Lady Gowrie Child Centre, in Carlton in 1938, which became a prototype for kindergarten planning at a time when new pre-school educational theories were developing. A partnership established with the younger Horace Tribe that year continued until 1949 when Tribe left to open his own office. Substantial contributions to the design of kindergartens in Victoria were made by the partnership and by Tribe in sole practice.

articles.title: René Ruitenberg
articles.text:
René Ruitenberg

René Ruitenberg (born 8 December 1970) is a Dutch former marathon speed skater and clergyman. He became the Dutch national champion on artificial ice once (1992) and won the Open Dutch national championship on natural ice once (2002). Furthermore, he won the Royal Dutch Skating Federation (Koninklijke Nederlandsche Schaatsenrijders Bond; KNSB) Cup in 1997. He competed in the Elfstedentocht once as a professional racer – a race in which he was disqualified – and won a total of three "natural ice classics": the Amstelmeer Marathon (1991), the Veluwemeertocht (1997), and the USA Marathon (1997). In 1993, he won the Alternative Elfstedentocht.


== Career ==


=== Early years ===
Ruitenberg grew up in a religious family with eight children. On Sundays, church was the central focus, and participating in sports was not permitted.
At the outset, football was his great passion. He played so well that Go Ahead Eagles, from the nearby city of Deventer, wanted to sign him as a professional footballer. On the very day that he was set to sign his contract, he saw his elder brother, Henri Ruitenberg, finish in second place in the Elfstedentocht on television. He thus chose to focus on speed skating instead, trading his football boots for ice skates. After this switch, he became the Dutch inline skating champion twice. He achieved his first great success on the ice at the 1991 Dutch National Marathon Skating Championships on natural ice, where he won the silver medal behind Dries van Wijhe, who had broken away solo thirty kilometres from the finish line. A week later, he won the Amstelmeer Marathon, one of that winter's toughest natural-ice races. He finished second in the Super Prestige standings that season.


=== Dutch artificial ice champion ===
In 1992, at the age of 21, Ruitenberg became the Dutch champion on artificial ice, making him one of the youngest champions ever, after Emiel Hopman, who had achieved the feat in 1984. He had not expected this victory, for he had never before won a race on artificial ice.
At the time, Ruitenberg combined marathon speed skating with inline skating, and he had intended to focus exclusively on speed skating only a few years later. Winning the national title changed these plans, and he decided to concentrate further on marathon speed skating.

articles.title: 2026–27 Memphis Tigers women's basketball team
articles.text:
2026–27 Memphis Tigers women's basketball team

The 2026–27 Memphis Tigers women's basketball team will represent the University of Memphis during the 2026–27 NCAA Division I women's basketball season. The Tigers, led by first-year head coach Hana Haden, will play their home games at the Elma Roane Fieldhouse in Memphis, Tennessee, and compete as a member of the American Conference.


== Previous season ==

The Tigers finished the 2025–26 season 10–22 overall and 4–14 in American play, finishing in a tie for tenth in the conference with UAB. They failed to qualify for the American tournament.
On March 9, two days after the conclusion of the season, it was announced that head coach Alex Simmons had been fired after three seasons with the program, in which she never posted a winning record and went 30–61. On March 26, Hana Haden was announced as the Tigers' new head coach. Most recently, she served for two years as the head coach for Georgia Southern, leading the team to a 23–8 record and the team's first regular season record in 25 years the previous season.
Simmons' final season was riddled with scandals; In early 2026, senior Chaé Harris was dismissed from the team for undisclosed reasons. On March 2, junior forward Paris Gaines was arrested on three counts of aggravated assault and subsequently did not finish the season with the team. She later entered the transfer portal and committed to play for Division II Eastern New Mexico.

articles.title: Verda Byrd
articles.text:
Verda Byrd

Verda Byrd is an American author. She is best known for identifying as African-American until discovering at the age of 70 that her birth parents were white.


== Life and career ==


=== Early life ===
Byrd was born on September 27, 1942, in Kansas City, Missouri as Jeanette Beagle to two white American parents: Daisy and Earl Beagle. In 1943, her biological father suffered an accident and Byrd along with her other siblings were placed in a children's home. Despite eventually taking back the rest of her children, Byrd remained and was adopted by an African-American couple: Edwinna and Ray Wagner. Byrd's name was changed to "Verda Ann Wagner". Byrd's adoptive parents never told her about her race and raised her as an African-American woman. According to Byrd, she was never questioned about her race as she resembled her adoptive mother. At the age of 10, she was told by her mother that she was adopted, but the rest of her background remained hidden. She attended a white school and claims her family did not face much discrimination aside from her adoptive father getting reduced pay. Byrd was friends with Linda Brown.


=== Adulthood ===
Byrd moved to St. Paul, Minnesota where her aunt and uncle lived at the age of 21. She believes this allowed her to "live the black experience" as she had black boyfriends, attended black churches and attended black social clubs. She also became more aware about black history.
Byrd married Trancle Byrd, an African-American man, who served in the Air Force. When they first met, he assumed Byrd was white, before she convinced him that she was in fact black. In the 1970s Byrd experienced her first perceived discrimination while dining at Denny's, recounting that the staff seated other patrons first and that she and her husband were told to show their ID. They were told to be seated on the second floor, despite there not being a second floor, alluding to the second floor of the local jailhouse. The couple have a daughter and they currently live in Texas.


=== Discovery of her birth family ===
When Byrd's mother died, Byrd uncovered an adoption document with her birth name. However, Byrd disregarded it at the time. In 2013, at the age of 70, Byrd reexamined these documents with the help of a researcher she hired. She learned that she had ten siblings (with only four of those still being alive), and that her biological parents were white. articles.title: Phanindra Narsetti
articles.text:
Phanindra Narsetti

Phanindra Narsetti is an Indian film director, screenwriter and editor who works in Telugu cinema. He first gained attention for his short films, including Backspace (2012) and Madhuram, before making his feature film debut with the crowdfunded Manu (2018). His second feature, 8 Vasantalu (2025), was produced by Mythri Movie Makers.


== Early life and education ==
Narsetti holds a Bachelor of Pharmacy degree. He has said that films were central to his life from a young age and that he laid the groundwork for his filmmaking career while still in college.


== Career ==


=== Short films ===
Narsetti began his career making short films. His 2012 short Backspace drew attention because it was shot, edited and dubbed entirely on an iPhone 4S. His short film Madhuram became one of the more widely viewed Telugu short films on YouTube, reaching close to three million views. He also directed the short film Her, starring Regina Cassandra, which was widely shared online.


=== Feature films ===
Narsetti made his feature debut with Manu, which he wrote, directed and edited. The film was financed through crowdfunding, and its production banner was named "The Crowd" in recognition of its backers. It starred Raja Goutham and Chandini Chowdary, and was released on 7 September 2018. Goutham reportedly agreed to the project after watching Narsetti's short films Madhuram and Backspace. Critics praised the film's visuals and background score but found fault with its storytelling.
In February 2024, Mythri Movie Makers announced 8 Vasantalu (Eight Springs), a coming of age romantic drama written and directed by Narsetti that follows a young woman's life over eight years. Starring Ananthika Sanilkumar, with music by Hesham Abdul Wahab, the film was released theatrically on 20 June 2025 and later streamed on Netflix. Reviewers commended its cinematography and lead performance, while some criticised its heavily poetic dialogue and second half.

articles.title: Viva Carmen
articles.text:
Viva Carmen

Viva Carmen (French: Carmen, l'oiseau rebelle) is a 2026 French animated adventure film directed by Sébastian Laudenbach. Adapted from the opera Carmen by Georges Bizet, it was written by Santiago Otheguy from an idea by Laudenbach.


== Plot ==
Salvador, a teenage orphan, apprenticing under a fortune-telling blade sharpener, arrives in his hometown of Seville with his master Antonio. Antonio is hired to sharpen the knife of a soldier, José, but tells him that he was unable to see his fortune. Camping outside the city, Salvador hears a Romani woman named Carmen singing as she bathes. Antonio tells Salvador he foresaw that José will kill Carmen during the next bullfight. 
Salvador meets his old friend Belén, a teenage orphan and thief, when he stops her and two younger orphans from robbing Antonio. Antonio sharpens Belén's scissors for her, and predicts that she will lose them in a river. Belén doesn't believe the prophecy, though Salvador attempts to recruit her to intervene in Carmen's fate. Salvador tries to warn Carmen, but she believes José is harmless, and she and José begin to fall in love after José is ordered to arrest her. Salvador, aided by Belén and the other children, free Carmen, which results in José's arrest and demotion. Antonio has taken on a new apprentice while Salvador was busy, telling Salvador that it's the right time for them to part ways.
Carmen visits José while he is confined. Belén steals a fish and, after being pursued by officers, loses her scissors in the river as foretold, and is rescued from the river by Salvador. With her prophecy come true, she and Salvador steal José's knife to prevent the murder, but the younger children sell it to buy food. One night, Carmen leads a group of women in song and dance outside of town. She begins to play her castanets and the gathering is broken up by soldiers. The commanding officer accosts Carmen, demanding a kiss, and José kills the officer with his knife. Carmen rejects him as a murderer, and he flees.
As the bullfight is about to start, Salvador and Belén see José disguised in the crowd. They follow him to his hiding spot, and when he goes to sleep, the teenagers tie him up. Salvador takes the knife, while Belén stays behind to guard José. At the bullfight, Carmen's friends dare her to get the matador's attention, which she does, but José has escaped and saw her. articles.title: 2nd Infantry Regiment of 2nd Call
articles.text:
2nd Infantry Regiment of 2nd Call

The 2nd Infantry Regiment of 2nd Call (Serbian: II пешадијски пук II позива) was a regiment of the Royal Serbian Army, belonging to the Morava Oblast Division. It was a 2nd Call-regiment, meaning it mobilized men between ages 31 and 38. It was one of three regiments organized in the Morava II Division (made up of the three 2nd Call regiments as well as a Cavalry Division and an Artillery Division), and included four battalions. The mobilization for the First Balkan War began at the beginning of October 1912. The men of the regiment all hailed from the Toplica region. The regiment's commander was potpukovnik (lieutenant colonel) Dušan Vasić.
During the Balkan Wars (1912–1913) the regiment was part of the Morava II Division under commander pukovnik (colonel) Milovan Nedić. The regiment was armed during the mobilization with refurbished M. 80 rifles which unfortunately were prone to break, as well as machine guns they had no training for. There was also incomplete supply of uniforms, which made the 2nd Class-regiments easy to spot with differing combinations of military uniform and peasant clothing. Despite this, the mobilized men were exalted, with very high moral.
The Morava II Division was part of the Serbian Third Field Army, which operated towards Kosovo and Metohija. The Division approached the border on 15 October, and the next day a clash ensued at Merdare, initiated independently by the Lab Chetnik commander Vojislav Tankosić. Tankosić's attack on Ottoman guard towers led to Ottoman border troops attacking the regiment, which managed to courageously fight them off with the help of the Šumadija 7th Infantry Regiment which on its own initiative attacked the Ottoman troops rear. The war on the Ottoman Empire was proclaimed on 18 October, and the next day victories on the battlefield opened the way to Podujevo and Pristina. The regiment fought off armed bands and distinguished itself in a battle outside Pristina, then entered the town as liberators. Next, the Morava II troops took Uroševac and Kačanik (25–26 October), and on 28 October the First and Third field armies united in liberated Skopje after defeating the Ottoman Vardar Army at Kumanovo. The Morava II troops were directed to Tetovo and set out on 30 October, and entered an empty town. articles.title: Berengar II (archbishop of Narbonne)
articles.text:
Berengar II (archbishop of Narbonne)

Berengar II (Catalan: Berenguer; French: Bérenger) was the archbishop of Narbonne from 1191 to 1211. He earlier served as the bishop of Lleida from 1177 to 1191 and concurrently served as abbot of Montearagón from 1170 to 1204.
Berengar was an illegitimate son of Count Raymond Berengar IV of Barcelona, born to a mistress taken between his father's betrothal to the child queen Petronilla of Aragon and their actual marriage in 1150. He was probably born around 1140. He was thus a half-brother of King Alfonso II of Aragon and uncle of Peter II. In 1170, he became abbot of Montearagón. He was elected bishop of Tarazona the same year, but was never consecrated. In 1176 or 1177, he became bishop of Lleida. He was given a dispensation to continue as abbot. He has been suspected of having never visited the diocese of Lleida. In 1179, he served Alfonso II as an ambassador to King Louis VII of France, seeking to avert a military campaign against the Cathar heresy in southern France. That year, he attended the Third Lateran Council. In 1191, through the influence of Viscountess Ermengarde, he was elected archbishop of Narbonne and the dispensation to continue as abbot was renewed.
Berengar's archiepiscopate coincided with rising concerns over the Cathars. In 1198, he met in Perpignan with Peter II, Count Raymond V of Toulouse and Count Bernard IV of Comminges to discuss the growing heresy. By 1200, Pope Innocent III was blaming him in strong terms for its growth in his diocese. In a letter to Cardinal Giovanni di San Paolo in 1200, the pope identified Berengar as "the fount and origin of so many and such great evils." He accused Berengar of having never made a canonical visitation; of simoniacally charging the bishop of Maguelone, Guillaume de Fleix, for his consecration; and of failing to hold a provincial synod to preach the crusade, as Innocent had ordered.
In May 1203, the pope wrote to Berengar that "fierce wolves attack the flocks entrusted to your care ... because like a dumb dog who refuses to bark, you neither put them to flight by barking nor do you, following the example of the good shepherd, lay down your life for your flock; but rather you flee, leaving them to the jaws of the wolves." He accused him of preferring to reside in Montearagón, neglecting his episcopal duties, and of being a lover of money. In January 1204, he wrote to him again, accusing him of mistreating the papal legates Pierre de Castelnau and Raoul

articles.title: Timeline of the Chester A. Arthur presidency
articles.text:
Timeline of the Chester A. Arthur presidency

The presidency of Chester A. Arthur began on September 19, 1881, when Chester A. Arthur became the twenty-first president of the United States upon the assassination of James A. Garfield, and ended on March 4, 1885, at the end of Garfield's term.


== 1881 ==


=== September 1881 ===
September 19 – Chester A. Arthur becomes the twenty-first president of the United States when James A. Garfield dies. Garfield had been shot and died from complications resulting from the treatment.
September 20 – James A. Garfield's death is announced and Arthur assumes the powers of the presidency.
September 22
Arthur is inaugurated as president of the United States. He speaks in praise of peaceful presidential succession.
Arthur issues a proclamation for a day of mourning following James A. Garfield's death.


=== October 1881 ===
October 19 – Arthur speaks at the Yorktown Centennial Celebration. He issues an executive order that the hundredth anniversary of the British surrender at Yorktown will be commemorated by having the United States military salute the British flag.


=== November 1881 ===
November 14 – Charles J. Guiteau goes to trial for the assassination of James A. Garfield.
November 29 – The United States invites nations of South America to a Pan-American Conference. The conference is Secretary of State James G. Blaine's idea, and Arthur does not strongly support it.


=== December 1881 ===
December 6 – Arthur delivers the 1881 State of the Union Address. He expresses support for funding education and Indian Schools.
December 8 – Arthur moves into the White House.
December 15 – James G. Blaine resigns as secretary of state after his political beliefs cone into conflict with Arthur's.


== 1882 ==


=== January 1882 ===
January 25 – Charles J. Guiteau is convicted of the assassination of James A. Garfield.


=== February 1882 ===
February 25 – The Apportionment Act of 1882 expands the House of Representatives to 325 seats.


=== March 1882 ===
March 1 – The United States signs the Geneva Convention of 1864 of 1864.
March 4 – Nine people are indicted in the Star Route scandal.
March 16 – The Senate ratifies the Geneva Convention of 1864. It also prohibits anyone practicing polygamy from voting or holding office, and it creates a commission to oversee voting in Utah Territory.
March 22 – The Edmunds Act makes it a felony to practice polygamy.

articles.title: Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening
articles.text:
Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening

"Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening" is the third episode of the thirty-eighth season of the American animated television series The Simpsons, and the 812th episode overall. The episode aired on the Fox network in the United States on October 18, 2026. The episode was written by Nick Dahan and directed by Eddie Rosas.
Departing from the traditional three-segment anthology format of the annual Treehouse of Horror specials, the episode serves as a standalone, full-length narrative where a serial killer hunts the people of Springfield. It is a parody of the 1997 horror film I Know What You Did Last Summer. The episode is notable for marking the first speaking appearance of the characters Apu Nahasapeemapetilon and his wife Manjula in nearly a decade, reintroducing them with new voice actors Sunil Malhotra and Janina Gavankar, respectively. It also features a guest appearance by Venezuelan conductor Gustavo Dudamel. The episode received positive reviews with fans praising the episode for finally addressing the controversy with Apu.

When they are too drunk to drive home, Homer, Dewey Largo, Superintendent Chalmers and Professor Frink decide to go home in the latter's self-driving car. While going over a bridge, the car loses control and hits a pedestrian wearing a hooded monk robe and full robot helmet who is seemingly killed. Afraid of the consequences, they throw the body over the bridge into the water. Homer feels guilty for the next year.
On the following Halloween, Homer receives a message that karma is coming. He meets with a guilty Largo and Frink while Chalmers reassures them. That night, Largo is killed with a machete by a person in the same outfit as the person they threw over the bridge. 
At Largo's funeral, Chalmers threatens Homer and Frink if they try to confess, so they suspect he killed Largo. The two go to Chalmers' home and see he has had trouble coping with the incident. When Chalmers returns, they hide in the closet. As he threatens to shoot into the closet, the helmeted person kills Chalmers. Homer escapes, but Frink is also killed. At home, Marge confesses that she was also involved in killing the helmet person.

articles.title: Konglingiphyton
articles.text:
Konglingiphyton

Konglingiphyton is an extinct genus of macro-algae fossil from the late Cryogenian to early Cambrian of South China. It is a ribbon-like branching algal fossil, with probable affinities to the Rhodophyta. It contains two species, K. erecta and K. (?) laterale.


== Discovery and naming ==
Fossils of Konglingiphyton erecta were first found in the Miaohe section in the Doushantuo Formation in Zigui County, Hubei Province of South China, and were formally described and named in 1992. Fossils of the second pontential species, K. (?) laterale, were also found in the Miaohe section of the Doushantuo Formation, being formally descrbied and named in 2019.
The specific name of K. (?) laterale derives direcrly from the Latin word "lateralis", to mean "lateral", in reference to the asymmetrical branching of the species.


== Description ==

Konglingiphyton is a small, ribbon-like macro-algae, with dichotomous branching. The branches taper outwards distally, ranging between 0.1–1.4 mm (0.004–0.055 in) in width. The overall length of the thallus ranges between 2.3–36.8 mm (0.1–1.4 in). Newer material has been found preserved with rhiozodal holdfast structures, with filaments up to 1.5 mm (0 in) in length and 0.07–0.2 mm (0.0028–0.0079 in) in width.


== Taphonomy ==
Konglingiphyton are commonly preserved with a rusty colour in the Doushantuo Formation, which is suggested to be due to the oxidation of pyrite in the fossils, which would have likely been cast or coated in the mineral, giving some parts of the fossils three-dimensional preservation, as well as sparse organic remains. Although, it is noted that other fossils from other sections of the formations are less influenced by pyrite mineralisation, thus presenting as range of preservation mods akin to the Burgess Shale, Chengjiang and Fezuouata biotas.


== Affinities ==
In 1999, Yuan et al. would describe Konglingiphyton from the Lantian Formation, and regarded it as a form of eukaryotic algae, although placement within a higher taxonomic level was precluded, with Konglingiphyton and other Lantian biota taxa either being Chlorophyta, Rhodophyta, or Phaeophyta based on their overall morphology. The placement as a eukaryotic algae has been supported since, with Xiao et al. in 2002 going further with a tenative placement to the Rhodophyta based on its gross morphogical similarities to the extant rhodophyte genera Pseudogloiophloea, Scinaia, and Galaxaura.

articles.title: Han Baltussen
articles.text:
Han Baltussen

Johannes Nicolaas Marie Baltussen is a Dutch classicist and historian of ancient philosophy. His research focuses on ancient philosophical commentary, the transmission of intellectual traditions, and consolation in Greco-Roman literature. He held the Walter W. Hughes Professorship of Classics at the University of Adelaide from 2011 to 2025 and subsequently became emeritus professor of Classics and Ancient Thought at Adelaide University.
Baltussen was born in Maastricht, and studied ancient Greek and Latin in college. He did his studies in Classics, gaining his Bachelor of Arts, Master of Arts, and his Doctor of Philosophy in Ancient Philosophy from Utrecht University in 1993. He focused on Theophrastus' views on theories of perception during his PhD studies with supervision by Jaap Mansfeld and Hans Gottschalk.
Baltussen was a postdoctoral fellow for the project Early Stoics at Utrecht between 1993 and 1996. He later became a fellow of the Center for Hellenic Studies at Harvard University. Baltussen was involved in the Ancient Commentators on Aristotle Project at King's College London from 1997 to 2002 and taught ancient Greek philosophy at that institution. He joined the University of Adelaide in 2002. Baltuss was Head of Classics from 2009 to 2013. Baltussen became Walter W. Hughes Professor of Classics in 2011. He was co-editor of Antichthon from 2015 to 2021.


== Early life and education ==
Johannes Nicolaas Marie Baltussen was born in Maastricht, Netherlands. He attended Henric van Veldeke College where he specialised in ancient Greek and Latin before moving to Utrecht University. In university, he obtained his Bachelor of Arts in Classics between 1978 and 1983, while his Master of Arts in Classics between 1983 and 1986.
Baltussen went on to study Ancient Philosophy from the same university in 1988, obtaining his Doctor of Philosophy in 1993. He authored his thesis on Theophrastus on Theories of Perception: Argument and Purpose in the De Sensibus. It was an investigation into Theophrastus dialectical defence of theories of perception. It was co-supervised by Jaap Mansfeld of Utrecht and Hans Gottschalk of the University of Leeds.


== Academic career ==
Between 1993 and 1996, Baltussen was a post-doctoral research associate at Utrecht University, working on the Early Stoics Project. After that, he worked at the Center for Hellenic Studies at Harvard University in Washington, D.C., as a post-doctoral research fellow between 1996 and 199

articles.title: Leo Gray
articles.text:
Leo Gray

Leonardo Bernard Gray (born January 8, 1957) is an American former professional football cornerback who played in the Canadian Football League (CFL) for the Toronto Argonauts. He played college football for the Los Angeles Harbor Seahawks, Los Angeles Southwest Cougars and UNLV Rebels. Gray also had stints in the National Football League (NFL) for the Dallas Cowboys and Oakland Raiders.


== Early life ==
Gray was born on January 13, 1968, in Los Angeles, California. He attended Mt. Carmel High School in San Diego, California.


== College career ==
Gray played college football for the Los Angeles Harbor Seahawks in 1975, Los Angeles Southwest Cougars in 1976 and UNLV Rebels from 1977 to 1978. At UNLV, he was a two-year letterman at wide receiver.


== Professional career ==


=== Dallas Cowboys ===
After going unselected in the 1979 NFL draft, Gray signed with the Dallas Cowboys as an undrafted free agent. On July 15, he was released by the team.


=== Oakland Raiders ===
During the 1980 offseason, Gray signed with Oakland Raiders. On August 19, he was placed on the injured reserve with a rib injury where he remained as the team won Super Bowl XV. On August 18, 1981, Gray was released by the Raiders.


=== BC Lions ===
On August 29, 1981, Gray signed with the BC Lions of the Canadian Football League (CFL). On April 12, 1982, he re-signed with the team. On June 19, Gray was waived.


=== Toronto Argonauts ===
On June 21, 1982, Gray was claimed off waivers by the Toronto Argonauts. He played in nine games, primarily as a cornerback but lined up at wide receiver against the Ottawa Rough Riders, catching three passes for 67 yards and one touchdown. On May 17, 1983, Gray was re-signed by the team.


=== Saskatchewan Roughriders (first stint) ===
On June 21, 1983, Gray was traded to the Saskatchewan Roughriders with John Lowe in exchange for Marcellus Greene and Lyall Woznesensky. On July 3, he was released by the team.


=== Los Angeles Express ===
On January 18, 1984, Gray was signed by the Los Angeles Express of the United States Football League (USFL). On February 6, he was released by the team.


=== Saskatchewan Roughriders (second stint) ===
On March 13, 1984, Gray was signed again by the Saskatchewan Roughriders. On June 22, he was released.

articles.title: Poligolet
articles.text:
Poligolet

Poligolet is a historic pastoral property and homestead near Derrinallum, in the Western District of Victoria, Australia. Originally part of the larger Larra pastoral estate, the property was established as a separate holding during the nineteenth century and subsequently passed through several owners, including the Dodds and Maconochie families. Portions of the estate were acquired for soldier settlement following the First World War. The homestead is classified by the National Trust of Australia (Victoria).


== History ==
Poligolet originally formed part of the extensive pastoral holdings of John Lang Currie, who acquired Larra in 1844. In 1857, John Dodds purchased the land comprising Poligolet from Currie, establishing it as a separate estate. Following his father's death, Thomas Dodds, who had previously lived at Larra, moved to Poligolet. The property remained associated with the Dodds family until September 1889, when it was purchased and occupied by James Machonochie.
The homestead likely dates from around 1880. Stonemason George Gemmell, who was also involved in building projects elsewhere in the Camperdown district, was credited with construction work at Poligolet.

On 3 July 1896, John Watts, a 29-year-old employee who had worked at Poligolet for approximately three years, died by suicide on the estate. Watts had been due to leave his employment following a discussion with James Maconochie the previous day. His body was discovered in Harney's paddock by fellow station worker Roderick McLennan, who had been carrying out his usual duties. Watts was survived by his wife and one child.
On 19 October 1904, Benjamin Sullivan, who had been employed at Poligolet since the beginning of the shearing season, was arrested and taken to the lock-up at Camperdown. His arrest concerned a time-payment arrangement for a bicycle purchased from the Davies-Franklin Depot in Port Fairy.
During the Machonochie family's ownership, Poligolet operated as a pastoral station, including sheep grazing and shearing activities. The property was affected by a substantial grass fire in early January 1908, which spread from Poligolet into the neighbouring Larra estate. Approximately 1,800 acres (730 ha) of land at Poligolet were burnt despite efforts to contain the fire. Another fire occurred in January 1914 after explosives used by fencing contractors ignited dry grass. articles.title: Clarence Brown (scholar)
articles.text:
Clarence Brown (scholar)

Clarence Brown (May 31 1929 - July 18, 2015) was an American literary scholar, translator, writer, and cartoonist. A scholar and translator of 20th century Russian literature, he was recognized as one of the world's foremost experts on Russian poet Osip Mandelstam.


== Education ==
Brown earned an undergraduate degree in Classics from Duke University in 1950. After graduating from Duke, Brown served for 3 years in the U.S. Army's signals intelligence branch, the Army Security Agency. During his duties in the Agency, Brown completed the rigorous language training program at the Army Language School in Monterey, California and served in West Berlin during the Cold War as a Russian and German translator. He then earned a Master's degree in Linguistics from The University of Michigan and a PhD from Harvard University in 1962. 


== Career ==
Brown joined Princeton University as an instructor in 1959 and became a professor in 1969. He taught at Princeton until his retirement in 1999. Initially a professor in the Department of Romance Languages, Brown joined the newly formed Program in Slavic Language and Literatures in 1967, and the Department of Comparative Literature in 1971. In researching his 1965 book The Prose of Osip Mandelstam, Brown travelled to the Soviet Union during the Cold War to interview Mandelstam's widow Nadezhda Mandelstam. Victims of Stalin's Great Purge in the 1930s, the Mandelstams had been exiled from Moscow. Osip was arrested in 1938 and died later that same year in the Soviet Gulags. Brown's corresponce with Nadezhda (herself a writer) over the course of one year when he lived in the Soviet Union, and his study of Mandelstam's papers culminated in the 1965 book. Before returning to the United States, Nadezhda gifted Osip's papers to Brown (the papers are currently housed in Princeton's Firestone Library). Brown's 1973 book Mandelstam was awarded the Christian Gauss Award in Literary Criticism and was a finalist for the National Book Award. His translation of Mandelstam's poems was anthologized in the book Mandelstam's Selected Poems which was a finalist for the National Book Award in the translation category in 1975. Current head of the Program in Slavic Language at Princeton Michael Wachtel described Brown as one of the pioneering scholars in the study of Mandelstam. Wachtel also stated that the Mandelstam papers, curated by Brown, is "the most valuable Russian literary archive outside Russia."

articles.title: Genrikh Gartung
articles.text:
Genrikh Gartung

Genrikh Gartung (Russian: Генрих Гартунг; born 25 October 2007) is a Russian-born figure skater who competes for Germany. He is the 2026 CS Nebelhorn Trophy silver medalist and the 2026 German national champion. At the junior level, he is a three-time ISU Junior Grand Prix bronze medalist and the 2025 German national champion.


== Personal life ==
Gartung was born 25 October 2007 in Nizhny Tagil, Russia. His great-grandfather was a Volga German, and his great-grandmother came from a German family based in Saint Petersburg. Growing up, Gartung often visited his aunt who lived in Germany, which influenced his decision to skate for Germany.


== Career ==


=== Early career ===
Skating for Russia, Gartung trained under Viktoria Volchkova. He competed in the 2022 Russian Junior Grand Prix series, coming in seventh place in Samara and tenth place in Kazan.
After deciding he wanted to compete for Germany, Gartung and his father reached out to German figure skating coach Niko Ulanovsky in 2023 to start the process. The Figure Skating Federation of Russia officially released Gartung in 2024, and he became a member of the German Ice Skating Union in July of that year.


=== 2024-2025 season ===
Gartung's first competition representing Germany was the 2024 Junior Grand Prix in Latvia in August, where he came in sixth place. At the 2024 Junior Grand Prix in Slovenia in October, he placed third, earning his first medal for Germany. In December, he earned the men's junior gold medal at the 2025 German Championships. Gartung ended the season in February at the 2025 World Junior Championships, where he placed seventh.


=== 2025-2026 season ===
Gartung's season began in August at the 2025 Junior Grand Prix in Latvia, where he earned a bronze medal.
In September, he competed in his first senior event, Skate to Milano, a qualifying event held in Beijing for the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan. He finished in ninth place and failed to secure a men's figure skating spot for Germany at the Olympics. Not yet a German citizen, Gartung would have been unable to compete at the Olympics, even if he had earned a spot.
In October, he earned his second bronze medal of the season at the in 2025 Junior Grand Prix in Poland. In November, he competed at the senior level at the 2025 Warsaw Cup and the 2025 Tallinn Trophy, coming in fourth place and sixth place, respectively. In December, he competed at the 2026 German Championships, where he won the men's senior gold medal

articles.title: Liberation of Skopje (1912)
articles.text:
Liberation of Skopje (1912)

The Liberation of Skopje (Serbian: Ослобођење Скопља) came after the Serbian Army victory over the Ottoman Vardar Army at Kumanovo (23–24 October 1912) and the subsequent retreat of the Ottoman army from Üsküb (Skopje), during the First Balkan War.
The Serbian Army, which had a central role in the Balkan Alliance, very quickly advanced towards Skopje which was a strategical goal. Even after the end of the battle at Kumanovo, the Serbian First Army still believed that it had fought against weaker Ottoman units and that the main enemy forces were on to Ovče Pole. Although the Ottoman army had exceptional defensive positions at Skopje, following their defeat at Kumanovo, they retreated further, towards Prilep and Bitola. Skopje was taken without a fight, with Serbian troops entering the town on 26 October [O.S. 13 October] 1912. The liberation of Skopje was symbolical in that it was once a possession of Serbian emperor Stefan Dušan, due to which it was called Dušanov grad ("Dušan's City"). 
The crown prince Alexander triumphantly entered the city with the First Army, which he commanded. He wrote an official congratulation that same day to the First Army, and the king also telegrammed a congratulation from Vranje. On 1 November [O.S. 19 October] 1912, the city declared the holding of a sabor ("assembly"), reminiscent of the Serbian Empire. The assembly was to guest Serbian parliamentary members, as well as guests from allied Montenegro, Greece and Bulgaria. The Serbian king Peter entered the city on 3 November [O.S. 21 October] 1912, arriving on train with prince Pavle, princess Jelena, Prime Minister Nikola Pašić and Assembly President Andra Nikolić. The king was welcomed by the new mayor, Spiro Hadži Ristić who spoke of Old Serbia and its legacy of the Nemanjić dynasty. The old Ottoman municipal president, Reşat, also welcomed king Peter in the name of all Muslim citizens. Peter answered that under his rule, Serbs and Turks would live in peace in Skopje. The Politika newspaper reported that some Ottoman prisoners of war from Skopje were paraded in Belgrade that same day. The king then went by car to the Church of Holy Ascension, and a photograph taken of him sitting in the car became the most widely surfaced photo of his visit to the liberated city; it showed an umpompous king in the midst of war. articles.title: Deniz Demirkapu
articles.text:
Deniz Demirkapu

Deniz Demirkapu is a Belgian-Turkish kickboxer, currently competing in the featherweight division of Glory. He is a former Enfusion World Featherweight Champion and Glory Featherweight world title challenger.


== Career ==


=== Early career ===
On April 22, 2017, Demirkapu faced Laurent Marie Françoise at King of the Ring 6. He won the fight by first-round knockout with a jumping knee.
On May 13, 2017, Demirkapu faced Ahmed Ferradji at La Nuit Des Titans 4. He won the bout by first-round technical knockout after three knockdowns.
Demirkapu faced Kenta Hayashi at K-1 World GP 2019: Japan vs World & Special Superfight in Osaka on August 24, 2019. Hayashi suffered a knockdown in the first round, but managed to rally back in the second round, winning the fight by a second-round technical knockout.
On June 25, 2021, Demirkpau faced Craig coakley at Muaythai Night 6. He lost the fight by split decision.
On November 5, 2022, Demirkapu faced Matěj Trčka at Glory Rivals 3. He won the fight by first-round knockout.

Demirkapu made his debut for the ONE Championship organization at ONE Friday Fights 53 on February 23, 2024, against Buakhiao Por.Paoin. He won the fight by first-round knockout with a body kick.

On September 20, 2024, Demirkapu faced Kongklai Sor.Sommai at ONE Friday Fights 80. He lost the fight by first-round knockout.
