articles.title: Stelling Kornwerderzand
articles.text:
Stelling Kornwerderzand

Redoubt Kornwerderzand (Dutch: Stelling Kornwerderzand) is a Dutch fortification group located on the Northeastern end of the Afsluitdijk, a dam stretching across the mouth of the Zuiderzee. The Dutch Defense Ministry demanded that the 32km (20mi) long dam be fortified since it connected the provinces of Friesland and North Holland, where the main Dutch naval base was. Work on the fortifications at Kornwerderzand started in 1931 and ended in 1936. The fortifications consisted of 17 reinforced concrete bunkers arrayed in 2 defense lines across 2 artificial islands. 9 bunkers were in the first defense line, and 8 in the second. This page also covers German defenses added during the occupation of the Netherlands. Stelling Kornwerderzand is the only place in the Netherlands that successfully resisted the German invasion. Battle of the Afsluitdijk 225 Dutch soldiers held back 17,500 German troops until the Netherlands surrendered. The Dutch used the term Kazemat, which translates to Casemate in English.


== First Defense Line ==
Machine Gun Casemate I

Machine Gun Casemate I was 1 of multiple MG casemates and bunkers built in Stelling Kornwerderzand. The casemate was located the farthest from the Afsluitdijk on a small man-made breakwater. MG Casemate I was armed with a Schwarzlose M.08/15 heavy machine gun in a casemate and a Lewis M20 light machine gun in an outdoor machine gun post protected by concrete walls on 3 sides.
Anti-tank Casemate II
Anti-tank Casemate II is located near the shipping locks on the northern side of the Afsluitdijk. The bunker was armed with a Schwarzloze M.08/15 heavy machine gun in a casemate and a 5cm Siderius anti-tank gun. The anti tank is mounted rather oddly, whereas most anti-tank bunker’s gun are mounted with just the barrel on a mount, Casemate II’s AT gun is the full gun, chassis and all. 2 large steel doors would be opened during combat and the whole gun would be exposed to enemy fire. The gun faced north-east, and the machine gun faced north, covering the road across the Afsluitdijk. Casemate II was also equipped with an armored observation dome. Most of the bunker was covered in earth to protect it against artillery fire. That same earth now grows foliage that covers the bunker today.

articles.title: Life Is Expensive

Life Is Expensive

Life Is Expensive is the second studio album by American hip-hop group Time Machine. It was released by Glow-in-the-Dark Records on May 16, 2008 in the United States, Australia and New Zealand, and by Miclife Recordings in Japan. The album was produced by Mekalek and Stoerok. It features guest appearances from Maya Jupiter, Shawn Jackson, Greg Nice, Cool Calm Pete, Two B. Era, Jahpan, Osandi and Maggie Horn.


== Critical reception ==
The album was featured in Billboard's "Your Guide to Unsigned Bands". Katie Hasty stated the album has "more complex lyrical content" compared to the "bouncy jams and old school beats" of their 2004 debut album. 
The Source said "By dropping sonic pretense and being sonically adventurous, Time Machine has created of one of the most distinctive rap albums of 2008."
Zoneil Maharaj of XLR8R called the album "a vibrant and bumpin' party album that's also smart and aware". He said it mixes '80s style electropop with golden era hip-hop, and compared the group to Jungle Brothers and early De La Soul.

articles.title: Allen A. Goldstein
articles.text:
Allen A. Goldstein

Allen Abbey Goldstein (January 7, 1925 – January 21, 2022) was an American mathematician and astrophysicist who worked at the University of Washington for most of his career. He is known for developing several methods in convex optimization and mathematical analysis, including the Kelley-Cheney-Goldstein method (an example of cutting-plane methods) for optimizing nondifferentiable functions, which he developed along with Ward Cheney. His other well-known contribution to optimization theory is the development of the Goldstein condition in line search methods which, along with the Wolfe conditions, is an important extension to the Armijo rule.


== Education and career ==
Goldstein was born in Baltimore, Maryland and studied flute at Peabody Conservatory on a scholarship and received a diploma for flute performance in 1943. He then attended St. John's College in Maryland, where he received a B.A. in liberal arts in 1947. He received an M.S. in astronomy in 1952 from Georgetown University. His master's thesis was on the collision events in three-body problem. During this time, he also worked part time at the Applied Mathematics Laboratory of the National Bureau of Standards. Goldstein continued his study at Georgetown for the Ph.D. program in astronomy with a minor in mathematics. He received his Ph.D. degree in 1954, with a thesis titled On the reduction of photoelectric measurements of a total solar eclipse.
After graduation, Goldstein initially worked as a design specialist for Convair Astronautics, a division of General Dynamics based in San Diego, California from 1955 to 1960. During this time, he also taught mathematics at University of California, Los Angeles as a part-time lecturer. He then moved to Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he worked as a research associate until 1963, when he became an associate professor of mathematics and computer science at the University of Texas at Austin. Goldstein moved to Seattle in 1964 and joined the University of Washington as an associate professor in mathematics and became a full professor in 1965. He was also appointed professor at the Department of Computer Science at the University of Washington in the early days of its history. Goldstein remained at the university for the next decades of his academic career.
In 1957, Goldstein was elected a member of the Mathematical Association of America.

articles.title: Browningia pilleifera
articles.text:
Browningia pilleifera

Browningia pilleifera is a species of succulent flowering plant in the genus Browningia, within the family Cactaceae. It is endemic to northwestern Peru.


== Description ==

Browningia pilleifera is a species of cactus with a treelike growth form. It is branched near the base and can grow to 3-4 m tall.
It has 7-9 triangular or rounded ribs. Upon the ribs are situated the areoles; on older stems, these fuse and form grayish spines. The areoles have a white to dark gray felt-like covering. There are up to 3 central spines measuring approximately 5 cm in length and approximately 3 marginal spines measuring 1-3 mm in length. The flower buds do not have spines, but they are sometimes covered in a few off-white trichomes.
The flowers are white in color and open at night. They grow to a length of 3.2-3.5 cm and are covered in scaled. The fruits are green in color and club-shaped; they measure up to 2 cm in diameter.


== Distribution and habitat ==
This specis is native to northwestern Peru, especially near Balsas along the Marañón River. It grows mainly in the seasonally-dry tropical biome.


== Taxonomy ==
Browningia pilleifera was first described as Gymnanthocereus pilleifer, a name published in 1967 by the German botanist Friedrich Ritter in the scientific journal Succulenta (Netherlands) 46: 24.
Later, the botanist Paul Clifford Hutchison transferred the species to the genus Browningia, renaming it Browningia pilleifera. He registered these changes in the scientific journal Cactus and Succulent Journal 40: 23, published in 1968.

Etymology
Browningia: The genus name honors Webster E. Browning (1869-1942), former director of the English Institute of Santiago de Chile.
pilleifera: The specific epithet is derived from the Latin terms pilleus (meaning "felt hat") and -fer (meaning "-bearing"), referring to the raised, trichome-covered areoles of this species.


== Conservation status ==
On the IUCN Red List, Browningia pilleifera is classified as being of Least Concern (LC).


== Cultivation ==
This species is mainly cultivated as an ornamental. It may be propagated vegetatively via cuttings, or via seed.

articles.title: Ta'Shawn James
articles.text:
Ta'Shawn James

Ta'Shawn James is an American college football safety for the UCLA Bruins. He previously played for the Iowa State Cyclones.


== Early life ==
James was inspired to start playing football by watching his older cousin, Tre' Porter, a local prep star who went on to play college football at Texas Tech. After convincing his mother, he was allowed to start playing the sport at age seven. James, who was often taller than his peers growing up, played the defensive end position in middle school.
James attended Carl Albert High School in Midwest City, Oklahoma, a suburb of Oklahoma City, where he helped the football team win three state championships in 2019, 2020, and 2022. In the 2022 title game, he caught a 35-yard touchdown pass and grabbed an interception in a 49–7 win over McAlester High School. As a senior, James recorded 74 tackles, including nine for a loss, four interceptions, a fumble recovery and a pass breakup. He also tallied 31 receptions for 535 yards and five touchdowns on offense and averaged 31.4 yards per kick return. James was named to The Oklahoman Super 30 as one of the top 30 recruits in the state. He also competed in basketball and track and field at Carl Albert.
James was rated as a consensus three-star recruit. He was ranked by ESPN as the 16th-best prospect in Oklahoma and the 90th-best safety nationally in the class of 2023. On June 24, 2022, James verbally committed to playing college football at Iowa State University over offers from Northern Iowa and Tulsa. He signed with the Cyclones during the early signing period in December 2022.


== College career ==
As a freshman in 2023, James appeared in four games and recorded five tackles, taking a redshirt. He played in all 14 games in 2024, making two starts, and registered 41 tackles, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery. James posted eight tackles and a fumble recovery in a 42–41 win over AP No. 13 Miami in the 2024 Pop-Tarts Bowl. The victory gave the Cyclones an 11–3 record, the best in program history. In 2025, James played in the first eight games, making six starts, before suffering a season-ending injury. He finished the year with 33 tackles and one fumble recovery. James entered the NCAA transfer portal after the season and was rated as a three-star transfer recruit by both On3 and 247Sports. On January 5, 2026, he committed to transferring to the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) to play for the Bruins.

articles.title: Seiko 9T82
articles.text:
Seiko 9T82

Seiko 9T82 is a chronograph watch movement developed by Seiko Epson and introduced commercially in 1999. It combines Seiko's Kinetic self-generating power system and quartz-controlled timekeeping with a mechanical heart-cam snap-to-zero mechanism for the chronograph hands.
The movement comprises 356 individual parts representing 250 part types, including 122 assembly components. It has 38 jewels, an outside diameter of 33.0 mm, a casing diameter of 30.0 mm and a height of 6.8 mm.
Seiko later included the 9T82 in its corporate watch history under the name “Ultimate Kinetic Chronograph cal. 9T82”, highlighting its heart-cam zero-reset mechanism and unusual movement construction.
New watches powered by the 9T82 continued to appear through 2008, including models in the Arctura, Sportura and MX collections.


== Development ==
Seiko's Kinetic system converts movement of the wearer's wrist into electrical energy, stores that energy and uses it to power a quartz-regulated watch. In a chronograph, however, additional hands must be driven continuously during elapsed-time measurement, creating substantially greater power requirements than in a conventional Kinetic watch.
The development paper by Hidehiro Akahane and Nobuhiro Koike refers to the movement as “CAL. 9T”. It describes the development of a high-output generating system, a drive system for the chronograph hands, a lever-based mechanical reset mechanism and the electronic control system required to coordinate them.
Development of the 9T82 took approximately two and a half years. Among the principal engineering challenges was the mechanism that returns all four chronograph hands instantaneously to zero by means of heart-shaped cams.


=== Engineers and patent inventors ===
Several engineers are documented as having participated in technologies associated with the 9T series.
The 1999 technical paper Development of the Kinetic Chronograph Watch was written by Seiko Epson engineers Hidehiro Akahane and Nobuhiro Koike.
A related Seiko Epson patent entitled Timing device, with a priority date of 10 September 1998, names Akihiko Maruyama, Nobuhiro Koike, Tsuneaki Furukawa and Eiichi Hiraya as inventors.
The patent describes a multifunction timekeeping device incorporating separate normal-time and elapsed-time sections, a power-generating system and a mechanical zero-return mechanism, among other features related to the architecture used in the 9T series.

articles.title: Adventure Weekly
articles.text:
Adventure Weekly

Adventure Weekly is a British children's television series following five young reporters as they run their newspaper, 'Adventure Weekly'. The series was created by Shaun Sutton and aired on BBC1 between 1968 and 1969.


== Story ==
At the Cliffsea Recorder, an ailing local paper, four boys create a junior newspaper, Adventure Weekly. The boys are Peter Perkins, the editor in chief and imaginative son of the proprietor of the Recorder, Andy Rogers, a combative boy with a mechanical know-how and  official photographer, making use of his high-quality camera, 'Tubby' Taylor, the papers well-padded sports editor who admired sports from a comfortable seat, and 'Swot' English the mostly serious note of the group who supplied news from the surrounding schools that were so scandalous, only Adventure Weekly would print. The four are soon joined by Frederica 'Fred' Somers, she makes a bad start after doing most things better then the boys but becomes one of the team after leading them to one of their biggest front-page stories. Together the five become involved in various adventures from capturing post office robbers to discovering an unexploded WWII bomb. The five befriend Mr Filling, a typesetter at the Recorder which faced closure until London-based newspaper magnet Lord Huntingford bought the paper out. The newspaper let's the five use their press to print Adventure Weekly while Mr Filling reluctantly gets involved in the kids schemes and plans which gets them in trouble with local bobby PC Cullis.

articles.title: Tulsa Bus Station
articles.text:
Tulsa Bus Station

The Tulsa Bus Station is an intercity bus station situated in downtown Tulsa, Oklahoma. The station, managed by Greyhound Lines, also serves Jefferson Lines. The current bus station was originally utilized by Trailways and has served as the only intercity bus station since 1987.
Tulsa has had an intercity bus terminal since at least 1926, when a union bus depot opened at the northeast corner of East 4th Street and South Cincinnati Avenue. Later stations were generally located in the vicinity, with new stations opening in 1934 and 1961. The present location has had intercity bus service since 1981.


== Attributes ==
The Greyhound station building sits at the northeast corner of East 4th Street and South Detroit Avenue in downtown Tulsa. The main entrance is located on South Detroit Avenue. The bus station is owned by Greyhound Lines, but also serves Jefferson Lines.


== History ==


=== Early stations ===
The first union bus station in Tulsa opened August 4, 1926 at the northeast corner of East 4th Street and South Cincinnati Avenue. The terminal replaced a handful of smaller stations scattered around Tulsa. Upon opening, the depot served six bus operators over 15 routes with 74 daily arrivals and departures using 128 buses. The terminal also served the interurban Oklahoma Union Railway.
At the start of the 1930s, Greyhound Lines was looking to establish a new terminal in Tulsa. Simultaneously, the Southern Kansas Stage Lines moved out of the union station to a new location at 211 South Cincinnati Avenue on August 13, 1932. 
In 1933, Waite Phillips, a local businessman, purchased the union depot property with the intent of remodeling the station. The Pickwick-Greyhound Lines, Southern Kansas Stage Lines, and Missouri Kansas and Oklahoma Lines signed ten-year leases for the proposed station. The new terra cotta and stucco station would feature six bus bays, a distinctive 47-foot sign, segregated waiting rooms, ticket offices, a newsstand, coffee shop, women's lounge, and passenger bathing facilities. The three story structure was designed by Smith & Senter and opened on February 3, 1934. Over 3,000 people participated in opening celebrations, which included a parade of buses, an orchestra performance, and ice cream sticks and cigars. Upon opening, there were 80 arrivals and departures daily.
According to the Tulsa World, the terminal was considered the finest in the southwest. By 1936, it served 118 daily schedules and 2,000 passengers.

articles.title: Octolasion tyrtaeum
articles.text:
Octolasion tyrtaeum

Octolasion tyrtaeum, also known as the woodland white worm, is a species of earthworm in the family Lumbricidae.


== Taxonomy ==
O. tyrtaeum is a species of earthworm in the genus Octolasion and the family Lumbricidae. It is believed that the species may be the same as O. lacteum.


== Habitat ==
Occurring in a large variety of soil and habitat types, O. tyrtaeum is widespread across the globe, and is more common in wet soil.


== Environmental impact ==
A large population of O. tyrtaeum in the Northwest Himalayan forest has been recorded influencing soil nutrient dynamics, reducing microbial and microarthropod communities, and significantly reducing litter thickness, organic layers, C/N ratio and soil PH. In 2023, it and O. cyaneum were recorded in Turtuk, a village in Ladakh which previously had no earthworm records.


== Description ==
The species is generally whitish-grey in colour. Can either be small (4-8 cm long) or large (10-14 cm). These differences in size are not environmental; they belong to different mtDNA lineages. The first dorsal pore 9/10-12/13, and the total number of segments generally ranges from 76-136.  Clitellum is saddle shaped on segments 30-35, the prostomium is epilobic, and the tubercula pubertatis on segments 31-34. Nedriphores are aligned and obvious. Bladders are elongated and ocarina-shaped, and the spermatheca are always empty.


== Life cycle ==
This species is parthenogenetic. Under lab conditions, the incubation period ranged from 30-45 days, with fertile cocoons changing colour from a pale yellow, to a light pink/red during hatching, then black. Infertile cocoons turned black after a few days. Most cocoons held 2-3 hatchlings. 


== References ==

articles.title: Henry Delp Styer
articles.text:
Henry Delp Styer

Henry Delp Styer (21 September 1862 – 11 May 1944) was a career officer in the United States Army. A native of Sellersville, Pennsylvania and an 1884 graduate of the United States Military Academy, he served from 1884 until retiring in 1922 and attained the rank of brigadier general. Styer was a veteran of the American Indian Wars, Spanish–American War, Philippine–American War, Mexican Border War, World War I, and North Russia intervention, and his commands included the 27th Infantry Regiment and 181st Infantry Brigade. His awards and decorations included the Japanese Order of the Rising Sun (3rd class) and Czechoslovak War Cross.


== Early life ==
Henry D. Styer was born in Sellersville, Pennsylvania on 21 September 1862, the son of William Barrett Styer and Katharine (Delp) Styer. He was raised and educated in Sellersville, attended Franklin & Marshall College from 1877 to 1879, and worked as a schoolteacher. In 1880, he received an appointment to the United States Military Academy at West Point from U.S. Representative Reuben K. Bachman. Styer graduated in 1884 ranked 29th of 37. At graduation, he received his commission as a second lieutenant of Infantry.
Among Styer's classmates who attained general officer rank were: Irving Hale; Hiram M. Chittenden; Harry Taylor; William L. Sibert; Stephen Miller Foote; Eugene Frederick Ladd; Samuel D. Sturgis Jr.; Everard Enos Hatch; DeRosey Caroll Cabell; Edwin Burr Babbitt; Wilds P. Richardson; Grote Hutcheson; George Oscar Cress; Robert Houston Noble; and David C. Shanks. Among his notable classmates who did not become generals were: David du Bose Gaillard; Isaac Newton Lewis; and Powhatan Henry Clarke.


== Start of career ==
In June 1884, Styer began his career with American Indian Wars assignment to the 21st Infantry Regiment at Fort Fred Steele, Wyoming. He served in Wyoming until July 1886, when he was posted to Fort Duchesne, Utah. Styer was also a member of the Department of the Platte's rifle team from September 1884 to September 1886. In February 1888, he escorted a detachment of recruits to Fort Sidney, Nebraska, after which he commanded the detachment and the post. In July 1888, he was assigned to duty at Fort Douglas, Utah. In May 1891, Styer was promoted to first lieutenant in the 22nd Infantry and continued to serve at Fort Douglas. In July 1891, Styer transferred to the 13th Infantry and was assigned to Fort Reno, Indian Territory, where he served until September 1892.

articles.title: Borzicactus plagiostoma
articles.text:
Borzicactus plagiostoma

Borzicactus plagiostoma is a species of succulent flowering plant in the genus Borzicactus, within the family Cactaceae. It is endemic to Peru.


== Description ==

Borzicactus plagiostoma is a species of cactus with a shrubby growth form, with vertical to ascendent stems that are branched at the base. They can reach 1.5 m in height and 5-7 cm in diameter.
There are 10-15 short, wavy ribs, which are divided into tubercles by grooves. Upon the tubercles are the areoles, which are situated very closely together and have straight spines which are black in color. Among these are 1-5 central spines measuring 1-3 cm in length and 12-16 marginal spines measuring 4-7 mm in length. 

The flowers are tubular with crooked edges, and are an intense purple or magenta color. They are somewhat bilaterally symmetrical and measure up to 8 cm in length.


== Distribution and habitat ==
This species is native to northwestern Peru, where it grows primarily in desert or dry scrubland biomes at altitudes between 2000 and 2200 meters above sea level.


== Taxonomy ==
Borzicactus plagiostoma was first described as Cereus plagiostoma, a name published in 1913 by the German botanist Friedrich Karl Johann Vaupel in the scientific journal Botanische Jahrbücher für Systematik, Pflanzengeschichte und Pflanzengeographie 111: 20.
Later, the American botanists Nathaniel Lord Britton and Joseph Nelson Rose transferred this species to the genus Borzicactus, renaming it Borzicactus plagiostoma. They registered these changes in their book The Cactaceae; descriptions and illustrations of plants of the cactus family 2: 163, published in 1920.

Etymology
Borzicactus: The genus name is derived from "Borzi" (honoring the Italian botanist Antonino Borzì (1852-1921), director del jardín botánico de Palermo) and the Greek term kaktos (meaning "thistle" or "spiny plant"), in reference to the spiny character of the species in this genus.
plagiostoma: The specific epithet is derived from the Greek words plagios (meaning "crooked") and stoma (meaning "mouth"), in reference to the floral morphology of this species.


== Cultivation ==
This species is cultivated mainly as an ornamental. It may be propagated vegetatively via cuttings, or via seed.


== References ==

articles.title: Evelyn Niemann Akeley
articles.text:
Evelyn Niemann Akeley

Evelyn Clara Niemann Akeley (August 24, 1907 – March 23, 1998) was an American mathematician and cryptanalyst. She taught at Skidmore College, and worked for American intelligence agencies during and after World War II. In 2023 she was inducted into the National Security Agency's Cryptologic Hall of Honor.


== Early life and education ==
Niemann was born in New York City and raised in Saratoga Springs, New York, the daughter of Albert Henry Niemann and Julia Dahin Niemann. Her father was a salesman. She was captain of the soccer team at Smith College, and graduated from Smith in 1928. She earned a master's degree in mathematics from Columbia University in 1931.


== Career ==
Akeley taught math and physics and directed the vocational bureau at Skidmore College until 1942, when she was recuited to train codebreakers in the Washington, D.C. area, during World War II. She was director of training at the Signal Intelligence Service and a researcher in cryptanalysis; her students, including Ann Z. Caracristi, were credited with breaking many Japanese Army codes important to the war effort. She retired from the National Security Agency in 1958. 
In retirement, she was a violist with the Florida West Coast Symphony, and a volunteer with the American Red Cross. She was also a competitive amateur golfer. 


== Personal life ==
Niemann married fellow academic Edward Stowe Akeley, son of Lewis Akeley, in 1935. They divorced before 1942, when he remarried, to Austrian physics lecturer Anna Akeley. Evelyn Niemann Akeley died in 1998, at age 90, in Sarasota, Florida. She was inducted into the National Security Agency's Cryptologic Hall of Honor in 2023.


== References ==

articles.title: Battle of Yegorlyk
articles.text:
Battle of Yegorlyk

The Battle of Yegorlyk was a military engagement that lasted from February 25 to March 1, 1920. The battle was fought between the Red Army's 1st Cavalry Army (Koniarmia) and the AFSRs Pavlov Cavalry Group. It was the largest cavalry battle of the Russian Civil War and one of the largest cavalry battles of the 20th century, involving even more cavalrymen than the Battle of Komarów.

As a result of this battle the red army advanced 100km southward and forced the white movement into a total retreat along with the red army started its third phase of the North Caucasus Operation (1920).


== Prelude ==

By February 1920, the offensive capabilities of the Red Army had run out, and, along with the freezing temperatures of nearly -20°C, a proper front was established on the Manych River. The exhausted nature of both the AFSR and the RKKA was shown in the fact that both Red and White commands placed their faith in their cavalry forces, which led to the deployment of major cavalry formations with 10.5 thousand Red sabers and 13 thousand White sabers.
The White movement was willing to do everything in order to keep its power in the area and began a wave of mobilization. However, because of Bolshevik victories in Donbas and Rostov, mutinies were common, both to the Green Army and the Reds. Nevertheless, the Whites planned to launch an offensive in the Rostov-on-Don direction, but on the 14th, they were met with a Bolshevik attack (by the 10th Army) on the Manych. The 10th Army defeated the Kuban Army and was able to create a small bridgehead with its victory in the Battle of Torgoyava, which allowed the konarmia to cross the Manych. After receiving news of the Bolshevik breakthrough, Pavlov's Cavalry Group, on the 19th, rushed in order to kick them out but was met with heavy resistance and was forced back to Sredny Yegorlyk. During this battle, the 20th, 34th and 50th Rifle Divisions of the 10th Army were incorporated into a shock group of the konarmia.
On the 22nd of February, units of the shock group and parts of the konarmia advanced in the southwestern direction and captured Belaya Glina, where they were able to gain information that Denikin's forces were retreating in an unorganized manner towards Pavlov's forces. Along with this information, the Reds gained the knowledge that the opposing forces had weakened the fronts with the 8th and 9th Armies, and the Bolsheviks became aware that they were planning on attacking the Bolsheviks at Sredny Ye

articles.title: Austrocylindropuntia shaferi
articles.text:
Austrocylindropuntia shaferi

Austrocylindropuntia shaferi is a species of succulent flowering plant in the genus Austrocylindropuntia, within the family Cactaceae. It is native from western Bolivia to northwestern Argentina. 


== Description ==

Austrocylindropuntia shaferi is a small species of cactus with an upright gworth, reaching 30 cm or more in height. The stems are slightly divided into sections or segments, which vary from cylindrical to slightly bulging in shape. They are green in color, and each measures approximately 15 cm in length and 3 cm in diameter. 
The stems exhibit a series of tubercles, upon which are situated small, tightly-spaced areoles with 15 narrow, needle-shaped spines each. These spines are weak, and measure up to 5 cm in length. Sometimes, trichomes or bristles also form on the areoles. Rudimentary leaves measuring up to 0.6 cm in length are present. 

The flowers are bright red in color and measure 3 cm in length. The pericarpel, which is pear-shaped, is covered in trichomes and does not have spines. The fruits are spherical in shape and bright red in color; they are covered in glochids and trichomes. They can grow to 1.5 cm in length.


== Distribution and habitat ==
This species is found from western Bolivia to northwestern Argentina. It grows primarily in desert and dry shrubland biomes, at altitudes between 2500 and 3500 meters above sea level. It has been introduced to the Canary Islands and Morocco.


== Taxonomy ==
Austrocylindropuntia shaferi was first described as Opuntia shaferi, a name published in 1919 by the American botanists Nathaniel Lord Britton and Joseph Nelson Rose in their book The Cactaceae; descriptions and illustrations of plants of the cactus family 1: 72.
Later, the German botanist Curt Backeberg transferred the species to the genus Austrocylindropuntia, renaming it Austrocylindropuntia shaferi. He registered these changes in the scientific journal Cactus and Succulent Journal 23: 14, published in 1951.


=== Etymology ===
Austrocylindropuntia: the genus name is derived from the Latin terms auster, -tralis; (meaning "southern"), the Greek term κύλινδρος (kýlindros); (meaning "cylinder"), and the genus Opuntia, (or, as a combination of the latter two terms, the genus Cylindropuntia); this references the cylindrical shape of the stems that appear similar to the genera Opuntia and Cylindropuntia.
shaferi: the specific epithet honors the American botanist John Adolph Shafer (1863–1918).

articles.title: Iggy San Pablo
articles.text:
Iggy San Pablo

Iggy San Pablo is a Filipino musician best known as the frontman and lead guitarist of the indie rock band Rusty Machines. In 2022, he started a solo music project called simple socks after moving to Toronto, Canada.


== Career ==


=== Rusty Machines ===
San Pablo is the frontman and lead guitarist of Rusty Machines, an indie rock band formed in 2012. The original lineup included San Pablo, guitarist Joshua Andres, bassist Leandro Fabregas, and drummer Miko Miso.
The band released its debut extended play (EP) City Lights in 2014. It later released songs including "Forget You", "Can't Hardly Wait", and "Trying Too Hard". In 2019, the band released its debut studio album Making Friends, which contains 11 tracks. Its single "Not so Fond" was released in 2023.
In 2019, San Pablo was featured in Scout magazine's music recommendations series, where he discussed songs he listened to during rainy days.
San Pablo moved to Toronto with his wife in 2022. He continued making music there while adjusting to life in a new country.


=== simple socks ===
While living in Toronto, San Pablo started simple socks, a solo project separate from Rusty Machines. Before the pandemic, he had also worked on thenils, a lo-fi music project influenced by the music of Diego Mapa and the American band the Drums.
On April 24, 2026, San Pablo released the debut single "Training Wheels", through Bandcamp, followed by its release on streaming platforms on April 27. The song is the first track from his planned debut EP Joanna Drive. "Training Wheels" is influenced by indie rock and reflects San Pablo's experience of balancing work and music while living abroad. He cited Death Cab for Cutie's The Photo Album, Into It. Over It.'s Proper, and susquatch's In This World as influences on the song.
San Pablo has said that his music deals with the demands of living as an immigrant while pursuing a music career. He also described the difficulty of communicating with audiences in Toronto because he thinks in Tagalog but often has to express himself in English. The name "simple socks" came from a phrase San Pablo and his wife used for comfortable clothes worn at home during Toronto's colder months. His songwriting has also shifted from themes of romance and young relationships to ideas about adulthood, distance, and life away from the Philippines.

articles.title: Austrocactus spiniflorus
articles.text:
Austrocactus spiniflorus

Austrocactus spiniflorus, commonly known in Spanish as espinifloro, is a succulent flowering plant in the genus Austrocactus, within the family Cactaceae. It is endemic to central Chile, from the east of the Santiago Metropolitan Region to the northeast of the O'Higgins Region.


== Description ==
Austrocactus spiniflorus is a species of cactus with a branching and spreading growth form. Its thin cylindrical stems can grow to 20 cm in length and 2 cm in diameter. The epidermis is green to dark red in color. This species has a tuberous root (which can grow to 20 cm in length) with a well-developed neck; this root can form rhizomes. 

The stem has 6-8 ribs, which do not have tubercles. The areoles are situated on the ribs; these are rounded and measure up to 2.5 mm in diameter. They have a white, felt-like covering and tiny deciduous leaves. This species has 1-3 central spines per areole; these point outwards. They are smooth, needle-shaped, and are bright red at the base when young. Furthermore, there are up to 8 spreading radial spines, which are also smooth and needle-shaped. The flowers are cup-shaped and grow to approximately 7 cm in length and 7.5 cm in width. The cavity of the ovary is oval in shape and measures approximately 2.5 cm in length and 1.2 cm in width. The tepals are spatulate. The internal tepals are off-white to yellowish in color; the external tepals are red. The style is white in color, and the stigma has approximately 10 light yellow lobes. The pericarpel is green, and is covered in fine reddish scales, some white woolly trichomes, and fine spines. 
The fruit becomes club-shaped as it matures, and it grows to approximately 5 cm in length and 2.5 cm in width. It is yellow in color, and the surface is covered in short spines. Unlike most other Austrocactus species, the fruit of Austrocactus spiniflorus is very mucilaginous. 
The seeds are black, matte, and somewhat comma-shaped. They measure approximately 3 mm in length and 2 mm in width. The hilum is small.


== Distribution and habitat ==
This species is native to central Chile, in the eastern Santiago Metropolitan Region and the northeastern O'Higgins Region.
It is found mainly in the subtropical biome at altitudes between 1200 and 1700 meters above sea level. It grows in Andean shrublands in open and sheltered areas with few rocks and moist soils into which water from snowmelt can remain for long periods of time. articles.title: Moonzy: The Other Side of the Moon
articles.text:
Moonzy: The Other Side of the Moon

Moonzy: The Other Side of the Moon (Russian: Лунтик. Обратная сторона Луны, romanized: Luntik. Obratnaya storona Luny, lit. 'Luntik. The Far Side of the Moon') is a 2026 Russian animated adventure film directed and written by Darina Shmidt. A direct sequel to Moonzy: Homecoming, the film follows Moonzy and her friends who build a rocket to the moon, to find Moonzy's lost father, going in adventures along the way.
The film was released in Russia on 27 August 2026.


== Plot ==

Following their previous adventure to the moon, that night, Moonzy sees an drawing of his mother. Later, he has an nightmare of, during the meteorite collision at his moon home, multiple moon bees, including Moonzy's father, were lost trying to rescue other moon bee children, while her mother desperately called for her child. Moonzy convinces his friend, Flip, about his father, and decide that they need to find and rescue him.
When Moonzy is unable to return to the moon when his mark on his tummy fails to glow, he and his grandparents, Annie and Stringer, visit the moth at his laboratory, who agrees to let Moonzy go to the moon. With the moth's help, the group, along with Flip and his other friends, the spider Mr. Webber, the earthworm named Mr. Diggins, twin caterpillars Woopie and Poopsie, Weebee the bee, and the ladybug Dottie build a rocket to go the moon. Only Moonzy, Flip, Woopsie and Poopsie launch the rocket, and, after braving a meteor shower, eventually reach the moon, and find a utopia filled with moon bees. There, Moonzy reconciles with his depressed mother, who explains that if he worries less, his mark on his tummy can glow again.
Returning to the surface, the group accidentally damage their rocket ship. When they go out to investigate, the group fall into a cave, the far side of the moon. While there, they encounter rolling ball-like creatures named the molesters. After evading them, Moonzy reconciles with his father, but initially claims not to be his father, but rather his uncle named Monty, also known as Grol, and says that his real father fell into the gorge. The group then decides to abandon Grol, but get attacked by more molesters. Grol arrives and rescues them, who reveals that the creatures can be driven away by a light source.
